paragraphs: This paper trains neural networks to evaluate Go positions using temporal difference learning. The motivation is that Go's many possible moves make tree search difficult, while interactions across space and time complicate position evaluation. Learning an evaluation function offers an alternative to relying on the extensive manually supplied knowledge required by conventional Go programs.

The approach combines architectures that reflect the board's spatial organization with training that exposes networks to competent but unlabeled play. Spatial organization applies to both inputs and reinforcement signals. The authors report that these choices produce much better performance than undifferentiated networks trained only through self-play, making architecture and training experience central to the result.

A network with fewer than 500 weights learned an evaluation function within 3,000 games on a 9-by-9 board. Coupled to a primitive one-ply search, it defeated a commercial Go program at a low playing level. This demonstrates useful learned position evaluation in the stated setting, with the shallow search relying on the network's assessment of positions.
summary.tldr: Spatially organized networks trained with temporal differences and competent play learn useful Go evaluation with fewer than 500 weights.

title: Temporal Difference Learning of Position Evaluation in the Game of Go

paragraphs: Applying discrete reinforcement-learning methods to continuous states often starts by dividing the state space into boxes. This creates a tradeoff: a coarse grid can yield poor control policies, while a fine grid becomes expensive as the number of dimensions increases. The paper investigates interpolation on a coarse grid as another way to represent the relevant functions.

Two methods are studied: multilinear interpolation and interpolation based on a regular triangulation of multidimensional space. Both use values associated with a grid to estimate values between its points. This lets the controller use a coarse representation while responding to states at locations that do not coincide with stored grid points.

The authors adapt the methods to model-based offline value iteration, Q-learning, and online value iteration with a model learned from data. They report empirical results and substantial improvements in the resulting systems' online behavior. The significance is a common approximation strategy usable across several learning settings for continuous nonlinear control, without requiring every distinction in state to have its own fine-grid entry.
summary.tldr: Interpolation on coarse multidimensional grids improves continuous-state control across several reinforcement-learning settings.

title: Multidimensional Triangulation and Interpolation for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper presents a method that decides which combinations of traffic can be accepted on a packet data link, so that quality of service (QoS) constraints can be met. The method uses samples of QoS results at dif(cid:173) ferent load conditions to build a neural network decision function. Pre(cid:173) vious similar approaches to the problem have a significant bias. This bias is likely to occur in any real system and results in accepting loads that miss QoS targets by orders of magnitude. Preprocessing the data to either remove the bias or provide a confidence level, the method was applied to sources based on difficult-to-analyze ethernet data traces. With this data, the method produces an accurate access control function that dramatically outperforms analytic alternatives. Interestingly, the results depend on throwing away more than 99% of the data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to decide which combinations of traffic a packet data link can accept while still meeting quality-of-service requirements. The method learns a neural network decision function from observed service outcomes at different traffic loads. Its purpose is to turn those observations into a rule for admitting or rejecting proposed loads.

The central difficulty is a significant bias in earlier approaches of this kind. According to the abstract, that bias is likely in real systems and can lead to accepting traffic whose service outcomes miss targets by orders of magnitude. The authors preprocess the observations either to remove the bias or to provide a confidence level for the decision.

Applied to sources constructed from difficult-to-analyze Ethernet traces, the method produces an accurate access-control function and substantially outperforms analytic alternatives. A striking finding is that success depends on discarding more than 99% of the data. This makes data preparation central to the contribution: the usefulness of the learned decision rule depends on addressing bias in the observations, rather than simply retaining every available sample.
summary.tldr: Bias-aware preprocessing enables a neural access-control rule to meet service targets on Ethernet-derived traffic.

title: Adaptive Access Control Applied to Ethernet Data

abstract: A Lyapunov function for excitatory-inhibitory networks is constructed. The construction assumes symmetric interactions within excitatory and inhibitory populations of neurons, and antisymmetric interactions between populations. The Lyapunov function yields sufficient conditions for the global asymptotic stability of fixed points. If these conditions are violated, limit cycles may be stable. The relations of the Lyapunov function to optimization theory and classical mechanics are revealed by minimax and dissipative Hamiltonian forms of the network dynamics.
originalAbstract: A Lyapunov function for excitatory-inhibitory networks is constructed. The construction assumes symmetric interactions within excitatory and inhibitory populations of neurons, and antisymmetric interactions between populations. The Lyapunov function yields sufficient conditions for the global asymptotic stability of fixed points. If these conditions are violated, limit cycles may be stable. The relations of the Lyapunov function to optimization theory and classical mechanics are revealed by minimax and dissipative Hamiltonian forms of the network dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes the dynamics of networks containing excitatory and inhibitory neuron populations. It constructs a Lyapunov function, a mathematical tool for establishing whether a dynamical system approaches a stable state. The construction assumes symmetric interactions within each population and antisymmetric interactions between the excitatory and inhibitory populations.

From this function, the authors derive sufficient conditions for global asymptotic stability of fixed points. These conditions provide a guarantee that the relevant dynamics settle toward fixed activity states. If the conditions are violated, stable limit cycles may occur, allowing activity to continue in a repeating pattern. Failure of the conditions permits this possibility without making oscillation inevitable.

The paper also expresses the dynamics in minimax and dissipative Hamiltonian forms, revealing connections to optimization and classical mechanics. These formulations give complementary mathematical views of the same network behavior. Together, they help explain how the assumed interaction structure can support either convergence to fixed points or sustained cyclic activity.
summary.tldr: A Lyapunov analysis gives stability conditions for structured excitatory-inhibitory networks and connects their dynamics to optimization and mechanics.

title: Minimax and Hamiltonian Dynamics of Excitatory-Inhibitory Networks

abstract: In adaptive boosting, several weak learners trained sequentially are combined to boost the overall algorithm performance. Recently adaptive boosting methods for classification problems have been derived as gradient descent algorithms. This formulation justifies key elements and parameters in the methods, all chosen to optimize a single common objective function. We propose an analogous formulation for adaptive boosting of regression problems, utilizing a novel objective function that leads to a simple boosting algorithm. We prove that this method reduces training error, and compare its performance to other regression methods.
originalAbstract: In adaptive boosting, several weak learners trained sequentially are combined to boost the overall algorithm performance. Recently adaptive boosting methods for classification problems have been derived as gradient descent algorithms. This formulation justifies key elements and parameters in the methods, all chosen to optimize a single common objective function. We propose an analogous formulation for adaptive boosting of regression problems, utilizing a novel objective function that leads to a simple boosting algorithm. We prove that this method reduces training error, and compare its performance to other regression methods.

paragraphs: Boosting combines several weak learners trained in sequence into a stronger predictor. This paper develops a gradient-based formulation of that process for regression, where the prediction is a numerical value. Its starting point is an interpretation already applied to classification: successive boosting steps can be understood as attempts to improve one shared objective.

The authors introduce a new objective function that produces a simple regression boosting algorithm. Having a common objective gives the procedure a coherent optimization basis: the choices made during training serve the same mathematical goal. The contribution therefore connects the construction of an ensemble to gradient descent, rather than treating the sequence of learners as an isolated recipe.

The paper proves that its method reduces training error and compares its performance with other regression methods. The proof supports improvement on the training examples; it does not itself establish an improvement on unseen examples. The abstract reports the comparison without claiming a particular ranking, so the clearest stated result is the training-error reduction guaranteed by the proposed formulation.
summary.tldr: The paper derives a simple regression boosting algorithm from a new objective function and proves that it reduces training error.

title: A Gradient-Based Boosting Algorithm for Regression Problems

abstract: We study the synthesis of neural coding, selective attention and percep- tual decision making. A hierarchical neural architecture is proposed, which implements Bayesian integration of noisy sensory input and top- down attentional priors, leading to sound perceptual discrimination. The model offers an explicit explanation for the experimentally observed modulation that prior information in one stimulus feature (location) can have on an independent feature (orientation). The network's intermediate levels of representation instantiate known physiological properties of vi- sual cortical neurons. The model also illustrates a possible reconciliation of cortical and neuromodulatory representations of uncertainty.

A hierarchical neural architecture is proposed, which implements Bayesian integration of noisy sensory input and top- down attentional priors, leading to sound perceptual discrimination. The model offers an explicit explanation for the experimentally observed modulation that prior information in one stimulus feature (location) can have on an independent feature (orientation). The network's intermediate levels of representation instantiate known physiological properties of vi- sual cortical neurons. The model also illustrates a possible reconciliation of cortical and neuromodulatory representations of uncertainty.

paragraphs: The paper brings together three questions: how neurons represent sensory information, how attention influences that information, and how perceptual decisions emerge. It proposes a hierarchical neural architecture that combines noisy sensory input with top-down attentional prior information through Bayesian integration. The resulting computation supports perceptual discrimination.

A central target is an observed interaction between stimulus features. Prior information about location can modulate processing of orientation even though the two features are independent. The model offers an explicit explanation for this effect within its combined treatment of sensory evidence and attention. This links a particular perceptual phenomenon to the architecture's inference process.

The intermediate representations also exhibit known physiological properties of visual cortical neurons. In addition, the model illustrates a possible reconciliation between cortical and neuromodulatory representations of uncertainty. These claims connect the computational account to both behavior and neural representation, while keeping the uncertainty proposal at the level of a possible explanation rather than an established biological mechanism.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian neural hierarchy combines sensory noise and attentional priors to explain perceptual decisions and interactions between location and orientation.

title: Inference, Attention, and Decision in a Bayesian Neural Architecture

abstract: This paper investigates the effect of Kernel Principal Component Analysis (KPCA) within the classification framework, essentially the regularization properties of this dimensionality reduction method. KPCA has been previously used as a pre-processing step before applying an SVM but we point out that this method is somewhat redundant from a regularization point of view and we propose a new algorithm called Kernel Projection Machine to avoid this redundancy, based on an analogy with the statistical framework of regression for a Gaussian white noise model. Preliminary experimental results show that this algorithm reaches the same performances as an SVM.
originalAbstract: This paper investigates the effect of Kernel Principal Component Analysis (KPCA) within the classification framework, essentially the regularization properties of this dimensionality reduction method. KPCA has been previously used as a pre-processing step before applying an SVM but we point out that this method is somewhat redundant from a regularization point of view and we propose a new algorithm called Kernel Projection Machine to avoid this redundancy, based on an analogy with the statistical framework of regression for a Gaussian white noise model. Preliminary experimental results show that this algorithm reaches the same performances as an SVM.

paragraphs: This paper examines kernel principal component analysis as part of a classification system, concentrating on its regularization properties. Regularization concerns how a learning method controls the complexity of its fitted solution. The authors ask what role this dimensionality-reduction step plays when it is followed by a support vector machine.

They argue that this combination is somewhat redundant from a regularization perspective. To address that overlap, they propose the Kernel Projection Machine. Its design draws on an analogy with regression under a Gaussian white noise model. The motivation is to use the regularizing role of projection more directly within a classification algorithm.

Preliminary experiments report performance matching that of a support vector machine. This suggests that the proposed construction can be competitive in the settings examined, while the preliminary character of the evidence remains important. The paper's main contribution is the connection it draws between kernel projection and regularization, together with an algorithm designed around that connection.
summary.tldr: The Kernel Projection Machine addresses overlapping regularization in KPCA-plus-SVM classification and preliminarily matches SVM performance.

title: Kernel Projection Machine: a New Tool for Pattern Recognition

abstract: Embedding algorithms search for low dimensional structure in complex data, but most algorithms only handle objects of a single type for which pairwise distances are specified. This paper describes a method for em- bedding objects of different types, such as images and text, into a single common Euclidean space based on their co-occurrence statistics. The joint distributions are modeled as exponentials of Euclidean distances in the low-dimensional embedding space, which links the problem to con- vex optimization over positive semidefinite matrices. The local struc- ture of our embedding corresponds to the statistical correlations via ran- dom walks in the Euclidean space. We quantify the performance of our method on two text datasets, and show that it consistently and signifi- cantly outperforms standard methods of statistical correspondence mod- eling, such as multidimensional scaling and correspondence analysis.

This paper describes a method for em- bedding objects of different types, such as images and text, into a single common Euclidean space based on their co-occurrence statistics. The joint distributions are modeled as exponentials of Euclidean distances in the low-dimensional embedding space, which links the problem to con- vex optimization over positive semidefinite matrices. The local struc- ture of our embedding corresponds to the statistical correlations via ran- dom walks in the Euclidean space. We quantify the performance of our method on two text datasets, and show that it consistently and signifi- cantly outperforms standard methods of statistical correspondence mod- eling, such as multidimensional scaling and correspondence analysis.

paragraphs: Many embedding methods start with distances between objects of one type. This paper instead learns a shared low-dimensional Euclidean space for different kinds of objects from how often they occur together. Images and text are given as an example of the kinds of heterogeneous objects that the formulation can place within one representation.

The method models joint probabilities through exponentials involving distances in the embedding space. This connects statistical association to geometry and links learning the embedding to convex optimization over positive semidefinite matrices. The paper also relates local geometric structure to statistical correlations through random walks in that space, explaining how nearby relationships reflect the observed co-occurrence information.

Evaluation uses two text datasets. On those datasets, the method consistently and significantly outperforms statistical correspondence approaches including multidimensional scaling and correspondence analysis. The results support the proposed probabilistic geometry for the tested text problems. The wider formulation accommodates different object types, while the stated comparative evidence comes specifically from text data rather than a reported image-and-text experiment.
summary.tldr: The paper learns a shared Euclidean embedding from co-occurrence probabilities and reports strong comparative results on two text datasets.

title: Euclidean Embedding of Co-Occurrence Data

abstract: Online mechanism design (OMD) addresses the problem of sequential decision making in a stochastic environment with multiple self-interested agents. The goal in OMD is to make value-maximizing decisions despite this self-interest. In previous work we presented a Markov decision process (MDP)-based approach to OMD in large-scale problem domains. In practice the underlying MDP needed to solve OMD is too large and hence the mechanism must consider approximations. This raises the possibility that agents may be able to exploit the approximation for selfish gain. We adopt sparse-sampling-based MDP algorithms to implement ϵefficient policies, and retain truth-revelation as an approximate Bayesian- Nash equilibrium. Our approach is empirically illustrated in the context of the dynamic allocation of WiFi connectivity to users in a coffeehouse.
originalAbstract: Online mechanism design (OMD) addresses the problem of sequential decision making in a stochastic environment with multiple self-interested agents. The goal in OMD is to make value-maximizing decisions despite this self-interest. In previous work we presented a Markov decision process (MDP)-based approach to OMD in large-scale problem domains. In practice the underlying MDP needed to solve OMD is too large and hence the mechanism must consider approximations. This raises the possibility that agents may be able to exploit the approximation for selfish gain. We adopt sparse-sampling-based MDP algorithms to implement ϵefficient policies, and retain truth-revelation as an approximate Bayesian- Nash equilibrium. Our approach is empirically illustrated in the context of the dynamic allocation of WiFi connectivity to users in a coffeehouse.

paragraphs: Online mechanism design studies sequential decisions involving self-interested participants in an uncertain environment. The objective is to maximize value even when participants have reasons to act strategically. This paper examines what happens when the decision problem is too large to solve exactly and the mechanism must use an approximation.

The difficulty is that approximation affects more than computational cost. It may create opportunities for a participant to benefit by misrepresenting information. Building on an approach based on Markov decision processes, the authors use sparse-sampling algorithms to construct policies that are approximately efficient while retaining truthful reporting as an approximate Bayesian-Nash equilibrium.

The equilibrium qualification matters: the stated result preserves an approximate incentive property, rather than making an unrestricted claim that manipulation can never help. The authors illustrate the method through dynamic allocation of WiFi connectivity among coffeehouse users. The contribution connects practical approximation of sequential planning with the strategic requirements that make a mechanism usable among self-interested agents.
summary.tldr: Sparse-sampling planning enables approximately efficient online mechanisms while preserving truthful reporting as an approximate Bayesian-Nash equilibrium.

title: Approximately Efficient Online Mechanism Design

abstract: Nonnegative matrix approximation (NNMA) is a recent technique for dimensionality reduction and data analysis that yields a parts based, sparse nonnegative representation for nonnegative input data. NNMA has found a wide variety of applications, including text analysis, document clustering, face/image recognition, language modeling, speech processing and many others. Despite these numerous applications, the algorithmic development for computing the NNMA factors has been relatively deficient. This paper makes algorithmic progress by modeling and solving (using multiplicative updates) new generalized NNMA problems that minimize Bregman divergences between the input matrix and its lowrank approximation. The multiplicative update formulae in the pioneering work by Lee and Seung [11] arise as a special case of our algorithms. In addition, the paper shows how to use penalty functions for incorporating constraints other than nonnegativity into the problem. Further, some interesting extensions to the use of "link" functions for modeling nonlinear relationships are also discussed.

paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix approximation represents nonnegative data through a smaller set of nonnegative factors. Such representations can be sparse and describe data in terms of component parts, making them useful for dimensionality reduction and analysis. This paper focuses on improving the algorithms used to compute those factors.

The authors formulate generalized approximation problems using Bregman divergences to measure the mismatch between an input matrix and its low-rank approximation. They derive multiplicative update algorithms for solving these problems. Previously established multiplicative updates arise as a special case, so the framework broadens the available objectives while retaining a connection to existing methods.

The paper also explains how penalty functions can incorporate constraints beyond nonnegativity. It discusses extensions using link functions to model nonlinear relationships. Together, these developments make the approximation framework more adaptable: the discrepancy measure, additional constraints, and relationship between the representation and the data can be modeled more flexibly. The stated contribution is primarily algorithmic, expanding how nonnegative approximations can be formulated and computed.
summary.tldr: The paper generalizes nonnegative matrix approximation through Bregman-divergence objectives, multiplicative updates, and additional modeling constraints.

title: Generalized Nonnegative Matrix Approximations with Bregman Divergences

abstract: Human listeners have the extraordinary ability to hear and recognize speech even when more than one person is talking. Their machine counterparts have historically been unable to compete with this ability, until now. We present a modelbased system that performs on par with humans in the task of separating speech of two talkers from a single-channel recording. Remarkably, the system surpasses human recognition performance in many conditions. The models of speech use temporal dynamics to help infer the source speech signals, given mixed speech signals. The estimated source signals are then recognized using a conventional speech recognition system. We demonstrate that the system achieves its best performance when the model of temporal dynamics closely captures the grammatical constraints of the task.
originalAbstract: Human listeners have the extraordinary ability to hear and recognize speech even when more than one person is talking. Their machine counterparts have historically been unable to compete with this ability, until now. We present a modelbased system that performs on par with humans in the task of separating speech of two talkers from a single-channel recording. Remarkably, the system surpasses human recognition performance in many conditions. The models of speech use temporal dynamics to help infer the source speech signals, given mixed speech signals. The estimated source signals are then recognized using a conventional speech recognition system. We demonstrate that the system achieves its best performance when the model of temporal dynamics closely captures the grammatical constraints of the task.

paragraphs: This paper tackles the problem of recovering two people's speech from a single recording in which their voices are mixed. The system uses models of how speech evolves over time to infer the individual source signals. Temporal structure supplies information for deciding which portions of the mixed sound belong to each talker.

After estimating the separate speech signals, the system passes them to a conventional speech recognizer. This separates the inference of source speech from the subsequent recognition step. The authors report performance on par with human listeners for the two-talker task, with recognition exceeding human performance under many of the evaluated conditions.

The system achieves its best results when its model of temporal dynamics closely reflects the task's grammatical constraints. This finding identifies the fit between the model and the speech task as an important part of the reported success. The contribution is evidence that suitable temporal models can support strong separation and recognition from one channel, with the strongest performance tied to accurately capturing the task's allowed speech structure.
summary.tldr: Temporal speech models enable human-comparable two-talker separation, with the best performance when their dynamics closely match the task's grammatical constraints.

title: Single Channel Speech Separation Using Factorial Dynamics

abstract: We present a new Bayesian skill rating system which can be viewed as a generalisation of the Elo system used in Chess. The new system tracks the uncertainty about player skills, explicitly models draws, can deal with any number of competing entities and can infer individual skills from team results. Inference is performed by approximate message passing on a factor graph representation of the model. We present experimental evidence on the increased accuracy and convergence speed of the system compared to Elo and report on our experience with the new rating system running in a large-scale commercial online gaming service under the name of TrueSkill.
originalAbstract: We present a new Bayesian skill rating system which can be viewed as a generalisation of the Elo system used in Chess. The new system tracks the uncertainty about player skills, explicitly models draws, can deal with any number of competing entities and can infer individual skills from team results. Inference is performed by approximate message passing on a factor graph representation of the model. We present experimental evidence on the increased accuracy and convergence speed of the system compared to Elo and report on our experience with the new rating system running in a large-scale commercial online gaming service under the name of TrueSkill.

paragraphs: A skill rating system must infer player ability from game outcomes. TrueSkill extends the Elo approach using a Bayesian model that tracks uncertainty about each player’s skill. This makes uncertainty part of the representation, alongside the estimate of ability itself, as the system interprets results.

The model explicitly accommodates draws, supports any number of competing entities, and can infer individual skills from team outcomes. Those capabilities let the same framework address several forms of competition. The authors express the model as a factor graph and use approximate message passing to perform inference about skills from the observed results.

Experiments provide evidence of better accuracy and faster convergence than Elo. The paper also reports experience operating TrueSkill within a large commercial online gaming service. Its contribution therefore includes both a broader probabilistic model of competition and evidence from evaluation and deployment. The comparative accuracy and convergence claims are experimental findings, while support for draws, multiple competitors, and team results describes the system’s modeling capabilities.
summary.tldr: TrueSkill models skill uncertainty, draws, multiple competitors, and team results, with experimental improvements over Elo.

title: TrueSkill™: A Bayesian Skill Rating System

abstract: A long-standing open research problem is how to use information from different experiments, including background knowledge, to infer causal relations. Recent developments have shown ways to use multiple data sets, provided they originate from identical experiments. We present the MCI-algorithm as the first method that can infer provably valid causal relations in the large sample limit from different experiments. It is fast, reliable and produces very clear and easily interpretable output. It is based on a result that shows that constraint-based causal discovery is decomposable into a candidate pair identification and subsequent elimination step that can be applied separately from different models. We test the algorithm on a variety of synthetic input model sets to assess its behavior and the quality of the output. The method shows promising signs that it can be adapted to suit causal discovery in real-world application areas as well, including large databases.

It is fast, reliable and produces very clear and easily interpretable output. paragraphs: Causal discovery becomes challenging when relevant information comes from different experiments and must be combined with background knowledge. Methods that combine datasets from identical experiments do not address this broader situation. The paper introduces MCI, an algorithm intended to infer causal relations from models associated with different experiments.

Its foundation is a decomposition of constraint-based causal discovery into two stages: identifying candidate pairs and then eliminating candidates. The authors show that these stages can be applied separately using different models. This creates a way to combine evidence without requiring all the contributing experiments to be identical, while producing an interpretable description of the inferred relationships.

The paper proves validity of the inferred causal relations in the large-sample limit. Tests on varied synthetic collections of input models examine the algorithm’s behavior and output quality. The authors describe the method as fast and reliable, while treating applications to real-world settings, including large databases, as promising directions for adaptation rather than established results of those tests.
summary.tldr: MCI combines models from different experiments to infer causal relations with a validity guarantee in the large-sample limit.

title: Causal discovery in multiple models from different experiments

abstract: It has been speculated that the human motion system combines noisy measurements with prior expectations in an optimal, or rational, manner. The basic goal of our work is to discover experimentally which prior distribution is used. More specifically, we seek to infer the functional form of the motion prior from the performance of human subjects on motion estimation tasks. We restricted ourselves to priors which combine three terms for motion slowness, first-order smoothness, and second-order smoothness. We focused on two functional forms for prior distributions: L2-norm and L1-norm regularization corresponding to the Gaussian and Laplace distributions respectively. In our first experimental session we estimate the weights of the three terms for each functional form to maximize the fit to human performance. We then measured human performance for motion tasks and found that we obtained better fit for the L1-norm (Laplace) than for the L2-norm (Gaussian). We note that the L1-norm is also a better fit to the statistics of motion in natural environments. In addition, we found large weights for the second-order smoothness term, indicating the importance of high-order smoothness compared to slowness and lower-order smoothness. To validate our results further, we used the best fit models using the L1-norm to predict human performance in a second session with different experimental setups. Our results showed excellent agreement between human performance and model prediction -- ranging from 3\% to 8\% for five human subjects over ten experimental conditions -- and give further support that the human visual system uses an L1-norm (Laplace) prior.

title: Functional form of motion priors in human motion perception

abstract: We address the challenging task of decoupling material properties from lighting properties given a single image. In the last two decades virtually all works have concentrated on exploiting edge information to address this problem. We take a different route by introducing a new prior on reflectance, that models reflectance values as being drawn from a sparse set of basis colors. This results in a Random Field model with global, latent variables (basis colors) and pixel-accurate output reflectance values. We show that without edge information high-quality results can be achieved, that are on par with methods exploiting this source of information. Finally, we present competitive results by integrating an additional edge model. We believe that our approach is a solid starting point for future development in this domain.

paragraphs: A single image mixes the appearance of materials with the effects of illumination. Recovering intrinsic images means separating those contributions. This paper approaches that problem through a prior on reflectance: the material-related colors are modeled as coming from a small set of basis colors shared across the image.

The resulting random field model contains global hidden variables for the basis colors while producing reflectance estimates at individual pixels. This links a scene-wide assumption about its color palette to detailed local output. The sparse palette provides information for the separation task that does not depend on detecting and interpreting image edges.

The authors show that their model can produce high-quality results without edge information, comparable to methods that use it. They also report competitive results after adding an edge model. These findings support global reflectance sparsity as a useful source of information for intrinsic-image recovery, and show that it can also be combined with edge-based evidence within the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: A sparse global palette of reflectance colors helps separate materials from lighting in a single image, even without edge information.

title: Recovering Intrinsic Images with a Global Sparsity Prior on Reflectance

abstract: This paper is concerned with the statistical consistency of ranking methods. Recently, it was proven that many commonly used pairwise ranking methods are inconsistent with the weighted pairwise disagreement loss (WPDL), which can be viewed as the true loss of ranking, even in a low-noise setting. This result is interesting but also surprising, given that the pairwise ranking methods have been shown very effective in practice. In this paper, we argue that the aforementioned result might not be conclusive, depending on what kind of assumptions are used. We give a new assumption that the labels of objects to rank lie in a rank-differentiable probability space (RDPS), and prove that the pairwise ranking methods become consistent with WPDL under this assumption. What is especially inspiring is that RDPS is actually not stronger than but similar to the low-noise setting. Our studies provide theoretical justifications of some empirical findings on pairwise ranking methods that are unexplained before, which bridge the gap between theory and applications.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a tension between theory and practice in ranking. Earlier results showed that many widely used pairwise ranking methods are inconsistent with weighted pairwise disagreement loss, even under low-noise conditions. Yet these methods often perform well empirically. The authors investigate whether different assumptions can help explain that apparent mismatch.

They introduce the assumption that the labels of the objects being ranked belong to a rank-differentiable probability space, abbreviated RDPS. Under this assumption, they prove that pairwise ranking methods are consistent with weighted pairwise disagreement loss. The result is conditional: it establishes consistency within the proposed setting, rather than overturning inconsistency results under other assumptions.

The authors describe RDPS as similar to, and not stronger than, the low-noise setting. Their analysis therefore highlights the importance of the kind of distributional assumptions used, rather than simply imposing a stronger low-noise requirement. The findings supply theoretical justification for previously unexplained empirical behavior and clarify how practical ranking success can coexist with negative results from a different mathematical setting.
summary.tldr: Pairwise ranking methods are consistent with weighted pairwise disagreement loss under a proposed rank-differentiable probability-space assumption.

title: Statistical Consistency of Ranking Methods in A Rank-Differentiable Probability Space

abstract: Learning temporal dependencies between variables over continuous time is an important and challenging task. Continuous-time Bayesian networks effectively model such processes but are limited by the number of conditional intensity matrices, which grows exponentially in the number of parents per variable. We develop a partition-based representation using regression trees and forests whose parameter spaces grow linearly in the number of node splits. Using a multiplicative assumption we show how to update the forest likelihood in closed form, producing efficient model updates. Our results show multiplicative forests can be learned from few temporal trajectories with large gains in performance and scalability.

Using a multiplicative assumption we show how to update the forest likelihood in closed form, producing efficient model updates. Our results show multiplicative forests can be learned from few temporal trajectories with large gains in performance and scalability.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning how variables influence one another over continuous time. Continuous-time Bayesian networks can represent these dependencies, but their conditional intensity matrices become costly as a variable gains more parents. The number of matrices grows exponentially with the parent count, creating a barrier to modeling richer dependency structures.

The authors introduce a partition-based representation built from regression trees and forests. Its parameter space grows linearly with the number of node splits, giving model complexity a different basis from enumerating parent configurations. Under a multiplicative assumption, the forest likelihood can be updated in closed form, enabling efficient changes to the model during learning.

The reported results show that multiplicative forests can be learned from only a few temporal trajectories, with large gains in performance and scalability. The contribution combines a compact way to represent conditional behavior with a convenient likelihood update. The multiplicative assumption is central to the computational result: it supplies the structure that makes those closed-form updates possible.
summary.tldr: Multiplicative regression forests provide a scalable representation of continuous-time dependencies with closed-form likelihood updates under a multiplicative assumption.

title: Multiplicative Forests for Continuous-Time Processes

abstract: We consider derivative-free algorithms for stochastic optimization problems that use only noisy function values rather than gradients, analyzing their finite-sample convergence rates. We show that if pairs of function values are available, algorithms that use gradient estimates based on random perturbations suffer a factor of at most $\sqrt{\dim}$ in convergence rate over traditional stochastic gradient methods, where $\dim$ is the dimension of the problem. We complement our algorithmic development with information-theoretic lower bounds on the minimax convergence rate of such problems, which show that our bounds are sharp with respect to all problem-dependent quantities: they cannot be improved by more than constant factors.
originalAbstract: We consider derivative-free algorithms for stochastic optimization problems that use only noisy function values rather than gradients, analyzing their finite-sample convergence rates. We show that if pairs of function values are available, algorithms that use gradient estimates based on random perturbations suffer a factor of at most $\sqrt{\dim}$ in convergence rate over traditional stochastic gradient methods, where $\dim$ is the dimension of the problem. We complement our algorithmic development with information-theoretic lower bounds on the minimax convergence rate of such problems, which show that our bounds are sharp with respect to all problem-dependent quantities: they cannot be improved by more than constant factors.

paragraphs: The paper studies stochastic optimization when an algorithm receives noisy function values but no gradients. Its central question is how quickly such methods can converge with a finite number of observations. This directly measures the price of using value information in place of the directional information supplied by a gradient.

When pairs of function values are available, the authors analyze algorithms that estimate gradients through random perturbations. They show that the convergence-rate penalty relative to traditional stochastic gradient methods is at most the square root of the problem dimension. The availability of paired values is a condition of this comparison and matters when interpreting the result.

The analysis also establishes information-theoretic lower bounds on minimax convergence rates. These show that the algorithmic bounds are sharp in all problem-dependent quantities, up to constant factors. Thus, within the studied setting, the dimension-dependent cost is supported by both an achievable method and a matching fundamental limit. The result explains how much can be recovered from noisy value queries and where further rate improvements are ruled out.
summary.tldr: With paired noisy function values, random-perturbation methods achieve sharp convergence bounds with at most a square-root dimension penalty.

title: Finite Sample Convergence Rates of Zero-Order Stochastic Optimization Methods

abstract: We study PCA as a stochastic optimization problem and propose a novel stochastic approximation algorithm which we refer to as Matrix Stochastic Gradient'' (MSG), as well as a practical variant, Capped MSG. We study the method both theoretically and empirically. "
originalAbstract: We study PCA as a stochastic optimization problem and propose a novel stochastic approximation algorithm which we refer to as Matrix Stochastic Gradient'' (MSG), as well as a practical variant, Capped MSG. We study the method both theoretically and empirically. "

paragraphs: This paper approaches principal component analysis, or PCA, as a stochastic optimization problem. The central contribution is an algorithmic treatment of that formulation: the authors propose a new stochastic approximation method called Matrix Stochastic Gradient, abbreviated MSG. Their focus is on how PCA can be solved through this optimization perspective.

Alongside MSG, the paper introduces Capped MSG as a practical variant. The contribution therefore includes both the proposed stochastic approximation algorithm and a version explicitly intended for practical use. These are presented as methods for the same PCA problem, with Capped MSG forming part of the paper's effort to connect the optimization formulation to an implementable procedure.

The authors study the method theoretically and empirically. The work thus combines mathematical investigation with experimental examination of the proposed approach. Its stated contribution is the formulation and study of MSG and its practical variant; the supplied abstract reports no particular comparative outcome. The supported takeaway is a new stochastic optimization route for PCA, investigated through both analysis and experiments.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces Matrix Stochastic Gradient and its practical Capped MSG variant for PCA, studying the approach theoretically and empirically.

title: Stochastic Optimization of PCA with Capped MSG

abstract: In stochastic optimal control the distribution of the exogenous noise is typically unknown and must be inferred from limited data before dynamic programming (DP)-based solution schemes can be applied. If the conditional expectations in the DP recursions are estimated via kernel regression, however, the historical sample paths enter the solution procedure directly as they determine the evaluation points of the cost-to-go functions. The resulting data-driven DP scheme is asymptotically consistent and admits efficient computational solution when combined with parametric value function approximations. If training data is sparse, however, the estimated cost-to-go functions display a high variability and an optimistic bias, while the corresponding control policies perform poorly in out-of-sample tests. To mitigate these small sample effects, we propose a robust data-driven DP scheme, which replaces the expectations in the DP recursions with worst-case expectations over a set of distributions close to the best estimate. We show that the arising min-max problems in the DP recursions reduce to tractable conic programs. We also demonstrate that this robust algorithm dominates state-of-the-art benchmark algorithms in out-of-sample tests across several application domains.

paragraphs: Stochastic control often requires decisions under a noise distribution estimated from limited data. A data-driven dynamic programming approach can estimate conditional expectations through kernel regression, using historical sample paths directly. Although this scheme is asymptotically consistent, sparse training data can produce variable, overly optimistic cost-to-go estimates and poor performance on new cases.

The paper proposes a robust alternative that accounts for uncertainty in the estimated distribution. At each dynamic programming step, it replaces the estimated expectation with a worst-case expectation over nearby distributions. This changes the decision calculation to consider plausible distributional alternatives, aiming to reduce the small-sample effects identified in the original scheme.

The authors show that the resulting min-max problems can be reduced to tractable conic programs. They also report that the robust algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art benchmark algorithms in out-of-sample tests across several application domains. The contribution combines a computationally manageable robustness mechanism with empirical evidence that it improves decisions when estimates based on limited training data would otherwise be too optimistic.
summary.tldr: Robust data-driven dynamic programming uses worst-case expectations over nearby distributions to reduce small-sample optimism, with tractable optimization and improved reported test performance.

title: Robust Data-Driven Dynamic Programming

abstract: Many single-channel signal decomposition techniques rely on a low-rank factorization of a time-frequency transform. In particular, nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) of the spectrogram -- the (power) magnitude of the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) -- has been considered in many audio applications. In this setting, NMF with the Itakura-Saito divergence was shown to underly a generative Gaussian composite model (GCM) of the STFT, a step forward from more empirical approaches based on ad-hoc transform and divergence specifications. Still, the GCM is not yet a generative model of the raw signal itself, but only of its STFT. The work presented in this paper fills in this ultimate gap by proposing a novel signal synthesis model with low-rank time-frequency structure. In particular, our new approach opens doors to multi-resolution representations, that were not possible in the traditional NMF setting. We describe two expectation-maximization algorithms for estimation in the new model and report audio signal processing results with music decomposition and speech enhancement.

paragraphs: Many single-channel audio decomposition methods factor a time-frequency representation into a low-rank structure. A common approach applies nonnegative matrix factorization to a spectrogram. Earlier work connected one such formulation to a Gaussian composite model of short-time Fourier-transform coefficients, giving a probabilistic interpretation to that transformed representation.

This paper moves the generative model to the raw signal itself. It proposes a signal-synthesis model with low-rank time-frequency structure, addressing the gap between explaining transform coefficients and explaining how the signal is generated. The authors state that this formulation also permits multi-resolution representations that were unavailable in the traditional nonnegative-matrix-factorization setting.

The paper develops two expectation-maximization algorithms for estimating the new model and reports applications to music decomposition and speech enhancement. Its contribution is therefore both representational and computational: a generative account of the waveform with the desired low-rank structure, together with procedures for fitting it. The audio results demonstrate uses of that formulation in two signal-processing tasks.
summary.tldr: A raw-signal generative model preserves low-rank time-frequency structure while enabling multi-resolution representations and audio-processing applications.

title: Low-Rank Time-Frequency Synthesis

abstract: We extend the multinomial logit model to represent some of the empirical phenomena that are frequently observed in the choices made by humans. These phenomena include the similarity effect, the attraction effect, and the compromise effect. We formally quantify the strength of these phenomena that can be represented by our choice model, which illuminates the flexibility of our choice model. We then show that our choice model can be represented as a restricted Boltzmann machine and that its parameters can be learned effectively from data. Our numerical experiments with real data of human choices suggest that we can train our choice model in such a way that it represents the typical phenomena of choice.

We formally quantify the strength of these phenomena that can be represented by our choice model, which illuminates the flexibility of our choice model. We then show that our choice model can be represented as a restricted Boltzmann machine and that its parameters can be learned effectively from data. Our numerical experiments with real data of human choices suggest that we can train our choice model in such a way that it represents the typical phenomena of choice.

paragraphs: Human choices exhibit recurring patterns that a choice model should be able to represent. This paper focuses on three such phenomena: similarity, attraction, and compromise effects. The authors extend the multinomial logit model to accommodate these patterns, making the representation of observed choice behavior the central modeling objective.

The work includes a formal analysis of how strongly the extended model can express each phenomenon. This goes beyond showing a few illustrative choices: it quantifies aspects of the model's flexibility. The authors then show that the choice model has a restricted Boltzmann machine representation and that its parameters can be learned effectively from data.

Numerical experiments use real human-choice data. The results suggest that training can produce a model exhibiting the characteristic choice phenomena considered in the paper. That empirical conclusion is appropriately narrower than claiming a complete account of human decisions. The contribution links a behavioral choice formulation, a formal description of its expressive capacity, and a learnable probabilistic model in one framework.
summary.tldr: An extended multinomial logit model represents characteristic human-choice effects and can be learned through a restricted Boltzmann machine formulation.

title: Restricted Boltzmann machines modeling human choice

abstract: Dropout training, originally designed for deep neural networks, has been successful on high-dimensional single-layer natural language tasks. This paper proposes a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon: we show that, under a generative Poisson topic model with long documents, dropout training improves the exponent in the generalization bound for empirical risk minimization. Dropout achieves this gain much like a marathon runner who practices at altitude: once a classifier learns to perform reasonably well on training examples that have been artificially corrupted by dropout, it will do very well on the uncorrupted test set. We also show that, under similar conditions, dropout preserves the Bayes decision boundary and should therefore induce minimal bias in high dimensions.
originalAbstract: Dropout training, originally designed for deep neural networks, has been successful on high-dimensional single-layer natural language tasks. This paper proposes a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon: we show that, under a generative Poisson topic model with long documents, dropout training improves the exponent in the generalization bound for empirical risk minimization. Dropout achieves this gain much like a marathon runner who practices at altitude: once a classifier learns to perform reasonably well on training examples that have been artificially corrupted by dropout, it will do very well on the uncorrupted test set. We also show that, under similar conditions, dropout preserves the Bayes decision boundary and should therefore induce minimal bias in high dimensions.

paragraphs: The paper asks why dropout can help high-dimensional language classifiers even when they have only a single layer. Its contribution is a theoretical explanation under a particular model of documents. The analysis assumes that documents are long and generated by a Poisson topic model, so the conclusions describe a specified statistical setting.

Under those assumptions, dropout improves the exponent in a generalization bound for empirical risk minimization. This strengthens the bound on how well a classifier trained on observed examples can perform beyond them. The authors explain the effect through training on artificially corrupted examples: learning to classify these harder examples reasonably well can translate into strong performance when the corruption is absent at test time.

The paper also shows that, under similar conditions, dropout leaves the Bayes decision boundary unchanged. In other words, the corruption preserves the ideal classification boundary associated with the assumed data distribution. This supports the expectation of minimal bias in high dimensions. Together, the results explain how dropout can strengthen generalization while preserving the underlying classification target within the analyzed setting.
summary.tldr: Under a Poisson topic model with long documents, single-layer dropout strengthens a generalization bound while preserving the Bayes decision boundary under similar conditions.

title: Altitude Training: Strong Bounds for Single-Layer Dropout

abstract: In this paper, we study the estimation of the $k$-dimensional sparse principal subspace of covariance matrix $\Sigma$ in the high-dimensional setting. We aim to recover the oracle principal subspace solution, i.e., the principal subspace estimator obtained assuming the true support is known a priori. To this end, we propose a family of estimators based on the semidefinite relaxation of sparse PCA with novel regularizations. In particular, under a weak assumption on the magnitude of the population projection matrix, one estimator within this family exactly recovers the true support with high probability, has exact rank-$k$, and attains a $\sqrt{s/n}$ statistical rate of convergence with $s$ being the subspace sparsity level and $n$ the sample size. Compared to existing support recovery results for sparse PCA, our approach does not hinge on the spiked covariance model or the limited correlation condition. As a complement to the first estimator that enjoys the oracle property, we prove that, another estimator within the family achieves a sharper statistical rate of convergence than the standard semidefinite relaxation of sparse PCA, even when the previous assumption on the magnitude of the projection matrix is violated. We validate the theoretical results by numerical experiments on synthetic datasets.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study the estimation of the $k$-dimensional sparse principal subspace of covariance matrix $\Sigma$ in the high-dimensional setting. We aim to recover the oracle principal subspace solution, i.e., the principal subspace estimator obtained assuming the true support is known a priori. To this end, we propose a family of estimators based on the semidefinite relaxation of sparse PCA with novel regularizations. In particular, under a weak assumption on the magnitude of the population projection matrix, one estimator within this family exactly recovers the true support with high probability, has exact rank-$k$, and attains a $\sqrt{s/n}$ statistical rate of convergence with $s$ being the subspace sparsity level and $n$ the sample size. Compared to existing support recovery results for sparse PCA, our approach does not hinge on the spiked covariance model or the limited correlation condition. As a complement to the first estimator that enjoys the oracle property, we prove that, another estimator within the family achieves a sharper statistical rate of convergence than the standard semidefinite relaxation of sparse PCA, even when the previous assumption on the magnitude of the projection matrix is violated. We validate the theoretical results by numerical experiments on synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: Sparse PCA seeks a principal subspace supported by a limited set of variables. This paper aims to match an oracle estimator that already knows which variables belong in that support. It proposes a family of estimators based on semidefinite relaxation, adding new regularization choices to recover the relevant subspace in high dimensions.

Under a weak assumption on the magnitude of the population projection matrix, one estimator recovers the true support with high probability, has exactly rank k, and achieves a statistical convergence rate of √(s/n). Here s is the subspace sparsity and n is the sample size. The support-recovery result does not require a spiked covariance model or the limited-correlation condition used in existing results.

A second estimator addresses cases where the projection-magnitude assumption fails. It still achieves a sharper statistical rate than the standard semidefinite relaxation, although the abstract does not assign it the first estimator’s oracle property. Synthetic-data experiments validate the theoretical results. The family therefore offers both a conditional oracle guarantee and a separate improvement beyond that condition.
summary.tldr: New sparse-PCA regularizations provide conditional oracle recovery and improved statistical rates when that oracle condition fails.

title: Sparse PCA with Oracle Property

abstract: We present a new algorithm for community detection. The algorithm uses random walks to embed the graph in a space of measures, after which a modification of $k$-means in that space is applied. The algorithm is therefore fast and easily parallelizable. We evaluate the algorithm on standard random graph benchmarks, including some overlapping community benchmarks, and find its performance to be better or at least as good as previously known algorithms. We also prove a linear time (in number of edges) guarantee for the algorithm on a $p,q$-stochastic block model with where $p \geq c\cdot N^{-\half + \epsilon}$ and $p-q \geq c' \sqrt{p N^{-\half + \epsilon} \log N}$.
originalAbstract: We present a new algorithm for community detection. The algorithm uses random walks to embed the graph in a space of measures, after which a modification of $k$-means in that space is applied. The algorithm is therefore fast and easily parallelizable. We evaluate the algorithm on standard random graph benchmarks, including some overlapping community benchmarks, and find its performance to be better or at least as good as previously known algorithms. We also prove a linear time (in number of edges) guarantee for the algorithm on a $p,q$-stochastic block model with where $p \geq c\cdot N^{-\half + \epsilon}$ and $p-q \geq c' \sqrt{p N^{-\half + \epsilon} \log N}$.

paragraphs: Community detection seeks groups within a graph, and this paper approaches the task by changing how the graph is represented. Random walks produce an embedding in a space of measures: the objects being compared are distributions rather than ordinary coordinate vectors. A modified form of k-means then clusters this representation.

This separates the method into a random-walk representation stage and a clustering stage suited to that representation. The authors describe the resulting algorithm as fast and readily parallelizable. On standard random-graph benchmarks, including some with overlapping communities, they report performance that matches or exceeds previously known algorithms. Those comparisons provide empirical support across the benchmark settings considered.

The paper also establishes a linear-in-edges time guarantee for a particular stochastic block model. That guarantee requires both a lower bound on p and a sufficiently large gap between p and q, with thresholds depending on graph size. Thus, the theoretical result identifies conditions supporting efficient operation, while the benchmark results supply a separate empirical assessment of community-detection performance.
summary.tldr: Random-walk distribution embeddings followed by modified k-means yield a parallelizable community detector with competitive benchmark results and a conditional linear-time guarantee.

title: Community Detection via Measure Space Embedding

abstract: We present the first application of the median of means in a PAC exploration algorithm for MDPs. Using the median of means allows us to significantly reduce the dependence of our bounds on the range of values that the value function can take, while introducing a dependence on the (potentially much smaller) variance of the Bellman operator. Additionally, our algorithm is the first algorithm with PAC bounds that can be applied to MDPs with unbounded rewards.
originalAbstract: We present the first application of the median of means in a PAC exploration algorithm for MDPs. Using the median of means allows us to significantly reduce the dependence of our bounds on the range of values that the value function can take, while introducing a dependence on the (potentially much smaller) variance of the Bellman operator. Additionally, our algorithm is the first algorithm with PAC bounds that can be applied to MDPs with unbounded rewards.

paragraphs: This paper addresses exploration in Markov decision processes using a probably approximately correct, or PAC, framework. Such a framework seeks guarantees about learning sufficiently good behavior with high probability. The authors introduce the median of means into a PAC exploration algorithm, presenting it as the first application of this estimation method in that setting.

The main result changes what the theoretical bounds depend on. Their dependence on the full range of possible value-function values is significantly reduced, while dependence on the variance of the Bellman operator is introduced. That variance can be much smaller, so the improvement is potentially substantial when the variability captured by this quantity is favorable.

The algorithm also extends the reach of PAC exploration guarantees to Markov decision processes with unbounded rewards, which the authors identify as a first. The contribution is therefore about both sharper dependence in the bounds and a broader reward setting. The abstract's potential advantage remains tied to the variance rather than asserting an unconditional improvement for every process.
summary.tldr: Using the median of means improves PAC exploration bounds through variance dependence and permits guarantees for MDPs with unbounded rewards.

title: Improving PAC Exploration Using the Median Of Means

abstract: We study the problem of learning influence functions under incomplete observations of node activations. Incomplete observations are a major concern as most (online and real-world) social networks are not fully observable. We establish both proper and improper PAC learnability of influence functions under randomly missing observations. Proper PAC learnability under the Discrete-Time Linear Threshold (DLT) and Discrete-Time Independent Cascade (DIC) models is established by reducing incomplete observations to complete observations in a modified graph. Our improper PAC learnability result applies for the DLT and DIC models as well as the Continuous-Time Independent Cascade (CIC) model. It is based on a parametrization in terms of reachability features, and also gives rise to an efficient and practical heuristic. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the ability of our method to compensate even for a fairly large fraction of missing observations.

This paper studies whether influence functions can still be learned when observations are randomly missing. That assumption is central to its theoretical results, which establish both proper and improper probably approximately correct learnability.

title: Learning Influence Functions from Incomplete Observations

abstract: Recently, several works have shown that natural modifications of the classical conditional gradient method (aka Frank-Wolfe algorithm) for constrained convex optimization, provably converge with a linear rate when the feasible set is a polytope, and the objective is smooth and strongly-convex. However, all of these results suffer from two significant shortcomings: i) large memory requirement due to the need to store an explicit convex decomposition of the current iterate, and as a consequence, large running-time overhead per iteration ii) the worst case convergence rate depends unfavorably on the dimension In this work we present a new conditional gradient variant and a corresponding analysis that improves on both of the above shortcomings. In particular, both memory and computation overheads are only linear in the dimension, and in addition, in case the optimal solution is sparse, the new convergence rate replaces a factor which is at least linear in the dimension in previous works, with a linear dependence on the number of non-zeros in the optimal solution At the heart of our method, and corresponding analysis, is a novel way to compute decomposition-invariant away-steps. While our theoretical guarantees do not apply to any polytope, they apply to several important structured polytopes that capture central concepts such as paths in graphs, perfect matchings in bipartite graphs, marginal distributions that arise in structured prediction tasks, and more. Our theoretical findings are complemented by empirical evidence that shows that our method delivers state-of-the-art performance.

summary.tldr: Decomposition-invariant away-steps reduce conditional gradient overhead and improve convergence dependence for sparse optima on supported structured polytopes.

title: Linear-Memory and Decomposition-Invariant Linearly Convergent Conditional Gradient Algorithm for Structured Polytopes

abstract: Decision-makers are faced with the challenge of estimating what is likely to happen when they take an action. For instance, if I choose not to treat this patient, are they likely to die? Practitioners commonly use supervised learning algorithms to fit predictive models that help decision-makers reason about likely future outcomes, but we show that this approach is unreliable, and sometimes even dangerous. The key issue is that supervised learning algorithms are highly sensitive to the policy used to choose actions in the training data, which causes the model to capture relationships that do not generalize. We propose using a different learning objective that predicts counterfactuals instead of predicting outcomes under an existing action policy as in supervised learning. To support decision-making in temporal settings, we introduce the Counterfactual Gaussian Process (CGP) to predict the counterfactual future progression of continuous-time trajectories under sequences of future actions. We demonstrate the benefits of the CGP on two important decision-support tasks: risk prediction and “what if?” reasoning for individualized treatment planning.

paragraphs: Decision support requires estimating what would happen if a particular action were taken. A model trained to predict observed outcomes may instead learn relationships tied to how actions were chosen in its training data. The paper shows that this sensitivity to the existing action policy can make conventional supervised prediction unreliable for guiding decisions.

The authors propose changing the learning objective to predict counterfactual outcomes. This targets the consequences of alternative actions rather than outcomes under the policy that generated the data. For decisions unfolding over time, they introduce the Counterfactual Gaussian Process, which predicts continuous-time trajectories under sequences of future actions.

The model is demonstrated on risk prediction and individualized treatment planning through what-if reasoning. In these tasks, the relevant output is a possible future progression associated with a proposed action sequence. The stated benefits support aligning prediction with the decision being considered. The central contribution is this shift in target, together with a temporal model designed to represent action-dependent future trajectories.
summary.tldr: Counterfactual Gaussian Processes predict future trajectories under alternative action sequences to improve decision support beyond policy-dependent outcome prediction.

title: Reliable Decision Support using Counterfactual Models

abstract: Thompson sampling has emerged as an effective heuristic for a broad range of online decision problems. In its basic form, the algorithm requires computing and sampling from a posterior distribution over models, which is tractable only for simple special cases. This paper develops ensemble sampling, which aims to approximate Thompson sampling while maintaining tractability even in the face of complex models such as neural networks. Ensemble sampling dramatically expands on the range of applications for which Thompson sampling is viable. We establish a theoretical basis that supports the approach and present computational results that offer further insight.

Ensemble sampling dramatically expands on the range of applications for which Thompson sampling is viable. We establish a theoretical basis that supports the approach and present computational results that offer further insight.

paragraphs: Online decision systems must choose actions while still learning which model best explains their observations. Thompson sampling addresses this by sampling from a posterior distribution over models. Although it has proved effective as a heuristic across many decision problems, directly computing and sampling from that posterior is tractable only in relatively simple cases.

This paper develops ensemble sampling as an approximation to Thompson sampling. The central aim is to retain a workable sampling-based decision procedure when the underlying models are complex, including neural networks. Using an ensemble provides an alternative basis for approximating the model uncertainty involved in Thompson sampling, making computational tractability a central design concern.

The authors establish theoretical support for the approach and provide computational results that add insight into its behavior. They present it as substantially broadening the range of applications where Thompson-style decision making is viable. The contribution concerns a tractable approximation with supporting analysis, so its significance lies in making the strategy usable with richer models rather than requiring exact posterior computation.
summary.tldr: Ensemble sampling approximates Thompson sampling to make uncertainty-driven online decisions tractable with complex models such as neural networks.

title: Ensemble Sampling

abstract: Stochastic gradient methods are the workhorse (algorithms) of large-scale optimization problems in machine learning, signal processing, and other computational sciences and engineering. This paper studies Markov chain gradient descent, a variant of stochastic gradient descent where the random samples are taken on the trajectory of a Markov chain. Existing results of this method assume convex objectives and a reversible Markov chain and thus have their limitations. We establish new non-ergodic convergence under wider step sizes, for nonconvex problems, and for non-reversible finite-state Markov chains. Nonconvexity makes our method applicable to broader problem classes. Non-reversible finite-state Markov chains, on the other hand, can mix substatially faster. To obtain these results, we introduce a new technique that varies the mixing levels of the Markov chains. The reported numerical results validate our contributions.

paragraphs: Markov chain gradient descent selects the samples used for gradient updates along a Markov chain trajectory. This creates a form of stochastic optimization in which successive sample choices are linked. Earlier analyses required convex objectives and reversible chains, restricting the kinds of optimization problems and sampling processes covered by the theory.

This paper establishes non-ergodic convergence results with a broader range of step sizes, including nonconvex objectives and non-reversible finite-state Markov chains. The analysis uses a technique that varies the chains' mixing levels. Mixing describes how the sampling process approaches its long-run behavior, making it central to understanding gradients obtained from a chain.

Allowing nonconvexity extends the analysis to a wider set of objectives. Allowing non-reversible chains is also useful because such chains can mix substantially faster, although that is a possibility rather than a guarantee for every chain. Numerical results support the contributions. The main advance is a convergence theory that accommodates more flexible objectives, sampling dynamics, and step-size choices.
summary.tldr: New convergence results extend Markov chain gradient descent to nonconvex objectives and non-reversible finite-state sampling chains.

title: On Markov Chain Gradient Descent

abstract: Machine learning models are vulnerable to adversarial examples: small changes to images can cause computer vision models to make mistakes such as identifying a school bus as an ostrich. However, it is still an open question whether humans are prone to similar mistakes. Here, we address this question by leveraging recent techniques that transfer adversarial examples from computer vision models with known parameters and architecture to other models with unknown parameters and architecture, and by matching the initial processing of the human visual system. We find that adversarial examples that strongly transfer across computer vision models influence the classifications made by time-limited human observers.
