paragraphs: Small changes to an image can cause a computer vision model to assign an incorrect label. The paper investigates whether adversarial images can also affect human judgments. It focuses on observers with limited viewing time, making the conditions of human perception central to the question being tested.

The approach builds on techniques for transferring adversarial examples between computer vision models. Such techniques construct examples using a model with known architecture and parameters, then seek effects on models whose details are unknown. The authors combine this transfer-based approach with matching the initial processing of the human visual system, connecting the attack design to the human viewing setting.

The reported finding is that adversarial examples with strong transfer across computer vision models influence classifications by time-limited human observers. This establishes an effect under the studied viewing conditions; it does not establish the same result for unrestricted inspection. The contribution connects model-to-model adversarial transfer with human classification behavior, showing that these perturbations can matter beyond the computer vision systems used to construct them.
summary.tldr: Adversarial images that transfer strongly between vision models also influence human classifications when viewing time is limited.

title: Adversarial Examples that Fool both Computer Vision and Time-Limited Humans

abstract: Progress in machine learning is measured by careful evaluation on problems of outstanding common interest. However, the proliferation of benchmark suites and environments, adversarial attacks, and other complications has diluted the basic evaluation model by overwhelming researchers with choices. Deliberate or accidental cherry picking is increasingly likely, and designing well-balanced evaluation suites requires increasing effort. In this paper we take a step back and propose Nash averaging. The approach builds on a detailed analysis of the algebraic structure of evaluation in two basic scenarios: agent-vs-agent and agent-vs-task. The key strength of Nash averaging is that it automatically adapts to redundancies in evaluation data, so that results are not biased by the incorporation of easy tasks or weak agents. Nash averaging thus encourages maximally inclusive evaluation -- since there is no harm (computational cost aside) from including all available tasks and agents.

paragraphs: Comparing machine learning systems becomes harder as researchers gain more choices of tasks, opponents, benchmarks, and attacks. Selecting among those choices can lead to deliberate or accidental cherry picking. This paper asks how evaluation can remain balanced as the amount and variety of available comparison data grow.

The authors propose Nash averaging, based on an analysis of the algebraic structure of two evaluation settings: agents competing against agents, and agents performing tasks. Its key property is automatic adaptation to redundancies in evaluation data. This prevents the inclusion of easy tasks or weak agents from biasing the resulting evaluation.

That property supports a more inclusive approach to testing. Researchers can include all available tasks and agents without the harm from redundancy addressed by the method, although computational cost remains a consideration. The contribution is an aggregation approach designed to reduce sensitivity to the composition of an evaluation collection, making broad inclusion compatible with meaningful comparisons.
summary.tldr: Nash averaging adjusts for redundant evaluation data so that easy tasks and weak agents do not bias comparisons.

title: Re-evaluating evaluation

abstract: Proximal policy optimization and trust region policy optimization (PPO and TRPO) with actor and critic parametrized by neural networks achieve significant empirical success in deep reinforcement learning. However, due to nonconvexity, the global convergence of PPO and TRPO remains less understood, which separates theory from practice. In this paper, we prove that a variant of PPO and TRPO equipped with overparametrized neural networks converges to the globally optimal policy at a sublinear rate. The key to our analysis is the global convergence of infinite-dimensional mirror descent under a notion of one-point monotonicity, where the gradient and iterate are instantiated by neural networks. In particular, the desirable representation power and optimization geometry induced by the overparametrization of such neural networks allow them to accurately approximate the infinite-dimensional gradient and iterate.

paragraphs: PPO and TRPO perform well empirically when neural networks represent both the policy and its critic. Explaining global convergence is harder because the resulting optimization is nonconvex. This paper provides a convergence theorem for a variant of these methods equipped with overparameterized neural networks, connecting their expressive capacity to the behavior of policy optimization.

The analysis starts from infinite-dimensional mirror descent and establishes global convergence under a property called one-point monotonicity. Neural networks then represent the gradient and the iterate appearing in that idealized procedure. Overparameterization supplies both representational power and favorable optimization geometry, allowing those networks to approximate the quantities needed by the analysis accurately.

The resulting theorem states that the studied variant converges to a globally optimal policy at a sublinear rate. Its significance is a mathematical explanation of how sufficiently expressive neural parameterizations can support global policy optimization despite nonconvexity. The guarantee concerns the overparameterized variant analyzed in the paper, with the approximation and monotonicity structure central to its proof.
summary.tldr: The paper proves sublinear convergence to a globally optimal policy for an overparameterized neural-network variant of PPO and TRPO.

title: Neural Trust Region/Proximal Policy Optimization Attains Globally Optimal Policy

abstract: Word embeddings are commonly obtained as optimisers of a criterion function f of a text corpus, but assessed on word-task performance using a different evaluation function g of the test data. We contend that a possible source of disparity in performance on tasks is the incompatibility between classes of transformations that leave f and g invariant. In particular, word embeddings defined by f are not unique; they are defined only up to a class of transformations to which f is invariant, and this class is larger than the class to which g is invariant. One implication of this is that the apparent superiority of one word embedding over another, as measured by word task performance, may largely be a consequence of the arbitrary elements selected from the respective solution sets. We provide a formal treatment of the above identifiability issue, present some numerical examples, and discuss possible resolutions.

paragraphs: Word embeddings are usually trained by optimizing one criterion and judged using a different function on language tasks. This paper argues that a mismatch between the symmetries of those two functions can help explain differences in measured performance. A transformation may preserve the training objective while changing the score used to evaluate the resulting embeddings.

The underlying issue is identifiability. A training criterion can define an entire family of equally valid embeddings rather than one unique representation. The authors examine the situation where the transformations preserving that criterion form a larger class than those preserving evaluation scores. Members of the same training solution family can therefore receive different task assessments.

One implication is that an embedding's apparent advantage may largely reflect an arbitrary choice from its solution family. The paper treats this as a possible explanation for performance disparities, not as proof that all embedding comparisons are misleading. It formalizes the issue, supplies numerical examples, and discusses possible resolutions. The contribution is a framework for examining whether training-equivalent representations are also equivalent under the evaluation being used.
summary.tldr: Different invariances in training and evaluation can make equally valid word embeddings receive different task scores.

title: Invariance and identifiability issues for word embeddings

abstract: Contemporary sensorimotor learning approaches typically start with an existing complex agent (e.g., a robotic arm), which they learn to control. In contrast, this paper investigates a modular co-evolution strategy: a collection of primitive agents learns to dynamically self-assemble into composite bodies while also learning to coordinate their behavior to control these bodies. Each primitive agent consists of a limb with a motor attached at one end. Limbs may choose to link up to form collectives. When a limb initiates a link-up action and there is another limb nearby, the latter is magnetically connected to the 'parent' limb's motor. This forms a new single agent, which may further link with other agents. In this way, complex morphologies can emerge, controlled by a policy whose architecture is in explicit correspondence with the morphology. We evaluate the performance of these dynamic and modular agents in simulated environments. We demonstrate better generalization to test-time changes both in the environment, as well as in the structure of the agent, compared to static and monolithic baselines. Project videos and source code are provided in the supplementary material.

paragraphs: Most sensorimotor learning starts with a fixed body and learns how to control it. This paper studies a different arrangement: simple agents learn both how to assemble larger bodies and how to coordinate those bodies' behavior. Body construction and control are therefore part of the same learning problem.

The resulting composite can connect with further agents. As bodies become more complex, the control policy has an architecture that explicitly corresponds to the assembled morphology.

The authors evaluate these dynamic, modular agents in simulation. They report better generalization than static, monolithic baselines when either the environment or the agent's structure changes at test time. The findings support modular co-evolution as a way to improve adaptability in the evaluated settings, tying the organization of the controller to the body's changing structure.
summary.tldr: Simulated modular limbs jointly learn self-assembly and control, improving generalization to changes in their environment and body structure.

title: Learning to Control Self-Assembling Morphologies: A Study of Generalization via Modularity

abstract: We investigate neural network representations from a probabilistic perspective. Specifically, we leverage Bayesian nonparametrics to construct models of neural activations in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and latent representations in Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). This allows us to formulate a tractable complexity measure for distributions of neural activations and to explore global structure of latent spaces learned by VAEs. We use this machinery to uncover how memorization and two common forms of regularization, i.e. dropout and input augmentation, influence representational complexity in CNNs. We demonstrate that networks that can exploit patterns in data learn vastly less complex representations than networks forced to memorize. We also show marked differences between effects of input augmentation and dropout, with the latter strongly depending on network width. Next, we investigate latent representations learned by standard $\beta$-VAEs and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) $\beta$-VAEs. We show that aggregated posterior in standard VAEs quickly collapses to the diagonal prior when regularization strength increases. MMD-VAEs, on the other hand, learn more complex posterior distributions, even with strong regularization. While this gives a richer sample space, MMD-VAEs do not exhibit independence of latent dimensions. Finally, we leverage our probabilistic models as an effective sampling strategy for latent codes, improving quality of samples in VAEs with rich posteriors.

It uses Bayesian nonparametric models to describe activations in convolutional networks and latent representations in variational autoencoders. These models provide a tractable measure of activation complexity and a way to examine the overall structure of a learned latent space.

Networks able to exploit patterns develop substantially less complex representations than networks forced to memorize. Together, these findings connect representation complexity, regularization, and sampling behavior.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic models of neural representations reveal how memorization and regularization affect complexity and improve sampling from VAEs with rich posteriors.

title: A Bayesian Nonparametrics View into Deep Representations

abstract: This paper re-examines a continuous optimization framework dubbed NOTEARS for learning Bayesian networks. We first generalize existing algebraic characterizations of acyclicity to a class of matrix polynomials. Next, focusing on a one-parameter-per-edge setting, it is shown that the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) optimality conditions for the NOTEARS formulation cannot be satisfied except in a trivial case, which explains a behavior of the associated algorithm. We then derive the KKT conditions for an equivalent reformulation, show that they are indeed necessary, and relate them to explicit constraints that certain edges be absent from the graph. If the score function is convex, these KKT conditions are also sufficient for local minimality despite the non-convexity of the constraint. Informed by the KKT conditions, a local search post-processing algorithm is proposed and shown to substantially and universally improve the structural Hamming distance of all tested algorithms, typically by a factor of 2 or more. Some combinations with local search are both more accurate and more efficient than the original NOTEARS.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network requires finding a directed graph without cycles. NOTEARS expresses this requirement within a continuous optimization problem. This paper revisits that formulation, first extending algebraic descriptions of acyclicity to a class of matrix polynomials and then examining whether the optimization conditions behave as expected.

For the setting with one parameter per edge, the authors show that the original formulation’s Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions can hold only in a trivial case. They derive necessary conditions for an equivalent reformulation and connect those conditions to requiring particular edges to be absent. summary.tldr: A reformulated analysis of NOTEARS yields meaningful optimality conditions and a local-search refinement that improves every tested algorithm.

title: DAGs with No Fears: A Closer Look at Continuous Optimization for Learning Bayesian Networks

abstract: We study the black-box attacks on graph neural networks (GNNs) under a novel and realistic constraint: attackers have access to only a subset of nodes in the network, and they can only attack a small number of them. A node selection step is essential under this setup. We demonstrate that the structural inductive biases of GNN models can be an effective source for this type of attacks. Specifically, by exploiting the connection between the backward propagation of GNNs and random walks, we show that the common gradient-based white-box attacks can be generalized to the black-box setting via the connection between the gradient and an importance score similar to PageRank. In practice, we find attacks based on this importance score indeed increase the classification loss by a large margin, but they fail to significantly increase the mis-classification rate. Our theoretical and empirical analyses suggest that there is a discrepancy between the loss and mis-classification rate, as the latter presents a diminishing-return pattern when the number of attacked nodes increases. Therefore, we propose a greedy procedure to correct the importance score that takes into account of the diminishing-return pattern. Experimental results show that the proposed procedure can significantly increase the mis-classification rate of common GNNs on real-world data without access to model parameters nor predictions.

paragraphs: This paper examines graph-neural-network attacks under restricted access: an attacker can reach only a subset of nodes and modify only a small number of them. Choosing which nodes to attack becomes essential. The authors investigate how the graph structure itself can guide that choice without access to model parameters or predictions.

The authors introduce a greedy correction to the importance score that accounts for this pattern. Experiments on real-world data show significant increases in misclassification rates for common graph neural networks. The finding highlights why an attack-selection criterion must reflect the outcome of interest, since loss increases alone may poorly track classification errors.
summary.tldr: A structure-based greedy node-selection method increases GNN misclassification under restricted access by accounting for diminishing attack returns.

title: Towards More Practical Adversarial Attacks on Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) are a new class of models that transform data continuously through infinite-depth architectures. The continuous nature of NODEs has made them particularly suitable for learning the dynamics of complex physical systems. While previous work has mostly been focused on first order ODEs, the dynamics of many systems, especially in classical physics, are governed by second order laws. In this work, we consider Second Order Neural ODEs (SONODEs). We show how the adjoint sensitivity method can be extended to SONODEs and prove that the optimisation of a first order coupled ODE is equivalent and computationally more efficient. Furthermore, we extend the theoretical understanding of the broader class of Augmented NODEs (ANODEs) by showing they can also learn higher order dynamics with a minimal number of augmented dimensions, but at the cost of interpretability. This indicates that the advantages of ANODEs go beyond the extra space offered by the augmented dimensions, as originally thought. Finally, we compare SONODEs and ANODEs on synthetic and real dynamical systems and demonstrate that the inductive biases of the former generally result in faster training and better performance.

The authors extend the adjoint sensitivity method to SONODEs, providing a route for optimizing these models. They also prove that optimizing an equivalent coupled first-order system is computationally more efficient. This connects the desired second-order dynamics with a practical first-order formulation for training, while preserving the stated equivalence.

These results favor explicit second-order structure in the studied settings while also clarifying the broader capabilities of augmented models.
summary.tldr: The paper develops second-order neural ODE training and shows how explicit second-order structure can improve learning relative to augmented neural ODEs.

title: On Second Order Behaviour in Augmented Neural ODEs

abstract: This article characterizes the exact asymptotics of random Fourier feature (RFF) regression, in the realistic setting where the number of data samples $n$, their dimension $p$, and the dimension of feature space $N$ are all large and comparable. In this regime, the random RFF Gram matrix no longer converges to the well-known limiting Gaussian kernel matrix (as it does when $N \to \infty$ alone), but it still has a tractable behavior that is captured by our analysis. This analysis also provides accurate estimates of training and test regression errors for large $n,p,N$. Based on these estimates, a precise characterization of two qualitatively different phases of learning, including the phase transition between them, is provided; and the corresponding double descent test error curve is derived from this phase transition behavior. These results do not depend on strong assumptions on the data distribution, and they perfectly match empirical results on real-world data sets.

paragraphs: Random Fourier feature regression is often understood through its connection to a limiting Gaussian kernel as the number of features grows. This paper studies a different regime: the sample count, input dimension, and feature count all grow together and remain comparable. That distinction matters because the familiar kernel limit no longer describes the random feature Gram matrix in this setting.

The authors use random matrix analysis to characterize the exact asymptotic behavior that replaces that limit. Their results provide accurate estimates of training and test regression errors when all three dimensions are large. The analysis therefore connects the relative sizes of the data and feature representation to prediction performance, rather than treating the feature count as independently approaching infinity.

From these error estimates, the paper identifies two qualitatively different learning phases and precisely describes the transition between them. It derives the associated double-descent test-error curve from that transition. The results do not require strong assumptions about the data distribution, and the authors report close agreement with experiments on real-world datasets. The stated theory concerns this joint large-dimension regime.
summary.tldr: A joint large-dimension analysis of random Fourier feature regression explains its learning phase transition and resulting double-descent test error.

title: A random matrix analysis of random Fourier features: beyond the Gaussian kernel, a precise phase transition, and the corresponding double descent

abstract: Multi-task reinforcement learning (RL) aims to simultaneously learn policies for solving many tasks. Several prior works have found that relabeling past experience with different reward functions can improve sample efficiency. Relabeling methods typically pose the question: if, in hindsight, we assume that our experience was optimal for some task, for what task was it optimal? Inverse RL answers this question. In this paper we show that inverse RL is a principled mechanism for reusing experience across tasks. We use this idea to generalize goal-relabeling techniques from prior work to arbitrary types of reward functions. Our experiments confirm that relabeling data using inverse RL outperforms prior relabeling methods on goal-reaching tasks, and accelerates learning on more general multi-task settings where prior methods are not applicable, such as domains with discrete sets of rewards and those with linear reward functions.

paragraphs: Multi-task reinforcement learning aims to learn behavior for many tasks at once. Experience collected for one task may also be useful for another if it is assigned a different reward function. Earlier relabeling methods exploit this reuse, improving how much learning can be extracted from interactions that have already occurred.

The paper connects hindsight relabeling to inverse reinforcement learning. If an observed experience is treated as optimal for some task, inverse RL asks which task could explain it. The authors use this connection as a principled mechanism for assigning past experience to other tasks, extending goal-relabeling techniques to arbitrary types of reward functions.

Experiments show that inverse-RL relabeling outperforms earlier relabeling methods on goal-reaching tasks. It also accelerates learning in broader multi-task settings where those methods do not apply, including discrete sets of rewards and linear reward functions. The findings support using inferred task explanations to reuse experience beyond settings defined only by reaching a different goal.
summary.tldr: Inverse reinforcement learning provides a principled way to relabel past experience for reuse across tasks with diverse reward functions.

title: Rewriting History with Inverse RL: Hindsight Inference for Policy Improvement

abstract: Variance reduction techniques have been successfully applied to temporal-difference (TD) learning and help to improve the sample complexity in policy evaluation. However, the existing work applied variance reduction to either the less popular one time-scale TD algorithm or the two time-scale GTD algorithm but with a finite number of i.i.d.\ samples, and both algorithms apply to only the on-policy setting. In this work, we develop a variance reduction scheme for the two time-scale TDC algorithm in the off-policy setting and analyze its non-asymptotic convergence rate over both i.i.d.\ and Markovian samples. In the i.i.d setting, our algorithm achieves an improved sample complexity $\calO(\epsilon^{-\frac{3}{5}} \log{\epsilon}^{-1})$ over the state-of-the-art result $\calO(\epsilon^{-1} \log {\epsilon}^{-1})$. In the Markovian setting, our algorithm achieves the state-of-the-art sample complexity $\calO(\epsilon^{-1} \log {\epsilon}^{-1})$ that is near-optimal. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed variance-reduced TDC achieves a smaller asymptotic convergence error than both the conventional TDC and the variance-reduced TD.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation estimates how a policy performs from experience. In the off-policy setting, that experience can come from a different policy. This paper develops variance reduction for TDC, a temporal-difference method with two time scales, and studies convergence after a finite number of samples rather than only eventual limiting behavior.

The analysis covers both independent samples and Markovian samples, which capture sequential dependence. With independent samples, the reported sample-complexity bound improves from order epsilon to the minus one times log of inverse epsilon to order epsilon to the minus three-fifths times that logarithm. Here epsilon represents the target error tolerance.

For Markovian samples, the method achieves the state-of-the-art bound of order inverse epsilon times log of inverse epsilon, described as near-optimal. Experiments also show smaller asymptotic convergence error than conventional TDC and variance-reduced TD. The distinction between sampling regimes matters: the improved independent-sample rate and the near-optimal sequential-sample rate are separate results for the same proposed scheme.
summary.tldr: Variance-reduced off-policy TDC improves independent-sample complexity and achieves a near-optimal bound for Markovian samples.

title: Variance-Reduced Off-Policy TDC Learning: Non-Asymptotic Convergence Analysis

abstract: We study the problem of efficient adversarial attacks on tree based ensembles such as gradient boosting decision trees (GBDTs) and random forests (RFs). Since these models are non-continuous step functions and gradient does not exist, most existing efficient adversarial attacks are not applicable. Although decision-based black-box attacks can be applied, they cannot utilize the special structure of trees. In our work, we transform the attack problem into a discrete search problem specially designed for tree ensembles, where the goal is to find a valid ``leaf tuple'' that leads to mis-classification while having the shortest distance to the original input. With this formulation, we show that a simple yet effective greedy algorithm can be applied to iteratively optimize the adversarial example by moving the leaf tuple to its neighborhood within hamming distance 1. Experimental results on several large GBDT and RF models with up to hundreds of trees demonstrate that our method can be thousands of times faster than the previous mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) based approach, while also providing smaller (better) adversarial examples than decision-based black-box attacks on general $\ell_p$ ($p=1, 2, \infty$) norm perturbations.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find small input changes that make ensembles of decision trees misclassify. These models behave like step functions, so the gradients used by many efficient attacks are unavailable. Attacks based only on the model's decisions remain possible, but they do not take advantage of how trees organize their predictions.

The authors reformulate the task as a discrete search over leaf tuples: combinations of leaves reached across the ensemble. The goal is to find a valid combination that produces a wrong prediction while remaining close to the original input. A greedy algorithm improves the candidate by exploring neighboring tuples that differ in one position.

Experiments cover large gradient boosting and random forest models with up to hundreds of trees. The method can be thousands of times faster than a mixed-integer programming approach and finds smaller perturbations than decision-based black-box attacks under the tested distance measures. These findings show the practical value of designing attacks around the model's discrete structure.
summary.tldr: A discrete search over tree leaves produces fast, small adversarial perturbations for tree ensembles.

title: An Efficient Adversarial Attack for Tree Ensembles

abstract: Sampling is a fundamental and arguably very important task with numerous applications in Machine Learning. One approach to sample from a high dimensional distribution $e^{-f}$ for some function $f$ is the Langevin Algorithm (LA). Recently, there has been a lot of progress in showing fast convergence of LA even in cases where $f$ is non-convex, notably \cite{VW19}, \cite{MoritaRisteski} in which the former paper focuses on functions $f$ defined in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and the latter paper focuses on functions with symmetries (like matrix completion type objectives) with manifold structure. Our work generalizes the results of \cite{VW19} where $f$ is defined on a manifold $M$ rather than $\mathbb{R}^n$. From technical point of view, we show that KL decreases in a geometric rate whenever the distribution $e^{-f}$ satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality on $M$.

paragraphs: The Langevin algorithm is a method for sampling from a distribution described through a function f, with probability density proportional to exp(-f). Understanding how quickly it approaches that target distribution is important in high-dimensional sampling. This paper studies the case where the function is defined on a manifold, a space whose geometry need not be ordinary Euclidean geometry.

The work extends an earlier convergence analysis from Euclidean space to this manifold setting. Its central result concerns Kullback–Leibler divergence, a measure of discrepancy between the sampling distribution and the target. The authors show that this discrepancy decreases at a geometric rate whenever the target distribution satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality on the manifold.

The log-Sobolev condition is central to the stated guarantee: the result does not assert fast convergence for every manifold distribution. Its significance is that convergence can be analyzed using a property of the distribution together with the geometry of its domain. This broadens the theoretical setting for fast Langevin sampling beyond functions defined on ordinary vector spaces.
summary.tldr: Langevin sampling on a manifold achieves geometric decay in KL divergence when the target distribution satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality.

title: Fast Convergence of Langevin Dynamics on Manifold: Geodesics meet Log-Sobolev

abstract: Motivated by neuroscientific and clinical applications, we empirically examine whether observational measures of information flow can suggest interventions. We do so by performing experiments on artificial neural networks in the context of fairness in machine learning, where the goal is to induce fairness in the system through interventions. Using our recently developed M-information flow framework, we measure the flow of information about the true label (responsible for accuracy, and hence desirable), and separately, the flow of information about a protected attribute (responsible for bias, and hence undesirable) on the edges of a trained neural network. We then compare the flow magnitudes against the effect of intervening on those edges by pruning. We show that pruning edges that carry larger information flows about the protected attribute reduces bias at the output to a greater extent. This demonstrates that M-information flow can meaningfully suggest targets for interventions, answering the title's question in the affirmative. We also evaluate bias-accuracy tradeoffs for different intervention strategies, to analyze how one might use estimates of desirable and undesirable information flows (here, accuracy and bias flows) to inform interventions that preserve the former while reducing the latter.

paragraphs: Can observing what information travels through a neural network help identify where to intervene? This paper investigates that question empirically through fairness in artificial neural networks. The aim is to reduce information associated with a protected attribute while retaining information about the correct prediction. Neuroscientific and clinical applications motivate the question, but the experiments concern artificial networks.

Using the authors' M-information flow framework, the study separately measures information about the true label and the protected attribute along network edges. It then prunes edges and compares the resulting changes with the previously measured flows. This directly tests whether an observational measurement can help select useful intervention targets.

In the experiments, removing edges with larger protected-attribute information flows reduces output bias more strongly. The study also compares intervention strategies through their bias–accuracy tradeoffs. These results support using flow estimates to guide interventions in the tested setting, while showing why both kinds of information matter: reducing undesirable information must be considered alongside preserving information that supports accuracy.
summary.tldr: Experiments show that measured information flows can help identify neural-network edges whose removal reduces bias.

title: Can Information Flows Suggest Targets for Interventions in Neural Circuits?

abstract: We quantify the robustness of a trained network to input uncertainties with a stochastic simulation inspired by the field of Statistical Reliability Engineering. The robustness assessment is cast as a statistical hypothesis test: the network is deemed as locally robust if the estimated probability of failure is lower than a critical level.The procedure is based on an Importance Splitting simulation generating samples of rare events. We derive theoretical guarantees that are non-asymptotic w.r.t. sample size. Experiments tackling large scale networks outline the efficiency of our method making a low number of calls to the network function.

paragraphs: The paper assesses how robust a trained neural network is to uncertainty in its inputs. It formulates this assessment as a statistical hypothesis test: local robustness depends on whether the estimated probability of failure falls below a chosen critical level. This turns robustness assessment into a question about failure frequency under the input uncertainties being considered.

The procedure uses Importance Splitting, a stochastic simulation method for generating samples of rare events. Its role is to make failures accessible to estimation even when they occur infrequently. The approach draws on statistical reliability engineering, connecting neural-network evaluation to methods designed to assess systems whose failures may be rare.

The authors derive theoretical guarantees that apply at finite sample sizes, rather than only in a large-sample limit. Experiments involving large networks indicate that the assessment can be efficient while requiring relatively few network evaluations. The resulting robustness judgment is specifically statistical and local: it concerns a failure-probability threshold under the assessed uncertainties.
summary.tldr: Rare-event simulation enables efficient statistical tests of local neural-network robustness with finite-sample guarantees.

title: Efficient Statistical Assessment of Neural Network Corruption Robustness

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a popular distributed learning framework that trains a global model through iterative communications between a central server and edge devices. Recent works have demonstrated that FL is vulnerable to model poisoning attacks. Several server-based defense approaches (e.g. robust aggregation), have been proposed to mitigate such attacks. However, we empirically show that under extremely strong attacks, these defensive methods fail to guarantee the robustness of FL. More importantly, we observe that as long as the global model is polluted, the impact of attacks on the global model will remain in subsequent rounds even if there are no subsequent attacks. In this work, we propose a client-based defense, named White Blood Cell for Federated Learning (FL-WBC), which can mitigate model poisoning attacks that have already polluted the global model. The key idea of FL-WBC is to identify the parameter space where long-lasting attack effect on parameters resides and perturb that space during local training. Furthermore, we derive a certified robustness guarantee against model poisoning attacks and a convergence guarantee to FedAvg after applying our FL-WBC. We conduct experiments on FasionMNIST and CIFAR10 to evaluate the defense against state-of-the-art model poisoning attacks. The results demonstrate that our method can effectively mitigate model poisoning attack impact on the global model within 5 communication rounds with nearly no accuracy drop under both IID and Non-IID settings. Our defense is also complementary to existing server-based robust aggregation approaches and can further improve the robustness of FL under extremely strong attacks.

The findings support combining client-side repair with server-side defenses to improve robustness in the evaluated attack settings.
summary.tldr: FL-WBC perturbs client-side parameters associated with persistent poisoning effects to help repair corrupted federated models and complement server defenses.

title: FL-WBC: Enhancing Robustness against Model Poisoning Attacks in Federated Learning from a Client Perspective

abstract: The backpropagation networks are notably susceptible to catastrophic forgetting, where networks tend to forget previously learned skills upon learning new ones. To address such the 'sensitivity-stability' dilemma, most previous efforts have been contributed to minimizing the empirical risk with different parameter regularization terms and episodic memory, but rarely exploring the usages of the weight loss landscape. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between the weight loss landscape and sensitivity-stability in the continual learning scenario, based on which, we propose a novel method, Flattening Sharpness for Dynamic Gradient Projection Memory (FS-DGPM). In particular, we introduce a soft weight to represent the importance of each basis representing past tasks in GPM, which can be adaptively learned during the learning process, so that less important bases can be dynamically released to improve the sensitivity of new skill learning. We further introduce Flattening Sharpness (FS) to reduce the generalization gap by explicitly regulating the flatness of the weight loss landscape of all seen tasks. As demonstrated empirically, our proposed method consistently outperforms baselines with the superior ability to learn new skills while alleviating forgetting effectively.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a network to acquire new skills while retaining earlier ones. Ordinary training can overwrite previous learning, creating a tension between responsiveness to new tasks and stability on old tasks. This paper studies that tension through the shape of the loss landscape over network weights.

The proposed FS-DGPM method modifies gradient projection memory by giving each basis representing past tasks a learnable soft importance weight. Less important bases can then be released dynamically, creating more flexibility for learning new skills. This makes the protection assigned to past-task information adaptable during learning rather than uniformly fixed.

A second component, Flattening Sharpness, explicitly regulates the flatness of the weight loss landscape across all tasks seen so far, with the aim of reducing the generalization gap. The experiments report consistent improvements over baselines in learning new skills while alleviating forgetting. The method therefore combines adaptable memory constraints with control of landscape shape to address both sides of the continual-learning tradeoff.
summary.tldr: FS-DGPM combines adaptive protection of past-task directions with loss-landscape flattening to improve continual learning and reduce forgetting.

title: Flattening Sharpness for Dynamic Gradient Projection Memory Benefits Continual Learning

abstract: Change point detection is becoming increasingly popular in many application areas. On one hand, most of the theoretically-justified methods are investigated in an ideal setting without model violations, or merely robust against identical heavy-tailed noise distribution across time and/or against isolate outliers; on the other hand, we are aware that there have been exponentially growing attacks from adversaries, who may pose systematic contamination on data to purposely create spurious change points or disguise true change points. In light of the timely need for a change point detection method that is robust against adversaries, we start with, arguably, the simplest univariate mean change point detection problem. The adversarial attacks are formulated through the Huber $\varepsilon$-contamination framework, which in particular allows the contamination distributions to be different at each time point. In this paper, we demonstrate a phase transition phenomenon in change point detection. This detection boundary is a function of the contamination proportion~$\varepsilon$ and is the first time shown in the literature. In addition, we derive the minimax-rate optimal localisation error rate, quantifying the cost of accuracy in terms of the contamination proportion. We propose a computationally feasible method, matching the minimax lower bound under certain conditions, saving for logarithmic factors. Extensive numerical experiments are conducted with comparisons to robust change point detection methods in the existing literature.

paragraphs: Change point detection tries to locate shifts in a sequence's underlying behavior. This paper studies changes in the mean of a single-variable sequence when an adversary can contaminate observations. Such contamination can manufacture apparent changes or conceal genuine ones, making the problem different from handling isolated outliers or an unchanged heavy-tailed noise distribution.

The analysis uses Huber's contamination framework, with contamination proportion epsilon and contaminating distributions that may vary at every time point. It establishes a phase transition in detectability whose boundary depends on that proportion. The contribution therefore addresses both whether a change can be detected and how precisely its location can be estimated, while explicitly accounting for systematic contamination.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes how adversarial contamination limits mean-change detection and develops a method with conditionally near-optimal localization accuracy.

title: Adversarially Robust Change Point Detection

abstract: Transformers have shown great potential in various computer vision tasks owing to their strong capability in modeling long-range dependency using the self-attention mechanism. Nevertheless, vision transformers treat an image as 1D sequence of visual tokens, lacking an intrinsic inductive bias (IB) in modeling local visual structures and dealing with scale variance. Alternatively, they require large-scale training data and longer training schedules to learn the IB implicitly. In this paper, we propose a new Vision Transformer Advanced by Exploring intrinsic IB from convolutions, i.e., ViTAE. Technically, ViTAE has several spatial pyramid reduction modules to downsample and embed the input image into tokens with rich multi-scale context by using multiple convolutions with different dilation rates. In this way, it acquires an intrinsic scale invariance IB and is able to learn robust feature representation for objects at various scales. Moreover, in each transformer layer, ViTAE has a convolution block in parallel to the multi-head self-attention module, whose features are fused and fed into the feed-forward network. Consequently, it has the intrinsic locality IB and is able to learn local features and global dependencies collaboratively. Experiments on ImageNet as well as downstream tasks prove the superiority of ViTAE over the baseline transformer and concurrent works. Source code and pretrained models will be available at https://github.com/Annbless/ViTAE.

paragraphs: Vision transformers model long-range relationships through self-attention, but their treatment of images as token sequences does not inherently encode local visual structure or variation in object scale. ViTAE incorporates convolutional structure to provide these inductive biases directly. The motivation is to help the model represent useful image properties that would otherwise need to be learned implicitly.

Spatial pyramid reduction modules use convolutions with different dilation rates to downsample images and produce tokens containing context at multiple scales. Within each transformer layer, a convolution block runs alongside multi-head self-attention. Their features are fused before entering the feed-forward network, allowing local feature learning and global relationship modeling to work together.

The architecture's contribution is the combination of scale-oriented token construction with local processing throughout the transformer. The findings support incorporating convolution-derived biases into attention models so that representations can use both nearby visual structure and relationships across distant parts of an image.
summary.tldr: ViTAE combines multiscale convolutions and self-attention to give vision transformers built-in biases for locality and scale variation.

title: ViTAE: Vision Transformer Advanced by Exploring Intrinsic Inductive Bias

abstract: Continual learning (CL) learns a sequence of tasks incrementally. There are two popular CL settings, class incremental learning (CIL) and task incremental learning (TIL). A major challenge of CL is catastrophic forgetting (CF). While a number of techniques are already available to effectively overcome CF for TIL, CIL remains to be highly challenging. So far, little theoretical study has been done to provide a principled guidance on how to solve the CIL problem. This paper performs such a study. It first shows that probabilistically, the CIL problem can be decomposed into two sub-problems: Within-task Prediction (WP) and Task-id Prediction (TP). It further proves that TP is correlated with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, which connects CIL and OOD detection. The key conclusion of this study is that regardless of whether WP and TP or OOD detection are defined explicitly or implicitly by a CIL algorithm, good WP and good TP or OOD detection are necessary and sufficient for good CIL performances. Additionally, TIL is simply WP. Based on the theoretical result, new CIL methods are also designed, which outperform strong baselines in both CIL and TIL settings by a large margin.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a model on a sequence of tasks, creating the risk that new learning will erase earlier capabilities. The paper focuses on why class incremental learning remains difficult even when methods can effectively address forgetting in task incremental learning. It seeks a theoretical account of the capabilities needed for successful class incremental prediction.

The analysis decomposes class incremental learning probabilistically into prediction within a task and prediction of the task identity. It then establishes a connection between task identity prediction and out-of-distribution detection. This connects recognizing which task an input belongs to with recognizing whether it falls outside a task's distribution.

The central theoretical conclusion is that good within-task prediction together with good task identity prediction, or the associated out-of-distribution detection capability, is necessary and sufficient for good class incremental performance. These capabilities can be implicit in an algorithm. Task incremental learning corresponds to the within-task component. Guided by this result, the authors design methods that substantially outperform strong baselines in both settings.
summary.tldr: The paper connects successful class incremental learning to both within-task prediction and identifying the relevant task through out-of-distribution detection.

title: A Theoretical Study on Solving Continual Learning

abstract: Cryo-Electron Microscopy (Cryo-EM) is an important imaging method which allows high-resolution reconstruction of the 3D structures of biomolecules. It produces highly noisy 2D images by projecting a molecule's 3D density from random viewing directions. Because the projection directions are unknown, estimating the images' poses is necessary to perform the reconstruction. We focus on this task and study it under the group synchronization framework: if the relative poses of pairs of images can be approximated from the data, an estimation of the images' poses is given by the assignment which is most consistent with the relative ones.In particular, by studying the symmetries of cryo-EM, we show that relative poses in the group O(2) provide sufficient constraints to identify the images' poses, up to the molecule's chirality. With this in mind, we improve the existing multi-frequency vector diffusion maps (MFVDM) method: by using O(2) relative poses, our method not only predicts the similarity between the images' viewing directions but also recovers their poses. Hence, we can leverage all input images in a 3D reconstruction algorithm by initializing the poses with our estimation rather than just clustering and averaging the input images. We validate the recovery capabilities and robustness of our method on randomly generated synchronization graphs and a synthetic cryo-EM dataset.

paragraphs: Cryo-electron microscopy reconstructs molecular structures from noisy two-dimensional projections taken from unknown directions. Recovering the images' poses is therefore a key step. This paper studies pose estimation through group synchronization: combining approximate pairwise relationships into a globally consistent assignment of poses.

By examining the problem's symmetries, the authors show that relative poses in O(2), which includes planar rotations and reflections, provide sufficient constraints to identify image poses up to the molecule's chirality. That qualification leaves an ambiguity in handedness. They use this result to extend multi-frequency vector diffusion maps so that the method estimates poses as well as similarities between viewing directions.

Pose estimates can then initialize a three-dimensional reconstruction algorithm using all the input images, extending the method's role beyond clustering and averaging images. The authors validate recovery and robustness on randomly generated synchronization graphs and synthetic cryo-EM data. The contribution links a symmetry-based identification result to a more directly useful output for molecular reconstruction.
summary.tldr: Using O(2) pairwise relationships, an extended diffusion-map method recovers cryo-EM image poses up to molecular handedness and supports reconstruction initialization.

title: On the symmetries of the synchronization problem in Cryo-EM: Multi-Frequency Vector Diffusion Maps on the Projective Plane

abstract: Calibrated probabilistic classifiers are models whose predicted probabilities can directly be interpreted as uncertainty estimates. It has been shown recently that deep neural networks are poorly calibrated and tend to output overconfident predictions. As a remedy, we propose a low-bias, trainable calibration error estimator based on Dirichlet kernel density estimates, which asymptotically converges to the true $L_p$ calibration error. This novel estimator enables us to tackle the strongest notion of multiclass calibration, called canonical (or distribution) calibration, while other common calibration methods are tractable only for top-label and marginal calibration. The computational complexity of our estimator is $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$, the convergence rate is $\mathcal{O}(n^{-1/2})$, and it is unbiased up to $\mathcal{O}(n^{-2})$, achieved by a geometric series debiasing scheme. In practice, this means that the estimator can be applied to small subsets of data, enabling efficient estimation and mini-batch updates. The proposed method has a natural choice of kernel, and can be used to generate consistent estimates of other quantities based on conditional expectation, such as the sharpness of a probabilistic classifier. Empirical results validate the correctness of our estimator, and demonstrate its utility in canonical calibration error estimation and calibration error regularized risk minimization.

paragraphs: A classifier’s probabilities are useful as uncertainty estimates only when they are calibrated. This paper targets canonical calibration, which evaluates the full distribution of predicted class probabilities. That is a stronger requirement than checking only the most confident label or treating each class separately. The goal is to make this demanding notion practical to estimate and incorporate into training.

The authors build a differentiable estimator using Dirichlet kernel density estimates. Its estimates converge asymptotically to the true Lp calibration error, while a geometric series correction reduces bias. For n observations, the stated computational cost is quadratic, the convergence rate is proportional to n to the power of minus one-half, and the remaining bias is of order n to the power of minus two.

The low bias makes estimation on small data subsets practical, supporting mini-batch training updates. Experiments support the estimator’s correctness and its usefulness both for measuring canonical calibration and for adding calibration penalties to learning objectives. The framework also extends to other conditional-expectation quantities, including classifier sharpness.
summary.tldr: A differentiable, low-bias estimator makes full-distribution calibration measurable and usable as a training objective.

title: A Consistent and Differentiable Lp Canonical Calibration Error Estimator

abstract: Thanks to the powerful representation capabilities, transformers have made impressive progress in image restoration. However, existing transformers-based methods do not carefully consider the particularities of image restoration. In general, image restoration requires that an ideal approach should be translation-invariant to the degradation, i.e., the undesirable degradation should be removed irrespective of its position within the image. Furthermore, the local relationships also play a vital role, which should be faithfully exploited for recovering clean images. Nevertheless, most transformers either adopt local attention with the fixed local window strategy or global attention, which unfortunately breaks the translation invariance and causes huge loss of local relationships. To address these issues, we propose an elegant stochastic window strategy for transformers. Specifically, we first introduce the window partition with stochastic shift to replace the original fixed window partition for training. Then, we design a new layer expectation propagation algorithm to efficiently approximate the expectation of the induced stochastic transformer for testing. Our stochastic window transformer not only enjoys powerful representation but also maintains the desired property of translation invariance and locality. Experiments validate the stochastic window strategy consistently improves performance on various image restoration tasks (deraining, denoising and deblurring) by significant margins. The code is available at https://github.com/jiexiaou/Stoformer.

paragraphs: Image restoration should remove degradation wherever it occurs while preserving the local relationships needed to recover a clean image. The paper argues that common transformer attention designs do not adequately respect these requirements. Fixed local windows and global attention can compromise the desired translation behavior and use of local information.

The proposed stochastic window transformer changes how attention windows are placed. During training, it randomly shifts the window partition instead of always using a fixed arrangement. At test time, a layer expectation propagation algorithm efficiently approximates the expected behavior of the resulting stochastic transformer. This provides a practical way to use the randomized design during inference.

The authors report that the approach retains strong representation capabilities while maintaining translation invariance and locality. Experiments show consistent, significant improvements on deraining, denoising, and deblurring. The contribution is a change to the organization of attention that reflects the structure of restoration tasks: image position should not determine whether a degradation is removed, and nearby visual relationships should remain available for reconstructing clean content.
summary.tldr: Randomly shifted attention windows and efficient expectation-based inference improve transformer restoration across deraining, denoising, and deblurring.

title: Stochastic Window Transformer for Image Restoration

abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) can automatically design promising neural architectures without artificial experience. Though it achieves great success, prohibitively high search cost is required to find a high-performance architecture, which blocks its practical implementation. Neural predictor can directly evaluate the performance of neural networks based on their architectures and thereby save much budget. However, existing neural predictors require substantial annotated architectures trained from scratch, which still consume many computational resources. To solve this issue, we propose a Cross-Domain Predictor (CDP), which is trained based on the existing NAS benchmark datasets (e.g., NAS-Bench-101), but can be used to find high-performance architectures in large-scale search spaces. Particularly, we propose a progressive subspace adaptation strategy to address the domain discrepancy between the source architecture space and the target space. Considering the large difference between two architecture spaces, an assistant space is developed to smooth the transfer process. Compared with existing NAS methods, the proposed CDP is much more efficient. For example, CDP only requires the search cost of 0.1 GPU Days to find architectures with 76.9% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet and 97.51% on CIFAR-10.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search aims to automate the design of effective neural networks, but evaluating candidate architectures can require substantial computation. Performance predictors help by estimating quality from architecture alone. However, training those predictors often requires many architectures whose performance has already been measured by training them from scratch, leaving a costly preparation step.

The paper introduces a Cross-Domain Predictor that learns from existing architecture benchmark datasets and transfers to larger search spaces. The central challenge is that architectures in the training benchmark can differ substantially from those in the target space. The method uses progressive subspace adaptation to address this mismatch and introduces an intermediate assistant space to make the transfer more gradual.

The authors report much lower search costs than existing neural architecture search methods. Their example uses 0.1 GPU days of search to find architectures reaching 76.9% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet and 97.51% on CIFAR-10. The contribution is a way to reuse existing architecture-performance evidence across search spaces, reducing the need to build a predictor entirely from newly trained candidates.
summary.tldr: A performance predictor transfers knowledge from existing architecture benchmarks to larger search spaces through progressive adaptation.

title: Bridge the Gap Between Architecture Spaces via A Cross-Domain Predictor

abstract: Generalization bounds which assess the difference between the true risk and the empirical risk have been studied extensively. However, to obtain bounds, current techniques use strict assumptions such as a uniformly bounded or a Lipschitz loss function. To avoid these assumptions, in this paper, we follow an alternative approach: we relax uniform bounds assumptions by using on-average bounded loss and on-average bounded gradient norm assumptions. Following this relaxation, we propose a new generalization bound that exploits the contractivity of the log-Sobolev inequalities. These inequalities add an additional loss-gradient norm term to the generalization bound, which is intuitively a surrogate of the model complexity. We apply the proposed bound on Bayesian deep nets and empirically analyze the effect of this new loss-gradient norm term on different neural architectures.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds describe how far a model's performance on training data can differ from its performance on the underlying population. Many existing techniques require strong restrictions, such as a loss that is uniformly bounded or Lipschitz. This paper develops a bound using average restrictions on the loss and its gradient norm instead.

The derivation exploits the contractivity of log-Sobolev inequalities. This introduces an additional term involving the loss-gradient norm into the generalization bound. Intuitively, that term acts as a surrogate for model complexity: the analysis makes gradient magnitude an explicit part of how generalization is assessed. The assumptions are relaxed from uniform control to on-average control, so the result still relies on boundedness conditions of the latter kind.

The authors apply the bound to Bayesian deep neural networks and empirically examine the gradient-norm term across different architectures. The contribution therefore includes both a theoretical route under weaker forms of boundedness and an investigation of how the new term behaves in neural-network applications.
summary.tldr: A new generalization bound replaces uniform restrictions with average loss and gradient-norm assumptions and explicitly incorporates gradient magnitude.

title: On the Importance of Gradient Norm in PAC-Bayesian Bounds

abstract: Bilevel optimization (BO) is useful for solving a variety of important machine learning problems including but not limited to hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, continual learning, and reinforcement learning.Conventional BO methods need to differentiate through the low-level optimization process with implicit differentiation, which requires expensive calculations related to the Hessian matrix. There has been a recent quest for first-order methods for BO, but the methods proposed to date tend to be complicated and impractical for large-scale deep learning applications. In this work, we propose a simple first-order BO algorithm that depends only on first-order gradient information, requires no implicit differentiation, and is practical and efficient for large-scale non-convex functions in deep learning. We provide non-asymptotic convergence analysis of the proposed method to stationary points for non-convex objectives and present empirical results that show its superior practical performance.

There has been a recent quest for first-order methods for BO, but the methods proposed to date tend to be complicated and impractical for large-scale deep learning applications. In this work, we propose a simple first-order BO algorithm that depends only on first-order gradient information, requires no implicit differentiation, and is practical and efficient for large-scale non-convex functions in deep learning. paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves a learning problem whose objective depends on another optimization problem. It appears in tasks including hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, continual learning, and reinforcement learning. The paper addresses the computational difficulty of connecting these two levels, particularly when the underlying functions are large and non-convex, as in deep learning.

Conventional approaches use implicit differentiation and calculations involving the Hessian matrix to account for the lower-level optimization. BOME instead relies only on first-order gradients. The authors present it as a simple, practical algorithm that avoids implicit differentiation, addressing both computational expense and the complexity of earlier attempts to make bilevel methods depend only on first-order information.

The paper provides a non-asymptotic convergence analysis, meaning that its guarantees concern finite computational progress rather than only eventual behavior. Those guarantees target stationary points for non-convex objectives, not globally optimal solutions. Empirical results show superior practical performance in the reported comparisons. Together, the analysis and experiments support the claim that a simpler gradient-only approach can make bilevel optimization practical for large-scale deep-learning problems.
summary.tldr: BOME uses only first-order gradients for bilevel optimization, with finite-time stationary-point guarantees and strong reported practical performance.

title: BOME! Bilevel Optimization Made Easy: A Simple First-Order Approach

abstract: For exact 3D shape correspondence (matching or alignment), i.e., the task of matching each point on a shape to its exact corresponding point on the other shape (or to be more specific, matching at geodesic error 0), most existing methods do not perform well due to two main problems. First, on nearly-isometric shapes (i.e., low noise levels), most existing methods use the eigen-vectors (eigen-functions) of the Laplace Beltrami Operator (LBO) or other shape descriptors to update an initialized correspondence which is not exact, leading to an accumulation of update errors. Thus, though the final correspondence may generally be smooth, it is generally inexact. Second, on non-isometric shapes (noisy shapes), existing methods are generally not robust to noise as they usually assume near-isometry. In addition, existing methods that attempt to address the non-isometric shape problem (e.g., GRAMPA) are generally computationally expensive and do not generalise to nearly-isometric shapes. To address these two problems, we propose a 2D graph convolution-based framework called 2D-GEM. 2D-GEM is robust to noise on non-isometric shapes and with a few additional constraints, it also addresses the errors in the update on nearly-isometric shapes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of 2D-GEM by achieving a high accuracy of 90.5$\%$ at geodesic error 0 on the non-isometric benchmark SHREC16, i.e., TOPKIDS (while being much faster than GRAMPA), and on nearly-isometric benchmarks by achieving a high accuracy of 92.5$\%$ on TOSCA and 84.9$\%$ on SCAPE at geodesic error 0.

paragraphs: Exact shape correspondence means identifying the precise matching point on another 3D shape, measured here by zero geodesic error. The paper distinguishes this goal from obtaining a generally smooth alignment. It identifies accumulated update errors as a problem for nearly-isometric shapes, and sensitivity to noise as a problem when shapes depart from near-isometry.

The authors introduce 2D-GEM, a framework based on two-dimensional graph convolution. It is designed to handle noise in non-isometric shapes. With a few additional constraints, it also addresses correspondence-update errors in nearly-isometric shapes. This gives the framework a role in both settings, where existing approaches face different obstacles.

The reported exact-match accuracies are 90.5% on the non-isometric SHREC16 TOPKIDS benchmark, 92.5% on TOSCA, and 84.9% on SCAPE. The latter two are nearly-isometric benchmarks. On TOPKIDS, the method is also reported to be much faster than GRAMPA. These results show substantial success at the strict zero-error criterion, while the percentages make clear that exact matching is achieved for many points rather than every point.
summary.tldr: 2D-GEM uses graph convolution to improve exact point matching across noisy and nearly-isometric 3D shapes.

title: Exact Shape Correspondence via 2D graph convolution

abstract: There continues to be a trade-off between the biological realism and performance of neural networks. Contemporary deep learning techniques allow neural networks to be trained to perform challenging computations at (near) human-level, but these networks typically violate key biological constraints. More detailed models of biological neural networks can incorporate many of these constraints but typically suffer from subpar performance and trainability. Here, we narrow this gap by developing an effective method for training a canonical model of cortical neural circuits, the stabilized supralinear network (SSN), that in previous work had to be constructed manually or trained with undue constraints. SSNs are particularly challenging to train for the same reasons that make them biologically realistic: they are characterized by strongly-connected excitatory cells and expansive firing rate non-linearities that together make them prone to dynamical instabilities unless stabilized by appropriately tuned recurrent inhibition. Our method avoids such instabilities by initializing a small network and gradually increasing network size via the dynamics-neutral addition of neurons during training. We first show how SSNs can be trained to perform typical machine learning tasks by training an SSN on MNIST classification. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by training an SSN on the challenging task of performing amortized Markov chain Monte Carlo-based inference under a Gaussian scale mixture generative model of natural image patches with a rich and diverse set of basis functions -- something that was not possible with previous methods. These results open the way to training realistic cortical-like neural networks on challenging tasks at scale.

This paper develops a training method that addresses those instabilities while retaining the features that motivate the model.

The method begins with a small network and gradually adds neurons during training through dynamics-neutral growth. The latter uses amortized Markov chain Monte Carlo inference under a Gaussian scale mixture model with diverse basis functions, which previous methods could not support. These demonstrations establish new training capabilities and open a path toward more scalable, computationally capable cortical-like networks.
summary.tldr: Gradually growing stabilized supralinear networks without disturbing their dynamics enables training on classification and challenging natural-image inference.

title: Training stochastic stabilized supralinear networks by dynamics-neutral growth

abstract: We present Myriad, a testbed written in JAX which enables machine learning researchers to benchmark imitation learning and reinforcement learning algorithms against trajectory optimization-based methods in real-world environments. Myriad contains 17 optimal control problems presented in continuous time which span medicine, ecology, epidemiology, and engineering. As such, Myriad strives to serve as a stepping stone towards application of modern machine learning techniques for impactful real-world tasks. The repository also provides machine learning practitioners access to trajectory optimization techniques, not only for standalone use, but also for integration within a typical automatic differentiation workflow. Indeed, the combination of classical control theory and deep learning in a fully GPU-compatible package unlocks potential for new algorithms to arise. We present one such novel approach for use in dynamics learning and control tasks. Trained in a fully end-to-end fashion, our model leverages an implicit planning module over neural ordinary differential equations, enabling simultaneous learning and planning with unknown environment dynamics. All environments, optimizers and tools are available in the software package at \url{https://github.com/nikihowe/myriad}.

summary.tldr: Myriad provides 17 continuous-time control benchmarks and differentiable optimization tools, including an end-to-end approach to learning dynamics while planning.

title: Myriad: a real-world testbed to bridge trajectory optimization and deep learning

abstract: As governments and corporations adopt deep learning systems to collect and analyze user-generated audio data, concerns about security and privacy naturally emerge in areas such as automatic speaker recognition. While audio adversarial examples offer one route to mislead or evade these invasive systems, they are typically crafted through time-intensive offline optimization, limiting their usefulness in streaming contexts. Inspired by architectures for audio-to-audio tasks such as denoising and speech enhancement, we propose a neural network model capable of adversarially modifying a user's audio stream in real-time. Our model learns to apply a time-varying finite impulse response (FIR) filter to outgoing audio, allowing for effective and inconspicuous perturbations on a small fixed delay suitable for streaming tasks. We demonstrate our model is highly effective at de-identifying user speech from speaker recognition and able to transfer to an unseen recognition system. We conduct a perceptual study and find that our method produces perturbations significantly less perceptible than baseline anonymization methods, when controlling for effectiveness. Finally, we provide an implementation of our model capable of running in real-time on a single CPU thread. Audio examples and code can be found at https://interactiveaudiolab.github.io/project/voiceblock.html.

Adversarial audio often requires slow offline optimization, making it awkward for live streams. VoiceBlock instead trains an audio-to-audio neural network to modify outgoing speech in real time, drawing inspiration from speech enhancement and denoising architectures.

The model learns a time-varying finite impulse response filter that applies perturbations with a small, fixed delay. This design makes streaming operation part of the method itself. The authors demonstrate effective de-identification against speaker recognition and show that the modifications can transfer to an unseen recognition system.

A perceptual study compares the method with baseline anonymization approaches while controlling for effectiveness. Under that comparison, VoiceBlock's perturbations are significantly less perceptible. The authors also provide an implementation that runs in real time on a single CPU thread. Together, the findings address both identity disruption and practical listening and deployment requirements, showing that a learned audio transformation can combine low delay with relatively inconspicuous modifications.
summary.tldr: VoiceBlock modifies streaming speech in real time to disrupt speaker recognition with comparatively inconspicuous audio changes.

title: VoiceBlock: Privacy through Real-Time Adversarial Attacks with Audio-to-Audio Models

abstract: Evaluating the performance of machine learning models on diverse and underrepresented subgroups is essential for ensuring fairness and reliability in real-world applications. However, accurately assessing model performance becomes challenging due to two main issues: (1) a scarcity of test data, especially for small subgroups, and (2) possible distributional shifts in the model's deployment setting, which may not align with the available test data. In this work, we introduce 3S Testing, a deep generative modeling framework to facilitate model evaluation by generating synthetic test sets for small subgroups and simulating distributional shifts. Our experiments demonstrate that 3S-Testing outperforms traditional baselines---including real test data alone---in estimating model performance on minority subgroups and under plausible distributional shifts. In addition, 3S offers intervals around its performance estimates, exhibiting superior coverage of the ground truth compared to existing approaches. Overall, these results raise the question of whether we need a paradigm shift away from limited real test data towards synthetic test data.
