paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks learn by combining information from connected nodes. The paper argues that using the graph Laplacian norm to suppress information from immediate neighbors can weaken valuable interactions. When useful relationships are sparse, this dilution may slow their discovery during training and reduce predictive performance. The work targets that particular aggregation behavior.

BoostGCN is a linear graph convolutional model that instead amplifies significant interactions with first-order neighbors. Its aim is to make important local relationships easier to capture accurately and quickly. The method keeps linear aggregation while changing the emphasis placed on useful neighbor interactions, making the treatment of local information its central design choice.

Experiments on four real-world datasets show improvements over existing state-of-the-art graph convolutional models in both performance and efficiency. The authors also describe BoostGCN as having relatively fixed parameters, supporting ease of use. These results provide empirical support for amplification in the evaluated settings, linking the proposed handling of neighbor information to both prediction quality and the efficiency of learning.
summary.tldr: BoostGCN amplifies significant immediate-neighbor interactions and improves performance and efficiency on four real-world datasets.

title: Revolutionizing Graph Aggregation: From Suppression to Amplification via BoostGCN

abstract: Selection bias poses a widely recognized challenge for unbiased evaluation and learning in many industrial scenarios. For example, in recommender systems, it arises from the users' selective interactions with items. Recently, doubly robust and its variants have been widely studied to achieve debiased learning of prediction models, however, all of them consider a simple exact matching scenario, i.e., the units (such as user-item pairs in a recommender system) are the same between the training and test sets. In practice, there may be limited or even no overlap in units between the training and test. In this paper, we consider a more practical scenario: the joint distribution of the feature and rating is the same in the training and test sets. Theoretical analysis shows that the previous DR estimator is biased even if the imputed errors and learned propensities are correct in this scenario. In addition, we propose a novel super-population doubly robust estimator (SuperDR), which can achieve a more accurate estimation and desirable generalization error bound compared to the existing DR estimators, and extend the joint learning algorithm for training the prediction and imputation models. We conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets, including a large-scale industrial dataset, to show the effectiveness of our method. The code is available at https://github.com/ChunyuanZheng/neurips-25-SuperDR.

paragraphs: Selection bias appears when observed data reflect selective behavior, such as users choosing which items to interact with. Doubly robust estimators are widely used to correct this bias. This paper examines an additional problem: existing approaches assume the same individual units appear in training and testing, although real datasets may contain little or no overlap.

The authors instead assume that training and test data share the joint distribution of features and ratings. Under this setting, they show that the previous doubly robust estimator remains biased even when its imputed errors and learned observation propensities are correct. The issue therefore involves how the datasets relate, beyond the accuracy of those correction components.

The proposed SuperDR estimator is designed for this population-based setting, with improved estimation and a favorable generalization-error bound compared with existing doubly robust estimators. The paper also extends joint training of the prediction and imputation models. Experiments on three real-world datasets, including a large industrial dataset, support its effectiveness. The contribution clarifies why correcting selective observations also requires accounting for sampling differences between training and evaluation units.
summary.tldr: SuperDR addresses bias that persists in existing doubly robust estimators when training and test units differ despite sharing a feature–rating distribution.

title: Unveiling Extraneous Sampling Bias with Data Missing-Not-At-Random

abstract: We study the problem of computing an optimal large language model (LLM) policy for the constrained alignment problem, where the goal is to maximize a primary reward objective while satisfying constraints on secondary utilities. Despite the popularity of Lagrangian-based LLM policy search in constrained alignment, iterative primal-dual methods often fail to converge, and non-iterative dual-based methods do not achieve optimality in the LLM parameter space. To address these challenges, we employ Lagrangian duality to develop an iterative dual-based alignment method that alternates between updating the LLM policy via Lagrangian maximization and updating the dual variable via dual descent. In theory, we characterize the primal-dual gap between the primal value in the distribution space and the dual value in the LLM parameter space. We further quantify the optimality gap of the learned LLM policies at near-optimal dual variables with respect to both the objective and the constraint functions. These results prove that dual-based alignment methods can find an optimal constrained LLM policy, up to an LLM parametrization gap. We demonstrate the effectiveness and merits of our approach through extensive experiments conducted on the PKU-SafeRLHF and Anthropic HH-RLHF datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies alignment as a constrained optimization problem: improve a language model's primary reward while meeting requirements on secondary utilities. The difficulty is finding a policy that balances both goals reliably. The authors identify shortcomings in existing approaches: iterative primal-dual methods can fail to converge, while non-iterative dual methods do not achieve optimality within the model's parameter space.

Their method alternates between two updates. First, it improves the language model using a Lagrangian objective, which combines the primary reward with weighted constraint terms. Then it adjusts the dual variables that control those weights through dual descent. This creates an iterative procedure for coordinating policy improvement with the importance assigned to constraint satisfaction.

The theoretical analysis connects optimization over distributions with optimization over parameterized language models. It also bounds objective and constraint errors near optimal dual variables. The resulting optimality claim is qualified by an LLM parametrization gap: what the model can represent remains relevant. Experiments on PKU-SafeRLHF and Anthropic HH-RLHF demonstrate the approach's effectiveness.
summary.tldr: An iterative dual-based alignment method optimizes rewards under utility constraints, with guarantees qualified by the language model's parametrization gap.

title: Alignment of Large Language Models with Constrained Learning

abstract: Learn to Optimize (L2O) trains deep neural network-based solvers for optimization, achieving success in accelerating convex problems and improving non-convex solutions. However, L2O lacks rigorous theoretical backing for its own training convergence, as existing analyses often use unrealistic assumptions-a gap this work highlights empirically. We bridge this gap by proving the training convergence of L2O models that learn Gradient Descent (GD) hyperparameters for quadratic programming, leveraging the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) theory. We propose a deterministic initialization strategy to support our theoretical results and promote stable training over extended optimization horizons by mitigating gradient explosion. Our L2O framework demonstrates over 50% better optimality than GD and superior robustness over state-of-the-art L2O methods on synthetic datasets. The code of our method can be found from https://github.com/NetX-lab/MathL2OProof-Official.

paragraphs: Learning to optimize trains a neural network to help solve optimization problems. Although such systems can work well empirically, understanding whether their own training converges is a separate challenge. This paper argues that earlier analyses often depend on unrealistic assumptions and presents empirical evidence highlighting that gap.

The authors prove training convergence for models that learn gradient-descent hyperparameters for quadratic programming. Their analysis uses Neural Tangent Kernel theory. They also propose deterministic initialization to support the proof and improve stability when the learned optimizer runs over longer horizons, specifically by mitigating exploding gradients.

On synthetic datasets, the framework reports more than 50% better optimality than gradient descent and stronger robustness than state-of-the-art learned optimization methods. The theoretical contribution concerns the training of the learned optimizer in the quadratic-programming setting; the experiments show how the proposed design performs in the tested problems. Together, the analysis and initialization strategy give a more grounded account of why this particular form of learned optimization can train successfully and improve solutions.
summary.tldr: The paper proves training convergence for learned gradient-descent hyperparameters in quadratic programming and reports improved synthetic-task results.

title: Learning Provably Improves the Convergence of Gradient Descent

abstract: We consider the problem of preprocessing an $n\times n$ matrix $\mathbf{M}$, and supporting queries that, for any vector $v$, returns the matrix-vector product $\mathbf{M} v$. This problem has been extensively studied in both theory and practice: on one side, practitioners have developed algorithms that are highly efficient in practice, whereas on the other side, theoreticians have proven that the problem cannot be solved faster than naive multiplication in the worst-case. This lower bound holds even in the average-case, implying that existing average-case analyses cannot explain this gap between theory and practice. Hence, we study the problem for \emph{structured} matrices. We show that for $n\times n$ Boolean matrices of VC-dimension $d$, the matrix-vector multiplication problem can be solved with $\smash{\tilde{O}(n^2)}$ preprocessing and $\smash{\tilde O(n^{2-1/d})}$ query time. Given the low constant VC-dimensions observed in most real-world data, our results posit an explanation for why the problem can be solved so much faster in practice. Furthermore, we show how to extend this result to the non-Boolean setting with the Pollard pseudodimension. Our results yield the first non-trivial upper bounds for many applications. In previous works, the online matrix-vector (OMv) hypothesis (conjecturing that quadratic time is needed per query, even over the boolean semi-ring) was used to prove many conditional lower bounds, showing that it is impossible to compute and maintain high-accuracy estimates for effective resistance, Laplacian solvers, shortest paths, and triangle detection in graphs subject to node insertions and deletions in subquadratic time. Yet, via a reduction to our matrix-vector-multiplication result, we show we can maintain these problems efficiently if the input is structured, providing the first subquadratic upper bounds in the high-accuracy regime.

paragraphs: Matrix-vector multiplication can be fast in practice even though worst-case and existing average-case analyses give strong barriers to improvement. This paper investigates whether structure in the matrix explains part of that gap. It studies preprocessing a fixed matrix so that products with subsequently supplied vectors can be answered efficiently.

For an n-by-n Boolean matrix with VC-dimension d, the authors obtain preprocessing time of approximately n squared and query time of approximately n raised to 2 minus 1/d, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The improvement depends on the structural dimension. Since low constant VC-dimensions are observed in much real-world data, the result offers a possible explanation for practical speedups. The authors also extend the approach beyond Boolean matrices using Pollard pseudodimension.

Reductions transfer these gains to dynamic graph problems involving effective resistance, Laplacian solvers, shortest paths, and triangle detection. The paper obtains subquadratic bounds in the high-accuracy regime when the input is structured. These results identify settings where structural restrictions permit efficient algorithms despite conditional lower bounds for more general inputs.
summary.tldr: Low structural dimension enables faster matrix-vector queries and subquadratic algorithms for related dynamic graph problems.

title: The Structural Complexity of Matrix-Vector Multiplication

abstract: We propose L2T, an advancement of visual instruction tuning (VIT). While VIT equips Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) with promising multimodal capabilities, the current design choices for VIT often result in overfitting and shortcut learning, potentially degrading performance. This gap arises from an overemphasis on instruction-following abilities, while neglecting the proactive understanding of visual information. Inspired by this, L2T adopts a simple yet effective approach by incorporating the loss function into both the instruction and response sequences. It seamlessly expands the training data, and regularizes the MLLMs from overly relying on language priors. Based on this merit, L2T achieves a significant relative improvement of up to 9% on comprehensive multimodal benchmarks, requiring no additional training data and incurring negligible computational overhead. Surprisingly, L2T attains exceptional fundamental visual capabilities, yielding up to an 18% improvement in captioning performance, while simultaneously alleviating hallucination in MLLMs. Github code: https://github.com/Feng-Hong/L2T.

paragraphs: Visual instruction tuning teaches multimodal language models to respond to instructions involving images. The paper argues that common training choices can overemphasize instruction following and encourage shortcuts, leaving models overly dependent on language patterns rather than visual understanding. This can produce overfitting and weaker performance.

L2T changes the training objective by applying the loss to both instruction and response sequences. Instructions therefore contribute directly to the learning signal alongside answers. The authors describe this as expanding the effective use of existing training data and regularizing reliance on language priors. The change requires no additional training examples and adds negligible computational overhead.

On comprehensive multimodal benchmarks, the authors report relative improvements of up to 9%. They also report captioning improvements of up to 18% and reduced hallucination. These findings connect a small change in where training loss is applied with improvements in both broad multimodal performance and fundamental visual capabilities. The results support using more of each training example to encourage visual understanding, with the reported gains varying across evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: L2T trains on both instructions and responses, improving evaluated visual capabilities and reducing hallucination without additional training data.

title: Learning to Instruct for Visual Instruction Tuning

abstract: Existing vision tokenization isolates the optimization of vision tokenizers from downstream training, implicitly assuming the visual tokens can generalize well across various tasks, e.g., image generation and visual question answering. The vision tokenizer optimized for low-level reconstruction is agnostic to downstream tasks requiring varied representations and semantics. This decoupled paradigm introduces a critical misalignment: The loss of the vision tokenization can be the representation bottleneck for target tasks. For example, errors in tokenizing text in a given image lead to poor results when recognizing or generating them. To address this, we propose ETT, an end-to-end vision tokenizer tuning approach that enables joint optimization between vision tokenization and target autoregressive tasks. Unlike prior autoregressive models that use only discrete indices from a frozen vision tokenizer, ETT leverages the visual embeddings of the tokenizer codebook, and optimizes the vision tokenizers end-to-end with both reconstruction and caption objectives. ETT can be seamlessly integrated into existing training pipelines with minimal architecture modifications. Our ETT is simple to implement and integrate, without the need to adjust the original codebooks or architectures of the employed large language models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed end-to-end vision tokenizer tuning unlocks significant performance gains, i.e., 2-6% for multimodal understanding and visual generation tasks compared to frozen tokenizer baselines, while preserving the original reconstruction capability. We hope this very simple and strong method can empower multimodal foundation models besides image generation and understanding.

paragraphs: A vision tokenizer trained only to reconstruct images may discard information important for later tasks, such as reading or generating text inside an image. Existing pipelines often freeze that tokenizer and assume its discrete codes are suitable for all downstream uses. ETT directly addresses this mismatch.

The method uses embeddings from the tokenizer’s codebook and jointly optimizes tokenization with reconstruction and caption objectives. It integrates with existing autoregressive training pipelines through small architectural changes, without redesigning the original codebooks or the language model.

Experiments report gains of 2–6% in multimodal understanding and visual generation relative to frozen-tokenizer baselines while preserving reconstruction ability. The finding makes tokenization part of task learning rather than a fixed preprocessing choice: improving the downstream model alone cannot recover visual information that its input representation has already lost.
summary.tldr: ETT jointly tunes visual tokenization with downstream autoregressive tasks to reduce representation bottlenecks.

title: End-to-End Vision Tokenizer Tuning

abstract: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has recently gained considerable attention as a method for reconstructing dynamic scenes. Despite achieving superior quality, 4DGS typically requires substantial storage and suffers from slow rendering speed. In this work, we delve into these issues and identify two key sources of temporal redundancy. (Q1) \textbf{Short-Lifespan Gaussians}: 4DGS uses a large portion of Gaussians with short temporal span to represent scene dynamics, leading to an excessive number of Gaussians. (Q2) \textbf{Inactive Gaussians}: When rendering, only a small subset of Gaussians contributes to each frame. Despite this, all Gaussians are processed during rasterization, resulting in redundant computation overhead. To address these redundancies, we present \textbf{4DGS-1K}, which runs at over 1000 FPS on modern GPUs. For Q1, we introduce the Spatial-Temporal Variation Score, a new pruning criterion that effectively removes short-lifespan Gaussians while encouraging 4DGS to capture scene dynamics using Gaussians with longer temporal spans. For Q2, we store a mask for active Gaussians across consecutive frames, significantly reducing redundant computations. Compared to vanilla 4DGS, our method achieves a $41\times$ reduction in storage and $9\times$ faster rasterization on complex dynamic scenes, while maintaining comparable visual quality.

paragraphs: Representing a moving scene with 4D Gaussian Splatting can produce high visual quality, but storing and rendering that representation is expensive. This paper identifies two sources of wasted work: many Gaussians represent only brief moments, and rendering processes Gaussians even when they contribute nothing to the current frame.

The proposed system, 4DGS-1K, addresses these problems separately. A Spatial-Temporal Variation Score guides pruning of short-lived Gaussians while encouraging the representation to describe motion using Gaussians that remain useful longer. An activity mask records which Gaussians contribute across consecutive frames, allowing rendering to avoid substantial computation on inactive elements.

On complex dynamic scenes, the authors report 41-fold lower storage requirements and ninefold faster rasterization than vanilla 4DGS, with comparable visual quality. The system exceeds 1,000 frames per second on modern GPUs. These findings show how reducing redundancy across time can improve both the compactness of a scene representation and the speed of producing its frames.
summary.tldr: 4DGS-1K reduces temporal redundancy to render dynamic scenes above 1,000 FPS while substantially cutting storage and preserving comparable visual quality.

title: 1000+ FPS 4D Gaussian Splatting for Dynamic Scene Rendering

abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) offers a flexible and general approach to performing Bayesian inference: In SBI, a neural network is trained on synthetic data simulated from a model and used to rapidly infer posterior distributions for observed data. A key goal for SBI is to achieve accurate inference with as few simulations as possible, especially for expensive simulators. In this work, we address this challenge by repurposing recent probabilistic foundation models for tabular data: We show how tabular foundation models---specifically TabPFN---can be used as pre-trained autoregressive conditional density estimators for SBI. We propose Neural Posterior Estimation with Prior-data Fitted Networks (NPE-PFN) and show that it is competitive with current SBI approaches in terms of accuracy for both benchmark tasks and two complex scientific inverse problems. Crucially, it often substantially outperforms them in terms of simulation efficiency, sometimes requiring orders of magnitude fewer simulations. NPE-PFN eliminates the need for selecting and training an inference network and tuning its hyperparameters. We also show that it exhibits superior robustness to model misspecification and can be scaled to simulation budgets that exceed the context size limit of TabPFN. NPE-PFN provides a new direction for SBI, where training-free, general-purpose inference models offer efficient, easy-to-use, and flexible solutions for a wide range of stochastic inverse problems.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference uses synthetic examples from a simulator to infer plausible model parameters from observed data. Typically, this involves training a neural network to estimate a posterior distribution. When simulations are expensive, the number required can become a major obstacle, alongside the work of choosing and tuning the inference network.

NPE-PFN repurposes TabPFN, a pretrained foundation model for tabular data, as a conditional density estimator. It uses an autoregressive formulation to estimate posterior distributions without selecting and training a new inference network for each task. This shifts the inference procedure toward using an already trained general-purpose model with the available simulated examples.

Across benchmark tasks and two complex scientific inverse problems, the method achieves accuracy competitive with current simulation-based approaches. It often needs substantially fewer simulations, with reductions of orders of magnitude in some cases. The authors also report better robustness to model misspecification and show how to use simulation budgets larger than TabPFN's context limit. These findings suggest a practical route to reducing both simulation costs and inference-model development effort.
summary.tldr: NPE-PFN uses pretrained TabPFN for Bayesian inference, often reducing simulation requirements while avoiding task-specific inference-network training.

title: Effortless, Simulation-Efficient Bayesian Inference using Tabular Foundation Models

abstract: Recent progress in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) has enabled promising applications in medical tasks, such as report generation and visual question answering. However, existing benchmarks focus mainly on the final diagnostic answer, offering limited insight into whether models engage in clinically meaningful reasoning. To address this, we present CheXStruct and CXReasonBench, a structured pipeline and benchmark built on the publicly available MIMIC-CXR-JPG dataset. CheXStruct automatically derives a sequence of intermediate reasoning steps directly from chest X-rays, such as segmenting anatomical regions, deriving anatomical landmarks and diagnostic measurements, computing diagnostic indices, and applying clinical thresholds. CXReasonBench leverages this pipeline to evaluate whether models can perform clinically valid reasoning steps and to what extent they can learn from structured guidance, enabling fine-grained and transparent assessment of diagnostic reasoning.The benchmark comprises 18,988 QA pairs across 12 diagnostic tasks and 1,200 cases, each paired with up to 4 visual inputs, and supports multi-path, multi-stage evaluation including visual grounding via anatomical region selection and diagnostic measurements.Even the strongest of 12 evaluated LVLMs struggle with structured reasoning and generalization, often failing to link abstract knowledge with anatomically grounded visual interpretation. The code is available at https://github.com/ttumyche/CXReasonBench

paragraphs: A correct diagnostic answer does not reveal whether a vision-language model can connect medical knowledge to the anatomy visible in an X-ray. This work introduces CheXStruct and CXReasonBench to evaluate that connection through intermediate steps. Both are built on the publicly available MIMIC-CXR-JPG dataset.

CheXStruct automatically derives a structured sequence from chest images: anatomical segmentation, landmarks and measurements, diagnostic indices, and application of clinical thresholds. CXReasonBench uses this pipeline to test whether models can carry out clinically meaningful steps and learn from structured guidance. Its evaluations include selecting anatomical regions and making diagnostic measurements across multiple stages and reasoning paths.

The benchmark contains 18,988 question-answer pairs covering 12 diagnostic tasks and 1,200 cases, with up to four visual inputs per case. All 12 evaluated models, including the strongest, struggle with structured reasoning and generalization. Their difficulty linking abstract knowledge to anatomically grounded interpretation shows why assessing intermediate reasoning provides information that final-answer evaluation alone can miss.
summary.tldr: CXReasonBench evaluates anatomical and measurement-based reasoning in chest X-rays, exposing difficulties even in the strongest of 12 tested vision-language models.

title: CXReasonBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Structured Diagnostic Reasoning in Chest X-rays

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$, where the pairs $(X,Y)$ are not observed together, but are instead separated co-ordinate-wise at two servers: server 1 contains all the $X$ observations, and server 2 contains the corresponding $Y$ observations. In this vertically distributed setting, we assume that each server has its own privacy constraints, owing to which they can only share suitably privatized statistics of their own component observations. We consider differing privacy budgets $(\varepsilon_1,\delta_1)$ and $(\varepsilon_2,\delta_2)$ for the two servers and determine the minimax optimal rates for correlation estimation allowing for both non-interactive and interactive mechanisms. We also provide correlation estimators that achieve these rates and further develop inference procedures, namely, confidence intervals, for the estimated correlations. Our results are characterized by an interesting rate in terms of the sample size $n$, $\varepsilon_1$, $\varepsilon_2$, which is strictly slower than the usual central privacy estimation rates. More interestingly, we find that the interactive mechanism is always better than its non-interactive counterpart whenever the two privacy budgets are different. Results from extensive numerical experiments support our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Estimating correlation usually relies on jointly observing two measurements for each sample. This paper studies a setting where one server holds all X measurements and another holds the corresponding Y measurements. Each server has its own privacy constraints and can share only appropriately privatized statistics of its component.

The authors allow the servers to have different privacy budgets and analyze both interactive and non-interactive communication. They determine minimax-optimal estimation rates, meaning the best achievable worst-case error rates in the studied setting, and construct estimators that attain them. They also develop confidence intervals so the estimated correlations can be accompanied by quantified uncertainty.

The resulting rates depend on sample size and both privacy budgets and are strictly slower than the usual central-privacy rates. Within the analyzed setting, interaction is always better than non-interactive communication when the privacy budgets differ. Numerical experiments support the theory. The findings identify both a statistical cost of keeping paired data separated and a benefit of allowing communication to adapt across servers.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal private correlation-estimation rates across two servers and shows interaction helps when their privacy budgets differ.

title: When Data Can't Meet: Estimating Correlation Across Privacy Barriers

abstract: Identifying the functional identity of individual neurons is essential for interpreting circuit dynamics, yet it remains a major challenge in large-scale _in vivo_ recordings where anatomical and molecular labels are often unavailable. Here we introduce NuCLR, a self-supervised framework that learns context-aware representations of neuron identity by modeling each neuron's role within the broader population. NuCLR employs a spatio-temporal transformer that captures both within-neuron dynamics and across-neuron interactions. It is trained with a sample-wise contrastive objective that encourages temporally-stable and discriminative embeddings. Across multiple open-access datasets, NuCLR outperforms prior methods in both cell type and brain region classification. Critically, it exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to entirely new populations, without any retraining or access to stimulus labels. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our framework scales effectively with data size. Overall, our results demonstrate that modeling population context is crucial for understanding neuron identity and that rich signal for cell-typing and neuron localization is present in neural activity alone. Code available at: https://github.com/nerdslab/nuclr.

paragraphs: Identifying a neuron's functional identity is difficult when large-scale recordings lack anatomical or molecular labels. NuCLR approaches this through recorded activity, treating a neuron's relationship to the surrounding population as useful evidence about its identity. The aim is to learn representations that capture more than an isolated activity trace.

A spatio-temporal transformer models both changes within each neuron's activity and interactions across neurons. Training uses a self-supervised contrastive objective to encourage representations that remain stable over time while distinguishing neurons. This connects the desired representation to persistent identity information rather than only momentary fluctuations in activity.

Across multiple open-access datasets, NuCLR outperforms prior methods on cell-type and brain-region classification. It also generalizes to entirely new populations without retraining or stimulus labels, and its performance scales effectively with data size. The results support population context as an important source of information for interpreting neuron identity, showing that activity recordings contain useful signals for both cell typing and localization.
summary.tldr: NuCLR learns neuron identity from individual activity and population interactions, generalizing to new populations without retraining.

title: Know Thyself by Knowing Others: Learning Neuron Identity from Population Context

abstract: The increasing utilization of graph databases across various fields stems from their capacity to represent intricate interconnections. Nonetheless, exploiting the full capabilities of graph databases continues to be a significant hurdle, largely because of the inherent difficulty in translating natural language into Cypher. Recognizing the critical role of schema selection in database query generation and drawing inspiration from recent progress in reasoning-augmented approaches trained through reinforcement learning to enhance inference capabilities and generalization, we introduce Cypher-RI, a specialized framework for the Text-to-Cypher task. Distinct from conventional approaches, our methodology seamlessly integrates schema selection within the Cypher generation pipeline, conceptualizing it as a critical element in the reasoning process. The schema selection mechanism is guided by textual context, with its outcomes recursively shaping subsequent inference processes. Impressively, our 7B-parameter model, trained through this RL paradigm, demonstrates superior performance compared to baselines, exhibiting a 9.41\% accuracy improvement over GPT-4o on CypherBench. These results underscore the effectiveness of our proposed reinforcement learning framework, which integrates schema selection to enhance both the accuracy and reasoning capabilities in Text-to-Cypher tasks.

paragraphs: Turning a natural-language request into a graph database query requires understanding both the request and the database structure. Selecting the relevant schema is therefore an important part of producing correct Cypher. Cypher-RI makes this selection part of the model's reasoning process, connecting it directly to query generation throughout the pipeline.

The framework uses reinforcement learning to train this integrated behavior. Textual context guides schema selection, and the selected schema feeds back into subsequent reasoning. This recursive relationship matters because decisions about which parts of the database are relevant can shape how the request is interpreted and expressed as a query.

The authors evaluate a seven-billion-parameter model trained with this approach and report stronger performance than the compared baselines. On CypherBench, they report a 9.41% accuracy improvement over GPT-4o. The finding supports incorporating schema selection into learned reasoning for Text-to-Cypher, with the reported advantage specifically demonstrated in the benchmark comparison described by the paper.
summary.tldr: Cypher-RI uses reinforcement learning to integrate schema selection into query reasoning, improving Text-to-Cypher accuracy on CypherBench.

title: Cypher-RI: Reinforcement Learning for Integrating Schema Selection into Cypher Generation

abstract: Learning rules—prescriptions for updating model parameters to improve performance—are typically assumed rather than derived. Why do some learning rules work better than others, and under what assumptions can a given rule be considered optimal? We propose a theoretical framework that casts learning rules as policies for navigating (partially observable) loss landscapes, and identifies optimal rules as solutions to an associated optimal control problem. A range of well-known rules emerge naturally within this framework under different assumptions: gradient descent from short-horizon optimization, momentum from longer-horizon planning, natural gradients from accounting for parameter space geometry, non-gradient rules from partial controllability, and adaptive optimizers like Adam from online Bayesian inference of loss landscape shape. We further show that continual learning strategies like weight resetting can be understood as optimal responses to task uncertainty. By unifying these phenomena under a single objective, our framework clarifies the computational structure of learning and offers a principled foundation for designing adaptive algorithms.

paragraphs: Learning algorithms prescribe how model parameters should change, but those prescriptions are often taken as starting points. This paper asks when particular update rules can be derived as optimal decisions. It treats learning as navigation through a partially observed loss landscape, with parameter updates acting as a policy in an optimal control problem.

Different assumptions produce different familiar rules. Short-horizon optimization yields gradient descent, while longer-horizon planning yields momentum. Accounting for parameter-space geometry leads to natural gradients, and partial controllability leads to non-gradient rules. Adaptive optimizers such as Adam arise through online Bayesian inference about the landscape's shape. The framework connects each rule to the information and planning structure under which it emerges.

The authors also interpret continual-learning strategies such as resetting weights as optimal responses to task uncertainty. The contribution is a unified account of why several learning behaviors can be appropriate under particular assumptions. It offers a basis for designing adaptive algorithms by making those assumptions explicit, rather than claiming one update rule is optimal in every setting.
summary.tldr: The paper derives familiar learning rules as optimal loss-landscape navigation policies under different planning, geometry, information, and uncertainty assumptions.

title: Gradient Descent as Loss Landscape Navigation: a Normative Framework for Deriving Learning Rules

abstract: Large language models with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures achieve efficiency and scalability, yet their routing mechanisms introduce safety alignment challenges insufficiently addressed by techniques developed for dense models. In this work, the MoE-specific safety risk of positional vulnerability—that safety-aligned behaviors rely on specific expert modules—is formalized and systematically analyzed. An analytical framework, SAFEx, is presented to robustly identify, characterize, and validate safety-critical experts via a stability-based expert selection procedure, and to decompose them into two functional groups: the Harmful Content Detection Group (HCDG), which specializes in identifying and recognizing harmful content within user inputs, and the Harmful Response Control Group (HRCG), which specializes in controlling and enforcing model behaviors to generate appropriate safety responses. Expert-level interventions are conducted to probe causality and to test mitigation. Targeted masking of SAFEx-selected experts reveals that safety behavior is highly concentrated. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, configured with 48 MoE-FFN layers and 128 experts per layer under top-8 routing (48×128=6,144 experts in total), disabling 12 selected experts reduces the refusal rate by 22%. In addition, lightweight adaptation is performed using LoRA under three configurations—the HRCG, the union of HCDG and HRCG, and all experts—and the resulting updates are composed through negative weight merging targeted at the HRCG, leading to improved refusal under adversarial prompts without full-model retraining. These results establish positional vulnerability as a distinct MoE-specific safety challenge and provide a practical, compute-efficient pathway for expert-level safety interventions within routed architectures.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts language models route computation through selected expert modules. SAFEx investigates a safety risk associated with this structure: aligned behavior may depend heavily on particular experts. The paper calls this positional vulnerability and develops a stability-based procedure for identifying and validating experts important to safety.

The framework distinguishes experts involved in detecting harmful user content from experts involved in controlling the model’s response. Targeted interventions test the causal role of the selected modules. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, which has 6,144 experts across its MoE layers, disabling 12 selected experts reduces the refusal rate by 22%. This provides evidence of concentrated safety behavior in that model.

The authors also test lightweight LoRA adaptation across different expert groups and compose the updates using negative weight merging targeted at response-control experts. This improves refusal under adversarial prompts without retraining the full model. The results connect a diagnosis of concentrated safety dependence with expert-level interventions intended to strengthen safety behavior in routed architectures.
summary.tldr: SAFEx identifies concentrated safety roles in MoE experts and tests targeted interventions that expose vulnerabilities and improve adversarial refusal.

title: SAFEx: Analyzing Vulnerabilities of MoE-Based LLMs via Stable Safety-critical Expert Identification

abstract: Accurately modeling complex dynamic spatio-temporal systems requires capturing flow-mediated interdependencies and context-sensitive interaction dynamics. Existing methods, predominantly graph-based or attention-driven, rely on similarity-driven connectivity assumptions, neglecting asymmetric flow exchanges that govern system evolution. We propose Spatio-Temporal Flow, a physics-inspired paradigm that explicitly models dynamic node couplings through quantifiable flow transfers governed by conservation principles. Building on this, we design FlowNet, a novel architecture leveraging flow tokens as information carriers to simulate source-to-destination transfers via Flow Allocation Modules, ensuring state redistribution aligns with physical laws. FlowNet dynamically adjusts the interaction radius through an Adaptive Spatial Masking module, suppressing irrelevant noise while enabling context-aware propagation. A cascaded architecture enhances scalability and nonlinear representation capacity. Experiments demonstrate that FlowNet significantly outperforms existing SOTA approaches on seven metrics in the modeling of three real-world systems, validating its efficiency and physical interpretability. We establish a principled methodology for modeling complex systems through spatio-temporal flow interactions.

paragraphs: FlowNet models systems whose states evolve across both space and time. The paper argues that connectivity based on similarity can miss an essential feature of these systems: exchanges have direction, and transfers between locations can be asymmetric. Its proposed Spatio-Temporal Flow paradigm represents interactions through measurable transfers governed by conservation principles.

The architecture uses flow tokens to carry information from sources to destinations. Flow Allocation Modules organize these transfers so that state redistribution follows the intended physical constraints. An Adaptive Spatial Masking module changes how far interactions reach according to context, reducing irrelevant information while retaining useful propagation. A cascaded architecture is designed to improve scalability and represent more complex nonlinear behavior.

Experiments on three real-world systems show improvements over existing state-of-the-art approaches across seven metrics. The authors present these results as evidence for both efficiency and physical interpretability. The central contribution is a structured way to model how state moves between locations, making directed transfers an explicit part of the architecture rather than relying primarily on similarity-based interactions.
summary.tldr: FlowNet models evolving systems through directed, conservation-guided transfers and context-dependent interaction ranges.

title: FlowNet: Modeling Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Systems via Flow Propagation

abstract: We study compute efficiency of LLM training when using different parameterizations, i.e., rules for adjusting model and optimizer hyperparameters (HPs) as model size changes. Some parameterizations fail to transfer optimal base HPs (such as learning rate) across changes in model depth, requiring practitioners to either re-tune these HPs as they scale up (expensive), or accept sub-optimal training when re-tuning is prohibitive. Even when they achieve HP transfer, we develop theory to show parameterizations may still exist in the lazy learning regime where layers learn only features close to their linearization, preventing effective use of depth and nonlinearity. Finally, we identify and adopt the parameterization we call CompleteP that achieves both depth-wise HP transfer and non-lazy learning in all layers. CompleteP enables a wider range of model width/depth ratios to remain compute-efficient, unlocking shapes better suited for different hardware settings and operational contexts. Moreover, CompleteP enables 12-34% compute efficiency improvements over the prior state-of-the-art. All experiments were run on Cerebras CS-3 systems. A minimal implementation is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/nanoGPT-mup/tree/completep.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the rules for scaling model and optimizer settings affect the efficiency of training deeper language models. A useful scaling rule should allow settings such as the learning rate to transfer from a smaller model to a deeper one. Otherwise, increasing depth requires expensive tuning or accepting training settings that are less effective.

The authors show theoretically that successful hyperparameter transfer is not enough. A parameterization can still leave layers in a lazy learning regime, where the features they learn stay close to a linear approximation. That limits how effectively additional depth and nonlinear computation are used. They identify CompleteP as a parameterization that combines depth-wise hyperparameter transfer with non-lazy learning in every layer.

CompleteP makes a broader range of width-to-depth ratios computationally efficient, giving practitioners more flexibility in choosing model shapes for different hardware and operational needs. The experiments report compute-efficiency improvements of 12–34% over the previous state of the art. All experiments used Cerebras CS-3 systems, which provides the concrete hardware context for those findings.
summary.tldr: CompleteP combines transferable training settings with non-lazy feature learning to make deeper Transformers more compute-efficient.

title: Don't be lazy: CompleteP enables compute-efficient deep transformers

abstract: We introduce **RESPIN-S1.0**, the largest publicly available dialect-rich read-speech corpus for Indian languages, comprising more than 10,000 hours of validated audio across nine major languages: Bengali, Bhojpuri, Chhattisgarhi, Hindi, Kannada, Magahi, Maithili, Marathi, and Telugu. Indian languages exhibit high dialectal variation and are spoken by populations that remain digitally underserved. Existing speech corpora typically represent only standard dialects and lack domain and linguistic diversity. RESPIN-S1.0 addresses this limitation by collecting speech across more than 38 dialects and two high-impact domains: agriculture and finance. Text data were composed by native dialect speakers and validated through a pipeline combining automated and manual checks. Over 200,000 unique sentences were recorded through a crowdsourced mobile platform and categorised into clean, semi-noisy, and noisy subsets based on transcription quality, with the clean portion alone exceeding 10,000 hours. Along with audio and transcriptions, RESPIN provides dialect-aware phonetic lexicons, speaker metadata, and reproducible train, development, and test splits. To benchmark performance, we evaluate multiple ASR models, including TDNN-HMM, E-Branchformer, Whisper, and wav2vec2-based self-supervised models, and find that fine-tuning on RESPIN significantly improves recognition accuracy over pretrained baselines. A subset of RESPIN-S1.0 has already supported community challenges such as the SLT Code Hackathon 2022 and MADASR@ASRU 2023 and 2025, releasing more than 1,200 hours publicly. This resource supports research in dialectal ASR, language identification, and related speech technologies, establishing a comprehensive benchmark for inclusive, dialect-rich ASR in multilingual low-resource settings. **Dataset:** https://spiredatasets.ee.iisc.ac.in/respincorpus **Code:** https://github.com/labspire/respin_baselines.git

paragraphs: Speech systems for Indian languages often lack training data representing the dialects people actually speak. RESPIN-S1.0 addresses this gap with validated read speech across nine languages and more than 38 dialects. Its agriculture and finance focus adds domain diversity alongside linguistic diversity, targeting areas highlighted as important in the paper.

Native dialect speakers composed the text, which passed automated and manual validation. Contributors recorded more than 200,000 distinct sentences through a mobile crowdsourcing platform. Recordings are grouped into clean, semi-noisy, and noisy subsets according to transcription quality, with the clean subset alone exceeding 10,000 hours. The resource also includes phonetic lexicons that account for dialect, speaker metadata, and reproducible training, development, and test splits.

The authors benchmark several speech-recognition approaches, including TDNN-HMM, E-Branchformer, Whisper, and wav2vec2-based models. Fine-tuning on RESPIN significantly improves recognition accuracy over pretrained baselines. The corpus therefore contributes both training material and a shared evaluation resource for dialect-aware recognition, language identification, and related speech technologies serving digitally underserved language communities.
summary.tldr: RESPIN-S1.0 provides over 10,000 hours of clean read speech across nine Indian languages and more than 38 dialects, improving recognition through fine-tuning.

title: RESPIN-S1.0: A read speech corpus of 10000+ hours in dialects of nine Indian Languages

abstract: While neural networks have demonstrated impressive performance across various tasks, accurately quantifying uncertainty in their predictions is essential to ensure their trustworthiness and enable widespread adoption in critical systems. Several Bayesian uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods exist that are either cheap or reliable, but not both. We propose a post-hoc, sampling-based UQ method for overparameterized networks at the end of training. Our approach constructs efficient and meaningful deep ensembles by employing a (stochastic) gradient-descent sampling process on appropriately linearized networks. We demonstrate that our method effectively approximates the posterior of a Gaussian Process using the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel. Through a series of numerical experiments, we show that our method not only outperforms competing approaches in computational efficiency--often reducing costs by multiple factors--but also maintains state-of-the-art performance across a variety of UQ metrics for both regression and classification tasks.

paragraphs: A neural network's prediction is more useful in critical applications when accompanied by a reliable estimate of uncertainty. Existing Bayesian approaches can force a tradeoff between computational cost and reliability. This paper proposes a sampling-based method applied after training an overparameterized network, aiming to construct useful uncertainty estimates without expensive ensemble construction.

The method uses a gradient-descent-based sampling process on appropriately linearized networks to create deep ensembles. The authors show that the resulting procedure effectively approximates a Gaussian-process posterior built with the empirical neural tangent kernel. This connects the sampled predictions to a specific posterior approximation, giving the ensemble a mathematical basis for expressing uncertainty.

Numerical experiments cover both regression and classification. The authors report computational savings, often by multiple factors compared with competing approaches, while maintaining state-of-the-art results across several uncertainty metrics. The contribution is a post-training route to efficient ensembles whose uncertainty behavior is supported by both the kernel-based approximation and the reported evaluations, addressing cost and prediction reliability together.
summary.tldr: Sampling linearized trained networks produces efficient uncertainty ensembles that approximate an empirical-neural-tangent-kernel Gaussian-process posterior.

title: Uncertainty Quantification with the Empirical Neural Tangent Kernel

abstract: We study the problem of controlling worst-case errors in misspecified linear regression under the random design setting, where the regression function is estimated via (penalized) least-squares. This setting arises naturally in value function approximation for bandit algorithms and reinforcement learning (RL). Our first main contribution is the observation that the amplification of the misspecification error when using least-squares is governed by the \emph{Lebesgue constant}, a classical quantity from approximation theory that depends on the choice of the feature subspace and the covariate distribution. We also show that this dependence on the misspecification error is tight for least-squares regression: in general, no method minimizing the empirical squared loss, including regularized least-squares, can improve it substantially. We argue this explains the empirical observation that some feature-maps (e.g., those derived from the Fourier bases) ``work better in RL'' than others (e.g., polynomials): given some covariate distribution, the Lebesgue constant is known to be highly sensitive to choice of the feature-map. As a second contribution, we propose a method that augments the original feature set with auxiliary features designed to reduce the error amplification. We then prove that the method successfully competes with an "oracle'' that knows the best way of using the auxiliary features to reduce this amplification. For example, when the domain is a real interval and the features are monomials, our method reduces the amplification factor to $O(1)$ as $d\to\infty$, while without our method, least-squares with the monomials (and in fact polynomials) will suffer a worst-case error amplification of order $\Omega(d)$. It follows that there are functions and feature maps for which our method is consistent, while least-squares is inconsistent.

paragraphs: Least-squares regression minimizes squared prediction errors, but this does not necessarily control the largest error when the chosen features cannot represent the true function. This paper studies that mismatch with randomly sampled inputs, a setting relevant to value-function approximation in bandits and reinforcement learning. It identifies the Lebesgue constant as the quantity governing how least squares amplifies approximation error.

That constant depends jointly on the feature space and the input distribution. The authors show that the resulting dependence is tight: methods minimizing empirical squared loss, including regularized least squares, generally cannot substantially improve it. This offers an explanation for why different feature families can behave differently in reinforcement learning even when each appears suitable for function approximation.

The proposed remedy adds auxiliary features and competes provably with an oracle that knows how best to use them. For monomials on a real interval, it reduces amplification to a bounded order as dimension grows, compared with at least linear growth without the method. Consequently, there are functions and feature choices where the new estimator is consistent and least squares is not.
summary.tldr: Auxiliary features can overcome worst-case error amplification that ordinary and regularized least squares cannot generally avoid.

title: Beyond Least Squares: Uniform Approximation and the Hidden Cost of Misspecification

abstract: Contrastive learning thrives—or fails—based on how we construct \emph{positive} and \emph{negative} pairs. In the absence of explicit labels, models must infer semantic structure from these proxy signals. Early work on Siamese networks \citep{chopra2005learning,hadsell2006dimensionality} already showed that pair construction directly shapes learned representations. In modern contrastive frameworks, poor pair selection remains a primary failure mode: it either causes collapse, where all embeddings converge to a point, or wastes the representational capacity of the space \citep{chen2020simple,tian2020makes,khosla2020supervised}. Contemporary methods typically generate positives via semantic-preserving augmentations (crop, jitter, view transform), while negatives are drawn from other elements in the mini-batch under the assumption that different images are semantically dissimilar. But this assumption breaks down in fine-grained, low-diversity, or high-resolution settings \citep{kalantidis2020hard,robinson2020contrastive,chuang2020debiased}, motivating techniques such as hard-negative mining and debiased losses \citep{bachman2019learning,tian2020makes}. \paragraph{Beyond pairs: batch-level diversity.} While most prior work focuses on \emph{which} individual negatives to select, we study the geometry of the entire batch. Our central observation is this: the overall \emph{diversity} of the batch embedding space strongly governs both training dynamics and representational quality. If diversity is too low, the model sees nearly identical negatives and gradients vanish—leading to collapse. If diversity is too high, negatives become almost orthogonal, but the resulting gradients shrink in magnitude, and learning slows. Optimal training thus occurs within a \emph{moderate diversity window}: high enough to avoid collapse, low enough to preserve update strength.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning uses positive and negative pairs to shape representations without explicit labels. Its usefulness depends on whether these pairs provide meaningful signals. Treating other images in a batch as semantically different can be problematic in settings where examples are similar, motivating closer attention to how training batches are constructed.

This paper shifts attention from choosing individual negative examples to the geometry of the batch as a whole. Its central observation is that diversity across the batch’s embeddings strongly influences both the strength of learning updates and the quality of the representation. Diversity here concerns how examples occupy the learned representation space.

The authors describe two unfavorable extremes. With too little diversity, negatives are nearly identical and gradients can vanish, leading to collapse. With too much diversity, negatives become nearly orthogonal and gradients also shrink, slowing learning. Their conclusion is that effective training occupies a moderate diversity window: enough variation to avoid collapse while retaining strong updates. The argument therefore favors balanced batch geometry rather than simply maximizing diversity.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that contrastive learning benefits from moderate batch diversity because both extremes weaken gradients.

title: Diversity Is All You Need for Contrastive Learning: Spectral Bounds on Gradient Magnitudes

abstract: Evaluation cost during test-time is becoming increasingly important as many real-world applications need fast evaluation (e.g. web search engines, email spam filtering) or use expensive features (e.g. medical diagnosis). We introduce Anytime Feature Representations (AFR), a novel algorithm that explicitly addresses this trade-off in the data representation rather than in the classifier. This enables us to turn conventional classifiers, in particular Support Vector Machines, into test-time cost sensitive anytime classifiers - combining the advantages of anytime learning and large-margin classification.
originalAbstract: Evaluation cost during test-time is becoming increasingly important as many real-world applications need fast evaluation (e.g. web search engines, email spam filtering) or use expensive features (e.g. medical diagnosis). We introduce Anytime Feature Representations (AFR), a novel algorithm that explicitly addresses this trade-off in the data representation rather than in the classifier. paragraphs: A classifier's usefulness can depend on how much computation or feature acquisition it requires when making a prediction. Search and spam filtering need quick decisions, while medical diagnosis can involve expensive features. The paper treats this test-time expense as a central design concern, alongside the ability to classify inputs.

The proposed algorithm, Anytime Feature Representations, addresses the trade-off through the data representation. Its key choice is to make the representation account for evaluation cost, allowing a conventional classifier to acquire anytime behavior. This places the mechanism for managing test-time expense in the features supplied to the classifier.

The authors state that the approach can turn conventional classifiers, particularly support vector machines, into cost-sensitive anytime classifiers. Its significance is the combination of flexible evaluation with large-margin classification: a familiar classification approach can participate in a system designed around test-time resource constraints. The contribution described here is this representational route to combining the two capabilities.
summary.tldr: Anytime Feature Representations make conventional classifiers sensitive to test-time costs by addressing the trade-off in the data representation.

title: Anytime Representation Learning

abstract: In many classification problems such as electroencephalogram (EEG) classification and image classification, the input features are naturally represented as matrices rather than vectors or scalars. In general, the structure information of the original feature matrix is useful and informative for data analysis tasks such as classification. One typical structure information is the correlation between columns or rows in the feature matrix. To leverage this kind of structure information, we propose a new classification method that we call support matrix machine (SMM). Specifically, SMM is defined as a hinge loss plus a so-called spectral elastic net penalty which is a spectral extension of the conventional elastic net over a matrix. The spectral elastic net enjoys a property of grouping effect, i.e., strongly correlated columns or rows tend to be selected altogether or not. Since the optimization problem for SMM is convex, this encourages us to devise an alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm for solving the problem. Experimental results on EEG and face image classification data show that our model is more robust and efficient than the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Some classification inputs, including EEG measurements and images, naturally take matrix form. Relationships among their rows or columns can carry useful information. This paper proposes the support matrix machine to incorporate that structure into classification, with particular attention to correlations among groups of matrix features.

The method combines hinge loss with a spectral elastic net penalty, a matrix-oriented extension of the conventional elastic net. The penalty has a grouping effect: strongly correlated rows or columns tend to be selected together or excluded together. This gives the classifier a way to reflect the relatedness of features when determining which matrix structure matters.

The resulting optimization problem is convex, and the authors develop an alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm to solve it. Experiments on EEG and face-image classification report greater robustness and efficiency than the leading methods considered. These findings support the practical value of combining matrix-aware regularization with a convex classification objective on the evaluated data.
summary.tldr: Support matrix machines use a convex matrix-aware penalty that tends to select correlated rows or columns together.

title: Support Matrix Machines

abstract: Subspace segmentation is the process of clustering a set of data points that are assumed to lie on the union of multiple linear or affine subspaces, and is increasingly being recognized as a fundamental tool for data analysis in high dimensional settings. Arguably one of the most successful approaches is based on the observation that the sparsest representation of a given point with respect to a dictionary formed by the others involves nonzero coefficients associated with points originating in the same subspace. Such sparse representations are computed independently for each data point via \ell_1-norm minimization and then combined into an affinity matrix for use by a final spectral clustering step. The downside of this procedure is two-fold. First, unlike canonical compressive sensing scenarios with ideally-randomized dictionaries, the data-dependent dictionaries here are unavoidably highly structured, disrupting many of the favorable properties of the \ell_1 norm. Secondly, by treating each data point independently, we ignore useful relationships between points that can be leveraged for jointly computing such sparse representations. Consequently, we motivate a multi-task learning-based framework for learning coupled sparse representations leading to a segmentation pipeline that is both robust against correlation structure and tailored to generate an optimal affinity matrix. Theoretical analysis and empirical tests are provided to support these claims.

paragraphs: Subspace segmentation clusters points assumed to lie in several linear or affine subspaces. A successful approach represents each point sparsely using the other points, then converts those representations into similarities for spectral clustering. The guiding idea is that a sparse representation should draw its nonzero coefficients from points in the same subspace.

The paper identifies two problems with computing each representation independently using L1 minimization. The available dictionary is built from the data and can have strong structure, undermining favorable properties associated with randomized dictionaries. Independent fitting also ignores useful relationships among the points that could inform the representations jointly.

The authors propose a multi-task learning framework that couples these sparse representations. Its design addresses correlation structure while tailoring the representations to produce an affinity matrix suited to segmentation. Theoretical analysis and empirical tests support the claims. The methodological shift is to treat representation learning across points as a connected problem whose output serves the final clustering stage.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning sparse representations helps subspace segmentation handle correlated data and build a better clustering affinity matrix.

title: Multi-Task Learning for Subspace Segmentation

abstract: In this paper, we consider the matrix completion problem when the observations are one-bit measurements of some underlying matrix M , and in particular the observed samples consist only of ones and no zeros. This problem is motivated by modern applications such as recommender systems and social networks where only “likes” or “friendships” are observed. The problem is an instance of PU (positive-unlabeled) learning, i.e. learning from only positive and unlabeled examples that has been studied in the context of binary classification. Under the assumption that M has bounded nuclear norm, we provide recovery guarantees for two different observation models: 1) M parameterizes a distribution that generates a binary matrix, 2) M is thresholded to obtain a binary matrix. For the first case, we propose a “shifted matrix completion” method that recovers M using only a subset of indices corresponding to ones; for the second case, we propose a “biased matrix completion” method that recovers the (thresholded) binary matrix. Both methods yield strong error bounds — if M ∈R^n \times n, the error is bounded as O(1-ρ) , where 1-ρdenotes the fraction of ones observed. This implies a sample complexity of O(n log n) ones to achieve a small error, when M is dense and n is large. We extend our analysis to the inductive matrix completion problem, where rows and columns of M have associated features. We develop efficient and scalable optimization procedures for both the proposed methods and demonstrate their effectiveness for link prediction (on real-world networks consisting of over 2 million nodes and 90 million links) and semi-supervised clustering tasks.

paragraphs: Matrix completion becomes a different learning problem when observed entries contain only positives, such as likes or friendships, and no confirmed negatives. Unobserved entries remain unlabeled. This paper treats that situation as positive-unlabeled learning and develops recovery methods under the assumption that the underlying matrix has bounded nuclear norm.

The authors distinguish two observation models. When the matrix specifies a distribution that generates binary entries, shifted matrix completion recovers the underlying matrix using observed ones. When thresholding produces the binary matrix, biased matrix completion instead recovers that thresholded matrix. Matching the recovery target to the observation mechanism is central to the formulation.

The paper derives error guarantees and states that, for a dense large n-by-n matrix, O(n log n) observed ones suffice for small error. It also extends the analysis to settings with row and column features. Efficient optimization procedures are evaluated on semi-supervised clustering and link prediction, including networks exceeding two million nodes and ninety million links. The findings combine recovery theory with evidence of scalability for positive-only observations.
summary.tldr: Positive-unlabeled matrix completion provides recovery guarantees and scalable algorithms for learning from observed ones without confirmed zeros.

title: PU Learning for Matrix Completion

abstract: Many clustering problems in computer vision and other contexts are also classification problems, where each cluster shares a meaningful label. Subspace clustering algorithms in particular are often applied to problems that fit this description, for example with face images or handwritten digits. While it is straightforward to request human input on these datasets, our goal is to reduce this input as much as possible. We present a pairwise-constrained clustering algorithm that actively selects queries based on the union-of-subspaces model. The central step of the algorithm is in querying points of minimum margin between estimated subspaces; analogous to classifier margin, these lie near the decision boundary. We prove that points lying near the intersection of subspaces are points with low margin. Our procedure can be used after any subspace clustering algorithm that outputs an affinity matrix. We demonstrate on several datasets that our algorithm drives the clustering error down considerably faster than the state-of-the-art active query algorithms on datasets with subspace structure and is competitive on other datasets.

paragraphs: Some clustering tasks group data into meaningful classes, making human feedback useful for correcting uncertain assignments. This paper aims to reduce the amount of feedback required when the data follow a union-of-subspaces model. It develops an active method for choosing pairwise queries rather than requesting input without regard to that structure.

The central rule selects points with the smallest margin between estimated subspaces. These points are analogous to examples near a classification boundary. The authors prove that points close to subspace intersections have low margin, linking the query rule to the geometry of ambiguity. Their procedure can follow any subspace clustering algorithm that produces an affinity matrix.

Across several datasets with subspace structure, the method reduces clustering error considerably faster than the compared state-of-the-art active-query algorithms. On other datasets, it remains competitive. The results support using the estimated geometry to prioritize human input, with the strongest reported comparative gains occurring where the subspace model fits the data structure.
summary.tldr: Querying low-margin points between estimated subspaces makes human-guided clustering more efficient on the reported datasets with subspace structure.

title: Leveraging Union of Subspace Structure to Improve Constrained Clustering

abstract: In lifelong reinforcement learning, agents must effectively transfer knowledge across tasks while simultaneously addressing exploration, credit assignment, and generalization. State abstraction can help overcome these hurdles by compressing the representation used by an agent, thereby reducing the computational and statistical burdens of learning. To this end, we here develop theory to compute and use state abstractions in lifelong reinforcement learning. We introduce two new classes of abstractions: (1) transitive state abstractions, whose optimal form can be computed efficiently, and (2) PAC state abstractions, which are guaranteed to hold with respect to a distribution of tasks. We show that the joint family of transitive PAC abstractions can be acquired efficiently, preserve near optimal-behavior, and experimentally reduce sample complexity in simple domains, thereby yielding a family of desirable abstractions for use in lifelong reinforcement learning. Along with these positive results, we show that there are pathological cases where state abstractions can negatively impact performance.

paragraphs: State abstraction compresses the representation an agent uses to learn and act. In lifelong reinforcement learning, such compression could reduce computational and data demands across multiple tasks. The challenge is to retain distinctions that matter for good decisions while simplifying enough to help exploration, credit assignment, and generalization.

The paper introduces two classes of abstractions. Transitive state abstractions have an optimal form that can be computed efficiently. PAC state abstractions provide guarantees with respect to a distribution of tasks. Combining these ideas yields transitive PAC abstractions, which the authors show can be acquired efficiently while preserving near-optimal behavior.

Experiments in simple domains show reduced sample complexity, meaning that the compressed representation can reduce the experience required for learning. The paper also identifies pathological cases in which state abstraction harms performance. Together, these results explain both the promise and the risk of compression: the proposed family has useful guarantees, but abstraction in general does not automatically preserve what an agent needs across tasks.
summary.tldr: Transitive PAC state abstractions can be learned efficiently and preserve near-optimal behavior across tasks, though abstraction can also harm performance.

title: State Abstractions for Lifelong Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are designed to handle sequential data but suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients. Recent work on Unitary Recurrent Neural Networks (uRNNs) have been used to address this issue and in some cases, exceed the capabilities of Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs). We propose a simpler and novel update scheme to maintain orthogonal recurrent weight matrices without using complex valued matrices. This is done by parametrizing with a skew-symmetric matrix using the Cayley transform; such a parametrization is unable to represent matrices with negative one eigenvalues, but this limitation is overcome by scaling the recurrent weight matrix by a diagonal matrix consisting of ones and negative ones. The proposed training scheme involves a straightforward gradient calculation and update step. In several experiments, the proposed scaled Cayley orthogonal recurrent neural network (scoRNN) achieves superior results with fewer trainable parameters than other unitary RNNs.

We propose a simpler and novel update scheme to maintain orthogonal recurrent weight matrices without using complex valued matrices. This is done by parametrizing with a skew-symmetric matrix using the Cayley transform; such a parametrization is unable to represent matrices with negative one eigenvalues, but this limitation is overcome by scaling the recurrent weight matrix by a diagonal matrix consisting of ones and negative ones.
