paragraphs: Recurrent networks process sequences but can suffer when training gradients shrink or grow excessively. Orthogonal and unitary recurrent weights are approaches to this difficulty. This paper introduces scoRNN, a training scheme that maintains orthogonal recurrent matrices using real-valued parameters, with a straightforward gradient calculation and update.

The construction starts with a skew-symmetric matrix and maps it through the Cayley transform. That parametrization alone cannot represent matrices with an eigenvalue of negative one. The authors address this representational restriction by scaling the recurrent matrix with a diagonal matrix whose entries are positive or negative one. This scaling is a specific fix to the limitation of the unscaled parametrization.

In several experiments, scoRNN achieves better results with fewer trainable parameters than the other unitary recurrent networks compared. The findings support the proposed parametrization as a practical way to train orthogonal recurrent weights. The reported advantage applies to those experiments, rather than establishing superiority for every sequential learning task.
summary.tldr: A scaled Cayley parametrization maintains real orthogonal recurrent weights and achieves strong experimental results with fewer parameters.

title: Orthogonal Recurrent Neural Networks with Scaled Cayley Transform

abstract: Our work addresses two important issues with recurrent neural networks: (1) they are over-parametrized, and (2) the recurrent weight matrix is ill-conditioned. The former increases the sample complexity of learning and the training time. The latter causes the vanishing and exploding gradient problem. We present a flexible recurrent neural network model called Kronecker Recurrent Units (KRU). KRU achieves parameter efficiency in RNNs through a Kronecker factored recurrent matrix. It overcomes the ill-conditioning of the recurrent matrix by enforcing soft unitary constraints on the factors. Thanks to the small dimensionality of the factors, maintaining these constraints is computationally efficient. Our experimental results on seven standard data-sets reveal that KRU can reduce the number of parameters by three orders of magnitude in the recurrent weight matrix compared to the existing recurrent models, without trading the statistical performance. These results in particular show that while there are advantages in having a high dimensional recurrent space, the capacity of the recurrent part of the model can be dramatically reduced.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks can suffer from both excessive parameter counts and poorly conditioned recurrent weight matrices. The paper connects the first issue to training time and the amount of data needed for learning, and the second to gradients that vanish or explode. Kronecker Recurrent Units address these two problems through the structure of the recurrent matrix.

KRU represents that matrix using Kronecker factors, allowing a large recurrent transformation to be described with fewer parameters. It also imposes soft unitary constraints on the factors to address ill-conditioning. Because the factors are small, maintaining those constraints is computationally efficient. The factorization and constraints therefore serve complementary purposes: compact representation and better conditioning.

Across seven standard datasets, the authors report reductions of three orders of magnitude in recurrent-matrix parameter counts compared with existing recurrent models, without sacrificing statistical performance. The results suggest that a high-dimensional recurrent space can remain useful even when the number of independently learned recurrent parameters is greatly reduced. This separates the size of the recurrent representation from the parameter capacity required to operate it.
summary.tldr: Kronecker-factored recurrent matrices with soft unitary constraints substantially reduce parameter counts while preserving reported performance.

title: Kronecker Recurrent Units

abstract: In this paper, we advocate for representation learning as the key to mitigating unfair prediction outcomes downstream. Motivated by a scenario where learned representations are used by third parties with unknown objectives, we propose and explore adversarial representation learning as a natural method of ensuring those parties act fairly. We connect group fairness (demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity) to different adversarial objectives. Through worst-case theoretical guarantees and experimental validation, we show that the choice of this objective is crucial to fair prediction. Furthermore, we present the first in-depth experimental demonstration of fair transfer learning and demonstrate empirically that our learned representations admit fair predictions on new tasks while maintaining utility, an essential goal of fair representation learning.

Through worst-case theoretical guarantees and experimental validation, we show that the choice of this objective is crucial to fair prediction. Furthermore, we present the first in-depth experimental demonstration of fair transfer learning and demonstrate empirically that our learned representations admit fair predictions on new tasks while maintaining utility, an essential goal of fair representation learning.

paragraphs: This paper considers learning representations that third parties will later use for prediction, even when their objectives are unknown during representation training. The goal is to reduce unfair downstream outcomes while preserving useful information. The authors investigate adversarial representation learning as a way to build fairness considerations into the representation before those later tasks are chosen.

A central contribution connects different adversarial objectives to demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity. These are distinct group-fairness criteria, so the training objective determines which fairness behavior the method supports. Worst-case theoretical guarantees and experimental validation show that choosing the adversarial objective is consequential; adversarial training alone does not specify a single interchangeable notion of fairness.

The paper also studies transfer to new prediction tasks. Its experiments show that the learned representations can support fair predictions while maintaining utility on those tasks. This provides empirical evidence for the intended use by downstream users. The contribution combines an analysis of objective choice with a demonstration that fairness-oriented representations can retain value beyond the task used to learn them.
summary.tldr: The paper links adversarial objectives to specific group-fairness criteria and empirically shows useful, fair transfer to new prediction tasks.

title: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations

abstract: We study the problem of repeated play in a zero-sum game in which the payoff matrix may change, in a possibly adversarial fashion, on each round; we call these Online Matrix Games. Finding the Nash Equilibrium (NE) of a two player zero-sum game is core to many problems in statistics, optimization, and economics, and for a fixed game matrix this can be easily reduced to solving a linear program. But when the payoff matrix evolves over time our goal is to find a sequential algorithm that can compete with, in a certain sense, the NE of the long-term-averaged payoff matrix. We design an algorithm with small NE regret–that is, we ensure that the long-term payoff of both players is close to minimax optimum in hindsight. Our algorithm achieves near-optimal dependence with respect to the number of rounds and depends poly-logarithmically on the number of available actions of the players. Additionally, we show that the naive reduction, where each player simply minimizes its own regret, fails to achieve the stated objective regardless of which algorithm is used. Lastly, we consider the so-called bandit setting, where the feedback is significantly limited, and we provide an algorithm with small NE regret using one-point estimates of each payoff matrix.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated zero-sum games whose payoff matrix can change on every round, including changes chosen adversarially. The goal is to compete with the Nash equilibrium of the payoff matrix averaged over the full sequence. This creates a hindsight benchmark for a learner that must act before the entire sequence is known.

The authors design an algorithm with small Nash-equilibrium regret, meaning the players' long-term payoffs remain close to the hindsight minimax optimum. Its dependence on the number of rounds is nearly optimal, and its dependence on the number of available actions is polylogarithmic. The latter result keeps the action-count contribution to the guarantee comparatively modest.

A key finding is that having each player independently minimize ordinary regret does not achieve this objective, regardless of which regret-minimization algorithm is chosen. The equilibrium benchmark therefore requires a distinct treatment. The paper also addresses bandit feedback, where information about payoffs is restricted, and provides an algorithm with small equilibrium regret using one-point estimates of the changing payoff matrices.
summary.tldr: New algorithms compete with the equilibrium of an averaged changing game, a guarantee independent regret minimization cannot provide.

title: Competing Against Nash Equilibria in Adversarially Changing Zero-Sum Games

abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in computer vision by supervisedly learning strong visual feature representations. However, training CNNs relies heavily on the availability of exhaustive training data annotations, limiting significantly their deployment and scalability in many application scenarios. In this work, we introduce a generic unsupervised deep learning approach to training deep models without the need for any manual label supervision. Specifically, we progressively discover sample anchored/centred neighbourhoods to reason and learn the underlying class decision boundaries iteratively and accumulatively. Every single neighbourhood is specially formulated so that all the member samples can share the same unseen class labels at high probability for facilitating the extraction of class discriminative feature representations during training. Experiments on image classification show the performance advantages of the proposed method over the state-of-the-art unsupervised learning models on six benchmarks including both coarse-grained and fine-grained object image categorisation.

paragraphs: Strong visual representations often depend on extensive manual labeling, which can restrict where deep image models are practical. This paper proposes training without manual label supervision by progressively discovering neighborhoods of examples around individual samples. These neighborhoods supply a structure from which the model can learn distinctions between unseen classes.

Each neighborhood is constructed so that its members have a high probability of sharing the same unknown class label. The method uses these groups to develop class-discriminative features and iteratively reason about class decision boundaries. Discovery and learning accumulate over time, allowing the training process to build on the neighborhoods it has identified.

Experiments on six image-classification benchmarks show advantages over state-of-the-art unsupervised methods. The benchmarks include both broad object categories and finer distinctions within categories. These results support neighborhood discovery as a source of supervision for visual feature learning. The approach relies on probable shared labels within groups; the abstract does not claim that every discovered neighborhood has perfectly uniform class membership.
summary.tldr: Progressively discovering likely same-class neighborhoods trains discriminative visual features without manual labels and improves results on six benchmarks.

title: Unsupervised Deep Learning by Neighbourhood Discovery

abstract: We identify a new variational inference scheme for dynamical systems whose transition function is modelled by a Gaussian process. Inference in this setting has either employed computationally intensive MCMC methods, or relied on factorisations of the variational posterior. As we demonstrate in our experiments, the factorisation between latent system states and transition function can lead to a miscalibrated posterior and to learning unnecessarily large noise terms. We eliminate this factorisation by explicitly modelling the dependence between state trajectories and the low-rank representation of our Gaussian process posterior. Samples of the latent states can then be tractably generated by conditioning on this representation. The method we obtain gives better predictive performance and more calibrated estimates of the transition function, yet maintains the same time and space complexities as mean-field methods.

As we demonstrate in our experiments, the factorisation between latent system states and transition function can lead to a miscalibrated posterior and to learning unnecessarily large noise terms. We eliminate this factorisation by explicitly modelling the dependence between state trajectories and the low-rank representation of our Gaussian process posterior. Samples of the latent states can then be tractably generated by conditioning on this representation. The method we obtain gives better predictive performance and more calibrated estimates of the transition function, yet maintains the same time and space complexities as mean-field methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies dynamical systems whose transition function is represented by a Gaussian process. Inference must account for uncertainty in both the hidden system states and the function that moves the system between states. Earlier approaches used expensive sampling methods or simplified the variational posterior by separating parts of that uncertainty.

The authors show experimentally that separating latent states from the transition function can produce poorly calibrated uncertainty and unnecessarily large learned noise terms. Their proposed variational method explicitly preserves dependence between state trajectories and a low-rank representation of the Gaussian process posterior. Conditioning on this representation makes it tractable to generate latent-state samples.

The resulting method improves predictive performance and yields better-calibrated estimates of the transition function. It maintains the same time and space complexity as mean-field methods. The contribution therefore addresses a specific approximation error while preserving computational scaling, showing that a richer treatment of dependence can improve both predictions and uncertainty estimates without changing those complexity classes.
summary.tldr: Preserving dependence between latent trajectories and Gaussian process dynamics improves prediction and uncertainty calibration at mean-field computational complexity.

title: Overcoming Mean-Field Approximations in Recurrent Gaussian Process Models

abstract: Triangular map is a recent construct in probability theory that allows one to transform any source probability density function to any target density function. Based on triangular maps, we propose a general framework for high-dimensional density estimation, by specifying one-dimensional transformations (equivalently conditional densities) and appropriate conditioner networks. This framework (a) reveals the commonalities and differences of existing autoregressive and flow based methods, (b) allows a unified understanding of the limitations and representation power of these recent approaches and, (c) motivates us to uncover a new Sum-of-Squares (SOS) flow that is interpretable, universal, and easy to train. We perform several synthetic experiments on various density geometries to demonstrate the benefits (and short-comings) of such transformations. SOS flows achieve competitive results in simulations and several real-world datasets.

SOS flows achieve competitive results in simulations and several real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Density estimation seeks a model of how probability is distributed across possible observations. This paper develops a framework for high-dimensional density estimation using triangular maps, which provide transformations between source and target probability densities. The framework specifies one-dimensional transformations, equivalently conditional densities, together with networks that condition those transformations.

This common description brings autoregressive and flow-based approaches into the same analytical framework. It exposes their shared structure, differences, representational capabilities, and limitations. The authors use that perspective to develop a Sum-of-Squares polynomial flow, describing the resulting model as interpretable, universal in representation, and easy to train.

Synthetic experiments examine transformations across different density geometries, illustrating both benefits and shortcomings. Additional evaluations on simulations and real-world datasets show competitive results for SOS flows. The paper’s contribution therefore has two connected parts: a framework for understanding existing density models and a new model motivated by that framework. Its representational claims and empirical competitiveness address different aspects of the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: A triangular-map framework unifies density-estimation approaches and motivates an interpretable, universal Sum-of-Squares polynomial flow.

title: Sum-of-Squares Polynomial Flow

abstract: Given the widespread popularity of spectral clustering (SC) for partitioning graph data, we study a version of constrained SC in which we try to incorporate the fairness notion proposed by Chierichetti et al. (2017). According to this notion, a clustering is fair if every demographic group is approximately proportionally represented in each cluster. To this end, we develop variants of both normalized and unnormalized constrained SC and show that they help find fairer clusterings on both synthetic and real data. We also provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of our algorithms on a natural variant of the stochastic block model, where $h$ groups have strong inter-group connectivity, but also exhibit a “natural” clustering structure which is fair. We prove that our algorithms can recover this fair clustering with high probability.

(2017). According to this notion, a clustering is fair if every demographic group is approximately proportionally represented in each cluster. To this end, we develop variants of both normalized and unnormalized constrained SC and show that they help find fairer clusterings on both synthetic and real data. We also provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of our algorithms on a natural variant of the stochastic block model, where $h$ groups have strong inter-group connectivity, but also exhibit a “natural” clustering structure which is fair. We prove that our algorithms can recover this fair clustering with high probability.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering partitions graph data, and this paper modifies it to incorporate a particular demographic fairness requirement. Under this definition, each demographic group should be represented in every cluster approximately in proportion to its overall presence. Fairness therefore concerns the composition of each cluster, rather than only the composition of the dataset as a whole.

The authors develop constrained versions of both normalized and unnormalized spectral clustering. On synthetic and real datasets, these methods help produce fairer clusterings. This empirical result addresses whether demographic constraints can influence the partitions produced by commonly used spectral approaches.

The paper also analyzes the algorithms under a variant of the stochastic block model. In that setting, demographic groups have strong inter-group connectivity, while a natural fair clustering structure is present. The authors prove recovery of that structure with high probability. This provides a model-based guarantee alongside the empirical findings, with the recovery claim tied to the specified graph-generation setting rather than arbitrary graphs.
summary.tldr: Fairness-constrained spectral clustering improves demographic representation empirically and recovers a fair partition with high probability under a specified graph model.

title: Guarantees for Spectral Clustering with Fairness Constraints

abstract: Standard sequential generation methods assume a pre-specified generation order, such as text generation methods which generate words from left to right. In this work, we propose a framework for training models of text generation that operate in non-monotonic orders; the model directly learns good orders, without any additional annotation. Our framework operates by generating a word at an arbitrary position, and then recursively generating words to its left and then words to its right, yielding a binary tree. Learning is framed as imitation learning, including a coaching method which moves from imitating an oracle to reinforcing the policy’s own preferences. Experimental results demonstrate that using the proposed method, it is possible to learn policies which generate text without pre-specifying a generation order, while achieving competitive performance with conventional left-to-right generation.

Our framework operates by generating a word at an arbitrary position, and then recursively generating words to its left and then words to its right, yielding a binary tree. paragraphs: Text generation usually follows an order fixed before learning, commonly producing words from left to right. This paper asks whether a model can learn useful generation orders itself. Its framework learns those orders without extra annotation, making the choice of where to generate a word part of the policy being trained.

Generation begins with a word at an arbitrary position. The model then recursively generates words to its left and afterward words to its right. These recursive decisions form a binary tree, providing an organized procedure for building a sequence even when its words are not produced in their final reading order.

Training is formulated as imitation learning. A coaching method gradually moves from following an oracle toward reinforcing the policy’s own preferences. Experiments demonstrate that the resulting policies can generate text without a prespecified order while achieving performance competitive with conventional left-to-right generation. The finding establishes the feasibility of learning generation order alongside word choices within this recursive framework.
summary.tldr: An imitation-learning framework learns recursive text-generation orders without additional annotation and achieves competitive performance with left-to-right generation.

title: Non-Monotonic Sequential Text Generation

abstract: The likelihood model of high dimensional data $X_n$ can often be expressed as $p(X_n|Z_n,\theta)$, where $\theta\mathrel{\mathop:}=(\theta_k)_{k\in[K]}$ is a collection of hidden features shared across objects, indexed by $n$, and $Z_n$ is a non-negative factor loading vector with $K$ entries where $Z_{nk}$ indicates the strength of $\theta_k$ used to express $X_n$. In this paper, we introduce random function priors for $Z_n$ for modeling correlations among its $K$ dimensions $Z_{n1}$ through $Z_{nK}$, which we call population random measure embedding (PRME). Our model can be viewed as a generalized paintbox model \cite{Broderick13} using random functions, and can be learned efficiently with neural networks via amortized variational inference. We derive our Bayesian nonparametric method by applying a representation theorem on separately exchangeable discrete random measures.

In this paper, we introduce random function priors for $Z_n$ for modeling correlations among its $K$ dimensions $Z_{n1}$ through $Z_{nK}$, which we call population random measure embedding (PRME). paragraphs: Many models describe a high-dimensional observation through shared hidden features and a separate vector of feature strengths for each object. Each non-negative entry indicates how strongly one feature contributes to that object. This paper focuses on modeling correlations among those strengths, allowing the use of one hidden feature to be statistically related to the use of others.

The authors introduce population random measure embedding, or PRME, which places random-function priors on the feature-loading vectors. They interpret the construction as a generalization of a paintbox model using random functions. Its Bayesian nonparametric foundation comes from applying a representation theorem for separately exchangeable discrete random measures.

To learn the model efficiently, the paper uses neural networks within amortized variational inference. The contribution thus joins a probabilistic construction for correlated feature loadings with a computational approach for fitting it. The correlations live in the strengths assigned to shared features, which directly determine how those features participate in explaining each observation. This gives the dependence model a clear role within the larger likelihood formulation.
summary.tldr: PRME uses random-function priors to model correlated feature strengths and neural amortized inference to learn the resulting Bayesian nonparametric model.

title: Random Function Priors for Correlation Modeling

abstract: Recent years have witnessed intensive research interests on training deep neural networks (DNNs) more efficiently by quantization-based compression methods, which facilitate DNNs training in two ways: (1) activations are quantized to shrink the memory consumption, and (2) gradients are quantized to decrease the communication cost. However, existing methods mostly use a uniform mechanism that quantizes the values evenly. Such a scheme may cause a large quantization variance and slow down the convergence in practice. In this work, we introduce TinyScript, which applies a non-uniform quantization algorithm to both activations and gradients. TinyScript models the original values by a family of Weibull distributions and searches for ”quantization knobs” that minimize quantization variance. We also discuss the convergence of the non-uniform quantization algorithm on DNNs with varying depths, shedding light on the number of bits required for convergence. Experiments show that TinyScript always obtains lower quantization variance, and achieves comparable model qualities against full precision training using 1-2 bits less than the uniform-based counterpart.

However, existing methods mostly use a uniform mechanism that quantizes the values evenly. Such a scheme may cause a large quantization variance and slow down the convergence in practice. In this work, we introduce TinyScript, which applies a non-uniform quantization algorithm to both activations and gradients. TinyScript models the original values by a family of Weibull distributions and searches for ”quantization knobs” that minimize quantization variance. We also discuss the convergence of the non-uniform quantization algorithm on DNNs with varying depths, shedding light on the number of bits required for convergence. Many methods assign values to evenly spaced quantization levels. The paper argues that this uniform treatment can introduce substantial quantization variance and slow convergence in practice.

TinyScript instead applies non-uniform quantization to both activations and gradients. It models their original values using a family of Weibull distributions, then searches for quantization settings that minimize variance. The central idea is to adapt the representation of values to their distribution, so the available bits are used more effectively. The authors also analyze convergence across networks of varying depths and discuss how many bits convergence requires.

In the reported experiments, TinyScript consistently produces lower quantization variance. It achieves model quality comparable to full-precision training while using one to two fewer bits than the uniform quantization counterpart. These findings connect the variance-minimizing design with a practical reduction in numerical precision, while retaining comparable quality in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: TinyScript adapts activation and gradient quantization to their distributions, retaining comparable model quality with fewer bits in experiments.

title: Don’t Waste Your Bits! Squeeze Activations and Gradients for Deep Neural Networks via TinyScript

abstract: We present a new discriminative technique for the multiple-source adaptation (MSA) problem. Unlike previous work, which relies on density estimation for each source domain, our solution only requires conditional probabilities that can be straightforwardly accurately estimated from unlabeled data from the source domains. We give a detailed analysis of our new technique, including general guarantees based on Rényi divergences, and learning bounds when conditional Maxent is used for estimating conditional probabilities for a point to belong to a source domain. We show that these guarantees compare favorably to those that can be derived for the generative solution, using kernel density estimation. Our experiments with real-world applications further demonstrate that our new discriminative MSA algorithm outperforms the previous generative solution as well as other domain adaptation baselines.

Earlier approaches estimate a separate probability density for each source, describing how its data are distributed. This paper proposes a discriminative alternative: estimate the probability that a data point belongs to each source domain. Those probabilities can be learned from source data without requiring task labels.

This changes the statistical problem underlying adaptation. Instead of reconstructing each source distribution, the method focuses on distinguishing the sources from one another. The authors analyze the resulting technique using Rényi divergences and provide learning bounds for conditional maximum-entropy estimation of source membership. They report that these guarantees compare favorably with guarantees for the generative approach using kernel density estimation.

Experiments on real-world applications also favor the proposed method over the previous generative solution and other domain-adaptation baselines. Together, the analysis and experiments support source-membership estimation as a useful alternative foundation for multiple-source adaptation. The stated advantage concerns both the theoretical guarantees and the observed predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Estimating source-membership probabilities offers a discriminative approach to multiple-source adaptation with favorable guarantees and experimental results.

title: A Discriminative Technique for Multiple-Source Adaptation

abstract: Noise injection is an effective way of circumventing overfitting and enhancing generalization in machine learning, the rationale of which has been validated in deep learning as well. Recently, noise injection exhibits surprising effectiveness when generating high-fidelity images in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) (e.g. StyleGAN). Despite its successful applications in GANs, the mechanism of its validity is still unclear. In this paper, we propose a geometric framework to theoretically analyze the role of noise injection in GANs. First, we point out the existence of the adversarial dimension trap inherent in GANs, which leads to the difficulty of learning a proper generator. Second, we successfully model the noise injection framework with exponential maps based on Riemannian geometry. Guided by our theories, we propose a general geometric realization for noise injection. Under our novel framework, the simple noise injection used in StyleGAN reduces to the Euclidean case. The goal of our work is to make theoretical steps towards understanding the underlying mechanism of state-of-the-art GAN algorithms. Experiments on image generation and GAN inversion validate our theory in practice.

Its aim is to develop a theoretical explanation for noise injection in GANs, rather than treating its successful use as sufficient understanding of the mechanism.

The authors identify an inherent difficulty they call the adversarial dimension trap, which makes learning a suitable generator harder. They then model noise injection using exponential maps from Riemannian geometry. This geometric treatment motivates a general realization of noise injection and places the simple mechanism used in StyleGAN within the framework as a Euclidean special case.

The contribution is a geometric account that links an identified learning difficulty to a broader family of noise-injection mechanisms. The authors frame this as theoretical progress toward understanding successful GAN algorithms, with the experimental results supporting that account in the studied applications.
summary.tldr: A Riemannian-geometric framework explains noise injection in GANs and treats StyleGAN’s mechanism as a Euclidean special case.

title: Understanding Noise Injection in GANs

abstract: In multi-dimensional classification (MDC), there are multiple class variables in the output space with each of them corresponding to one heterogeneous class space. Due to the heterogeneity of class spaces, it is quite challenging to consider the dependencies among class variables when learning from MDC examples. In this paper, we propose a novel MDC approach named SLEM which learns the predictive model in an encoded label space instead of the original heterogeneous one. Specifically, SLEM works in an encoding-training-decoding framework. In the encoding phase, each class vector is mapped into a real-valued one via three cascaded operations including pairwise grouping, one-hot conversion and sparse linear encoding. In the training phase, a multi-output regression model is learned within the encoded label space. In the decoding phase, the predicted class vector is obtained by adapting orthogonal matching pursuit over outputs of the learned multi-output regression model. Experimental results clearly validate the superiority of SLEM against state-of-the-art MDC approaches.

paragraphs: Multi-dimensional classification predicts several categorical variables at once, with each variable drawing from its own class space. The variables may depend on one another, but their heterogeneous categories make those relationships difficult to incorporate into learning. This paper proposes SLEM, which moves prediction into an encoded numerical label space.

SLEM follows three stages: encoding, training, and decoding. First, it transforms each class vector through pairwise grouping, one-hot conversion, and sparse linear encoding. It then trains a multi-output regression model to predict the resulting real-valued representation. Finally, it adapts orthogonal matching pursuit to translate the regression outputs back into a predicted vector of classes.

This design puts a shared numerical representation between the original labels and the predictive model, giving the method a way to address dependencies among heterogeneous outputs. Experiments show SLEM outperforming the leading multi-dimensional classification methods used in the comparison. The stated findings support the overall encoding–prediction–decoding approach as an effective alternative to learning directly in the original label space.
summary.tldr: SLEM encodes heterogeneous categorical outputs into a sparse numerical space, learns there, and decodes predictions to improve multi-dimensional classification.

title: Multi-Dimensional Classification via Sparse Label Encoding

abstract: We study the online load balancing problem with machine learned predictions, and give results that improve upon and extend those in a recent paper by Lattanzi et al. (2020). First, we design deterministic and randomized online rounding algorithms for the problem in the unrelated machine setting, with $O(\frac{\log m}{\log \log m})$- and $O(\frac{\log \log m}{\log \log \log m})$-competitive ratios. They respectively improve upon the previous ratios of $O(\log m)$ and $O(\log^3\log m)$, and match the lower bounds given by Lattanzi et al. Second, we extend their prediction scheme from the identical machine restricted assignment setting to the unrelated machine setting. With the knowledge of two vectors over machines, a dual vector and a weight vector, we can construct a good fractional assignment online, that can be passed to an online rounding algorithm. Finally, we consider the learning model introduced by Lavastida et al. (2020), and show that under the model, the two vectors can be learned efficiently with a few samples of instances.

paragraphs: Online load balancing assigns work as it arrives. This paper studies how learned predictions can help in the unrelated-machine setting, where assigning a job to different machines can incur different processing costs. It develops both the machinery for turning fractional assignments into actual assignments and a prediction scheme that supplies those fractional assignments.

For m machines, the deterministic rounding algorithm achieves an O(log m / log log m) competitive ratio. The randomized algorithm achieves O(log log m / log log log m). Both improve the corresponding previous bounds and match the cited lower bounds. These guarantees quantify assignment quality relative to an optimum, rather than reporting empirical speed improvements.

The authors also extend a prediction scheme previously used in a more restricted machine setting. Given two machine-indexed vectors, a dual vector and a weight vector, their method constructs a good fractional assignment online and passes it to a rounding algorithm. Under the learning model they study, both vectors can be learned efficiently from a few sampled instances, connecting the improved rounding guarantees to learnable predictions.
summary.tldr: Improved online rounding algorithms and two learnable prediction vectors extend prediction-assisted load balancing to unrelated machines.

title: Online Unrelated Machine Load Balancing with Predictions Revisited

abstract: Scalable Gaussian Process methods are computationally attractive, yet introduce modeling biases that require rigorous study. This paper analyzes two common techniques: early truncated conjugate gradients (CG) and random Fourier features (RFF). We find that both methods introduce a systematic bias on the learned hyperparameters: CG tends to underfit while RFF tends to overfit. We address these issues using randomized truncation estimators that eliminate bias in exchange for increased variance. In the case of RFF, we show that the bias-to-variance conversion is indeed a trade-off: the additional variance proves detrimental to optimization. However, in the case of CG, our unbiased learning procedure meaningfully outperforms its biased counterpart with minimal additional computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/ cunningham-lab/RTGPS.

paragraphs: Scalable Gaussian process methods reduce computational cost, but their approximations can also change what a model learns. This paper examines two common approaches: stopping conjugate gradients early and using random Fourier features. It finds systematic effects on learned hyperparameters, with the first tending toward underfitting and the second toward overfitting.

The authors introduce randomized truncation estimators to remove this bias. The central exchange is between systematic error and variability: eliminating bias comes with increased variance. Consequently, a mathematically unbiased learning procedure need not be easier to optimize or yield a better practical result.

The two methods illustrate that distinction. For random Fourier features, the additional variance harms optimization, making the correction a consequential trade-off. For conjugate gradients, the unbiased procedure meaningfully improves on its biased counterpart while requiring little extra computation. The findings therefore identify both a useful correction for one scalable Gaussian process approach and a reason to evaluate bias removal together with its effect on optimization.
summary.tldr: Randomized truncation removes bias from two Gaussian process approximations, helping conjugate-gradient learning but harming random-feature optimization through added variance.

title: Bias-Free Scalable Gaussian Processes via Randomized Truncations

abstract: Ad hoc teamwork is the challenging problem of designing an autonomous agent which can adapt quickly to collaborate with teammates without prior coordination mechanisms, including joint training. Prior work in this area has focused on closed teams in which the number of agents is fixed. In this work, we consider open teams by allowing agents with different fixed policies to enter and leave the environment without prior notification. Our solution builds on graph neural networks to learn agent models and joint-action value models under varying team compositions. We contribute a novel action-value computation that integrates the agent model and joint-action value model to produce action-value estimates. We empirically demonstrate that our approach successfully models the effects other agents have on the learner, leading to policies that robustly adapt to dynamic team compositions and significantly outperform several alternative methods.

paragraphs: Ad hoc teamwork asks an agent to cooperate with teammates without prior coordination or joint training. This paper extends that challenge to open teams, where agents may arrive or leave without warning. The teammates can follow different fixed policies, so the learner must adapt both to their behavior and to changing team composition.

The proposed approach uses graph neural networks to learn models of agents and models of joint-action values. A new action-value computation integrates those two sources of information to estimate the value of the learner's choices. This links predictions about other agents with assessments of how combinations of actions affect the learner.

Experiments show that the approach successfully models other agents' effects and produces policies that adapt robustly to changing teams. It significantly outperforms several alternative methods in the reported evaluations. The contribution concerns cooperation under changing membership, with fixed teammate policies as the stated setting. The graph-based models and integrated value computation provide a way to account for whoever is currently participating.
summary.tldr: Graph-based agent and joint-action models help a learner cooperate with teammates who enter and leave without warning.

title: Towards Open Ad Hoc Teamwork Using Graph-based Policy Learning

abstract: Data subset selection from a large number of training instances has been a successful approach toward efficient and cost-effective machine learning. However, models trained on a smaller subset may show poor generalization ability. In this paper, our goal is to design an algorithm for selecting a subset of the training data, so that the model can be trained quickly, without significantly sacrificing on accuracy. More specifically, we focus on data subset selection for $L_2$ regularized regression problems and provide a novel problem formulation which seeks to minimize the training loss with respect to both the trainable parameters and the subset of training data, subject to error bounds on the validation set. We tackle this problem using several technical innovations. First, we represent this problem with simplified constraints using the dual of the original training problem and show that the objective of this new representation is a monotone and $\alpha$-submodular function, for a wide variety of modeling choices. Such properties lead us to develop SELCON, an efficient majorization-minimization algorithm for data subset selection, that admits an approximation guarantee even when the training provides an imperfect estimate of the trained model. Finally, our experiments on several datasets show that SELCON trades off accuracy and efficiency more effectively than the current state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Training on a smaller data subset can save computation but may damage performance on unseen data. This paper addresses that tradeoff for L2-regularized regression. Its formulation jointly selects training examples and model parameters to minimize training loss while enforcing error bounds on a validation set.

The authors reformulate the problem through its dual to simplify the constraints. For a wide range of modeling choices, they show that the resulting objective is monotone and alpha-submodular. These mathematical properties support SELCON, an efficient subset-selection algorithm based on majorization-minimization. The algorithm comes with an approximation guarantee even when training supplies an imperfect estimate of the fitted model.

Experiments across several datasets show a more effective accuracy-efficiency tradeoff than the state of the art considered in the paper. The key design choice is to make validation error part of the selection problem itself. That gives the method an explicit way to balance reducing the training set against preserving predictive quality, supported by both an approximation analysis and empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: SELCON selects regression training subsets under validation-error constraints, with an approximation guarantee and improved reported accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs.

title: Training Data Subset Selection for Regression with Controlled Generalization Error

abstract: We show the formal equivalence of linearised self-attention mechanisms and fast weight controllers from the early ’90s, where a slow neural net learns by gradient descent to program the fast weights of another net through sequences of elementary programming instructions which are additive outer products of self-invented activation patterns (today called keys and values). Such Fast Weight Programmers (FWPs) learn to manipulate the contents of a finite memory and dynamically interact with it. We infer a memory capacity limitation of recent linearised softmax attention variants, and replace the purely additive outer products by a delta rule-like programming instruction, such that the FWP can more easily learn to correct the current mapping from keys to values. The FWP also learns to compute dynamically changing learning rates. We also propose a new kernel function to linearise attention which balances simplicity and effectiveness. We conduct experiments on synthetic retrieval problems as well as standard machine translation and language modelling tasks which demonstrate the benefits of our methods.

paragraphs: This paper establishes a formal equivalence between linearized self-attention and fast weight programmers. In that interpretation, a slowly learned neural network writes into another network’s rapidly changing weights. Keys and values supply patterns whose outer products act as elementary writing instructions, making attention a way to manipulate a finite memory.

The authors use this connection to infer a memory-capacity limitation of recent linearized softmax-attention variants. They replace purely additive writing with an update resembling a delta rule. This lets the model more easily correct its existing mapping from keys to values. The fast weight programmer also learns changing learning rates, allowing the strength of these updates to vary dynamically.

A further contribution is a new kernel for linearizing attention that aims to combine simplicity with effectiveness. Experiments on synthetic retrieval, machine translation, and language modeling demonstrate benefits from the proposed methods. The equivalence thus serves both as an interpretation of linear attention and as a basis for changing how its memory is updated.
summary.tldr: Viewing linear attention as fast weight programming motivates corrective memory updates and a new attention kernel with demonstrated benefits.

title: Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers

abstract: Domain adaptation algorithms and theory have relied upon an assumption that the observed data uniquely specify the correct correspondence between the domains. Unfortunately, it is unclear under what conditions this identifiability assumption holds, even when restricting ourselves to the case where a correct bijective map between domains exists. We study this bijective domain mapping problem and provide several new sufficient conditions for the identifiability of linear domain maps. As a consequence of our analysis, we show that weak constraints on the third moment tensor suffice for identifiability, prove identifiability for common latent variable models such as topic models, and give a computationally tractable method for generating certificates for the identifiability of linear maps. Inspired by our certification method, we derive a new objective function for domain mapping that explicitly accounts for uncertainty over maps arising from unidentifiability. We demonstrate that our objective leads to improvements in uncertainty quantification and model performance estimation.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation often assumes that observed data determine the correct correspondence between two domains. This paper asks when that assumption is justified. Even if a correct one-to-one mapping exists, the available observations may leave several mappings plausible. Establishing identifiability means showing that the data distinguish the correct correspondence.

The authors provide several sufficient conditions for identifying linear domain maps. Their analysis shows that weak constraints on third-moment tensors can suffice, and establishes identifiability for common latent-variable models, including topic models. They also develop a computationally tractable method for producing certificates of identifiability, giving a way to substantiate uniqueness in the studied setting.

The paper demonstrates improvements in uncertainty quantification and model performance estimation. Its contribution combines conditions that establish when a mapping can be uniquely determined with an objective that accounts for ambiguity when uniqueness is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Sufficient conditions and practical certificates establish identifiability of linear domain maps, while a new objective accounts for mapping ambiguity.

title: Identifiability Conditions for Domain Adaptation

abstract: Transformer-based models such as BERT have proven successful in information retrieval problem, which seek to identify relevant documents for a given query. There are two broad flavours of such models: cross-attention (CA) models, which learn a joint embedding for the query and document, and dual-encoder (DE) models, which learn separate embeddings for the query and document. Empirically, CA models are often found to be more accurate, which has motivated a series of works seeking to bridge this gap. However, a more fundamental question remains less explored: does this performance gap reflect an inherent limitation in the capacity of DE models, or a limitation in the training of such models? And does such an understanding suggest a principled means of improving DE models? In this paper, we study these questions, with three contributions. First, we establish theoretically that with a sufficiently large embedding dimension, DE models have the capacity to model a broad class of score distributions. Second, we show empirically that on real-world problems, DE models may overfit to spurious correlations in the training set, and thus under-perform on test samples. To mitigate this behaviour, we propose a suitable distillation strategy, and confirm its practical efficacy on the MSMARCO-Passage and Natural Questions benchmarks.

paragraphs: Neural retrieval systems score how relevant a document is to a query. Cross-attention models represent the query and document jointly, while dual encoders represent them separately. Cross-attention often performs better empirically. This paper asks whether that gap reflects an inherent restriction in dual encoders or problems with how they are trained.

The theoretical result shows that dual encoders can represent a broad class of score distributions when their embedding dimension is sufficiently large. This establishes a capacity result under an explicit dimensionality condition. It gives a reason to investigate training behavior rather than attributing every observed accuracy gap to the separate-embedding design.

The empirical analysis finds that dual encoders may overfit to spurious correlations in training data and consequently perform worse on test examples. The authors propose a distillation strategy to mitigate that behavior and demonstrate its effectiveness on MSMARCO-Passage and Natural Questions. The findings connect a theoretical account of model capacity with a practical explanation for underperformance and a training-based remedy.
summary.tldr: Dual encoders have broad capacity with sufficiently large embeddings, and targeted distillation can mitigate harmful training correlations.

title: In defense of dual-encoders for neural ranking

abstract: One of the arguments to explain the success of deep learning is the powerful approximation capacity of deep neural networks. Such capacity is generally accompanied by the explosive growth of the number of parameters, which, in turn, leads to high computational costs. It is of great interest to ask whether we can achieve successful deep learning with a small number of learnable parameters adapting to the target function. From an approximation perspective, this paper shows that the number of parameters that need to be learned can be significantly smaller than people typically expect. First, we theoretically design ReLU networks with a few learnable parameters to achieve an attractive approximation. We prove by construction that, for any Lipschitz continuous function $f$ on $[0,1]^d$ with a Lipschitz constant $\lambda>0$, a ReLU network with $n+2$ intrinsic parameters (those depending on $f$) can approximate $f$ with an exponentially small error $5 \lambda \sqrt{d} \, 2^{-n}$. Such a result is generalized to generic continuous functions. Furthermore, we show that the idea of learning a small number of parameters to achieve a good approximation can be numerically observed. We conduct several experiments to verify that training a small part of parameters can also achieve good results for classification problems if other parameters are pre-specified or pre-trained from a related problem.

Such a result is generalized to generic continuous functions. Furthermore, we show that the idea of learning a small number of parameters to achieve a good approximation can be numerically observed. We conduct several experiments to verify that training a small part of parameters can also achieve good results for classification problems if other parameters are pre-specified or pre-trained from a related problem.

paragraphs: A neural network’s total parameter count need not equal the number of parameters that must adapt to a particular target function. This paper studies that distinction through approximation theory. It asks how much function-specific information must be learned when the remaining network structure and parameters can be specified separately.

For any Lipschitz-continuous function on the d-dimensional unit cube with Lipschitz constant λ, the authors construct a ReLU network with n + 2 target-dependent parameters and approximation error bounded by 5λ√d times 2 to the power −n. The bound decreases exponentially with n. They also generalize the construction to continuous functions beyond the Lipschitz case.

These are statements about intrinsic, function-dependent parameters rather than a claim that the entire network has only n + 2 parameters. The authors complement the theory with classification experiments in which only a small subset of parameters is trained. They report good results when the other parameters are predetermined or pretrained on a related problem, illustrating the practical relevance of selective adaptation.
summary.tldr: Constructed ReLU networks can approximate functions accurately with few target-dependent parameters, with experiments supporting selective parameter training.

title: Deep Network Approximation in Terms of Intrinsic Parameters

abstract: Curriculum learning (CL) is a commonly used machine learning training strategy. However, we still lack a clear theoretical understanding of CL’s benefits. In this paper, we study the benefits of CL in the multitask linear regression problem under both structured and unstructured settings. For both settings, we derive the minimax rates for CL with the oracle that provides the optimal curriculum and without the oracle, where the agent has to adaptively learn a good curriculum. Our results reveal that adaptive learning can be fundamentally harder than the oracle learning in the unstructured setting, but it merely introduces a small extra term in the structured setting. To connect theory with practice, we provide justification for a popular empirical method that selects tasks with highest local prediction gain by comparing its guarantees with the minimax rates mentioned above.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning chooses which tasks to learn from during training, but explaining its statistical benefits requires separating a good curriculum from the effort needed to discover one. This paper makes that distinction in multitask linear regression. It considers both structured and unstructured settings and compares an optimal curriculum supplied by an oracle with one learned adaptively by the agent.

For each setting, the authors derive minimax rates, which characterize the best achievable worst-case statistical performance. Their results show that discovering a curriculum can be fundamentally harder than receiving the optimal one in the unstructured setting. In the structured setting, adaptive discovery introduces only a small additional term. Thus, the cost of learning how to allocate training depends substantially on the setting’s structure.

The paper also studies a practical rule that selects tasks with the largest local prediction gain. By comparing its guarantees with the derived minimax rates, the authors provide theoretical justification for this empirical strategy. The contribution connects the potential value of an ideal curriculum with the feasibility of finding a useful one during learning.
summary.tldr: In multitask linear regression, discovering a curriculum can be costly without structure but adds only a small statistical penalty in the structured setting.

title: On the Statistical Benefits of Curriculum Learning

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection plays a crucial role in ensuring the safe deployment of deep neural network (DNN) classifiers. While a myriad of methods have focused on improving the performance of OOD detectors, a critical gap remains in interpreting their decisions. We help bridge this gap by providing explanations for OOD detectors based on learned high-level concepts. We first propose two new metrics for assessing the effectiveness of a particular set of concepts for explaining OOD detectors: 1) detection completeness, which quantifies the sufficiency of concepts for explaining an OOD-detector’s decisions, and 2) concept separability, which captures the distributional separation between in-distribution and OOD data in the concept space. Based on these metrics, we propose an unsupervised framework for learning a set of concepts that satisfy the desired properties of high detection completeness and concept separability, and demonstrate its effectiveness in providing concept-based explanations for diverse off-the-shelf OOD detectors. We also show how to identify prominent concepts contributing to the detection results, and provide further reasoning about their decisions.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detectors help identify inputs that fall outside a classifier's familiar data distribution. A detector can flag an input without making its reasoning understandable. This paper addresses that interpretability problem by explaining detection decisions through learned high-level concepts.

The authors introduce two measures of how useful a concept set is. Detection completeness assesses whether the concepts contain enough information to explain the detector's decisions. Concept separability assesses how distinctly familiar and unfamiliar data are distributed in the concept representation. These measures address complementary questions: whether concepts account for the detector's behavior and whether they reveal differences between the two kinds of data.

An unsupervised learning framework seeks concept sets that score well on both properties. The authors demonstrate explanations for a variety of existing detectors and show how to identify concepts that contribute prominently to particular detection results. The contribution therefore extends beyond giving inputs a detection score: it provides a structured way to inspect what distinctions support that score.
summary.tldr: Learned high-level concepts explain out-of-distribution decisions using measures of decision coverage and distributional separation.

title: Concept-based Explanations for Out-of-Distribution Detectors

abstract: Population Based Training (PBT) is an efficient hyperparameter optimization algorithm. PBT is a single-objective algorithm, but many real-world hyperparameter optimization problems involve two or more conflicting objectives. In this work, we therefore introduce a multi-objective version of PBT, MO-PBT. Our experiments on diverse multi-objective hyperparameter optimization problems (Precision/Recall, Accuracy/Fairness, Accuracy/Adversarial Robustness) show that MO-PBT outperforms random search, single-objective PBT, and the state-of-the-art multi-objective hyperparameter optimization algorithm MO-ASHA.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization often involves competing goals. A setting that improves one measure may make another worse, so a single objective may not capture what a practitioner wants. This paper addresses that issue for Population Based Training, an efficient hyperparameter optimization algorithm originally designed around one objective.

The authors introduce MO-PBT, a version of Population Based Training for multiple objectives. Its purpose is to extend that optimization approach to problems where several performance criteria matter together. The experimental settings examine precision versus recall, accuracy versus fairness, and accuracy versus adversarial robustness, covering different kinds of conflict that can arise when choosing a model.

Across the evaluated problems, the authors report that MO-PBT outperforms random search, single-objective Population Based Training, and MO-ASHA, a state-of-the-art multi-objective hyperparameter optimizer. These findings support extending Population Based Training to account explicitly for competing criteria. The evidence concerns the optimization problems studied; the contribution is an empirically successful multi-objective variant rather than a claim that conflicts between desirable properties disappear.
summary.tldr: MO-PBT extends Population Based Training to competing objectives and outperforms the compared optimizers on the evaluated problems.

title: Multi-Objective Population Based Training

abstract: Parallel neurosymbolic architectures have been applied effectively in NLP by distilling knowledge from a logic theory into a deep model. However, prior art faces several limitations including supporting restricted forms of logic theories and relying on the assumption of independence between the logic and the deep network. We present Concordia, a framework overcoming the limitations of prior art. Concordia is agnostic both to the deep network and the logic theory offering support for a wide range of probabilistic theories. Our framework can support supervised training of both components and unsupervised training of the neural component. Concordia has been successfully applied to tasks beyond NLP and data classification, improving the accuracy of state-of-the-art on collective activity detection, entity linking and recommendation tasks.

paragraphs: Neurosymbolic systems combine neural learning with knowledge expressed through logic. Earlier parallel architectures have transferred logical knowledge into deep models, particularly for language tasks. The paper identifies two restrictions in that work: limited support for different logic theories and an assumption that the logic component and neural network are independent.

Concordia is a framework designed to overcome those restrictions. It is agnostic to the choice of deep network and logic theory, supporting a wide range of probabilistic theories. It can train both components with supervision and can also support unsupervised training of the neural component. These capabilities broaden the kinds of components and training settings that can be brought together.

The authors apply Concordia beyond language processing and data classification, reporting improved accuracy over state-of-the-art methods on collective activity detection, entity linking, and recommendation tasks. These findings support the framework's usefulness across the evaluated applications. Its contribution combines greater flexibility in neural and logical integration with empirical evidence that the resulting systems can improve task accuracy.
summary.tldr: Concordia flexibly integrates neural networks and probabilistic logic, with reported accuracy gains across activity detection, entity linking, and recommendation.

title: Parallel Neurosymbolic Integration with Concordia

abstract: Learning-based high-fidelity reconstruction of 3D shapes with varying topology is a fundamental problem in computer vision and computer graphics. Recent advances in learning 3D shapes using explicit and implicit representations have achieved impressive results in 3D modeling. However, the template-based explicit representation is limited by fixed topology, and the implicit representation, although flexible with arbitrary topology, requires a large number of sampled points to regress the surface, which is computationally expensive. In this work, we propose a novel 3D shape representation named NeuralSlice, which represents a 3D shape as the intersection of a 4D tetrahedral mesh and a 4D hyperplane. A novel network is designed to incorporate the proposed representation flexibly, which learns a deformable 4D template and a parameter for slicing 4D hyperplane to reconstruct the 3D object. To learn the local deformation of the 4D template, we further propose a spatial-aware network to locate the 4D points within the 3D feature volume of input shape via positional encoding, which leverages the local geometrical feature to guide the 4D deformation. By addressing the 3D problem in a higher 4D space, our method supports flexible topology changes while being highly efficient. Our method is guaranteed to produce manifold meshes. NeuralSlice outperforms the state-of-the-art explicit-based approaches in terms of reconstruction quality. Compared with implicit approaches, by avoiding point sampling, our method is 10 times faster than the implicit approaches, and better preserves thin structures. NeuralSlice has the capability of representing various shapes and topologies using a single 4D tetrahedral mesh. The corresponding code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/IGLICT/NEURALSLICE

paragraphs: Reconstructing three-dimensional shapes requires representing both surface geometry and topology, including changes in connectivity. Explicit template methods are constrained by a fixed topology, while implicit methods can handle varied topology but need expensive point sampling. NeuralSlice represents a 3D surface as the intersection of a four-dimensional tetrahedral mesh and a slicing hyperplane.

The network learns both how to deform the 4D template and how to set the slice. A spatially aware component uses positional encoding to relate 4D points to a 3D feature volume, allowing local geometric information to guide deformation. Moving the representation into four dimensions lets a single template support different resulting shapes and topologies.

The method guarantees manifold meshes and surpasses state-of-the-art explicit approaches in reconstruction quality. Compared with the implicit approaches evaluated, it is ten times faster and better preserves thin structures, with its efficiency attributed to avoiding point sampling. These findings show how a higher-dimensional construction can provide flexible surface topology while retaining an efficient route to an explicit triangle mesh.
summary.tldr: NeuralSlice reconstructs flexible-topology 3D meshes by slicing a learned 4D mesh, improving quality and speed in the reported comparisons.

title: NeuralSlice: Neural 3D Triangle Mesh Reconstruction via Slicing 4D Tetrahedral Meshes

abstract: Mirror descent value iteration (MDVI), an abstraction of Kullback-Leibler (KL) and entropy-regularized reinforcement learning (RL), has served as the basis for recent high-performing practical RL algorithms. However, despite the use of function approximation in practice, the theoretical understanding of MDVI has been limited to tabular Markov decision processes (MDPs). We study MDVI with linear function approximation through its sample complexity required to identify an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy with probability $1-\delta$ under the settings of an infinite-horizon linear MDP, generative model, and G-optimal design. We demonstrate that least-squares regression weighted by the variance of an estimated optimal value function of the next state is crucial to achieving minimax optimality. Based on this observation, we present Variance-Weighted Least-Squares MDVI (VWLS-MDVI), the first theoretical algorithm that achieves nearly minimax optimal sample complexity for infinite-horizon linear MDPs. Furthermore, we propose a practical VWLS algorithm for value-based deep RL, Deep Variance Weighting (DVW). Our experiments demonstrate that DVW improves the performance of popular value-based deep RL algorithms on a set of MinAtar benchmarks.

paragraphs: Mirror descent value iteration underlies reinforcement-learning methods using KL or entropy regularization. Despite practical use with function approximation, its theoretical understanding had largely concerned tabular problems. This paper studies its sample requirements with linear function approximation, asking how much data is needed to identify a near-optimal policy with high probability.

The analysis assumes an infinite-horizon linear Markov decision process, access to a generative model, and G-optimal design. Within this setting, the authors identify variance-weighted least-squares regression as crucial to minimax optimality. The weights use the variance of an estimated optimal value function at the next state, making that uncertainty part of the value-estimation procedure.

The resulting VWLS-MDVI algorithm achieves nearly minimax-optimal sample complexity for infinite-horizon linear MDPs. The authors also translate the weighting idea into Deep Variance Weighting, a practical method for value-based deep reinforcement learning. Experiments show improvements to popular algorithms on a set of MinAtar benchmarks. These are complementary contributions: a sample-efficiency guarantee in the specified linear setting and empirical evidence for a related technique in deep RL.
summary.tldr: Variance-weighted regression yields nearly minimax-optimal MDVI in the specified linear-MDP setting and improves deep RL performance on MinAtar.

title: Regularization and Variance-Weighted Regression Achieves Minimax Optimality in Linear MDPs: Theory and Practice

abstract: The average reward criterion is relatively less studied as most existing works in the Reinforcement Learning literature consider the discounted reward criterion. There are few recent works that present on-policy average reward actor-critic algorithms, but average reward off-policy actor-critic is relatively less explored. In this work, we present both on-policy and off-policy deterministic policy gradient theorems for the average reward performance criterion. Using these theorems, we also present an Average Reward Off-Policy Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (ARO-DDPG) Algorithm. We first show asymptotic convergence analysis using the ODE-based method. Subsequently, we provide a finite time analysis of the resulting stochastic approximation scheme with linear function approximator and obtain an $\epsilon$-optimal stationary policy with a sample complexity of $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2.5})$. We compare the average reward performance of our proposed ARO-DDPG algorithm and observe better empirical performance compared to state-of-the-art on-policy average reward actor-critic algorithms over MuJoCo-based environments.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning under an average-reward objective, which evaluates sustained reward rather than discounting rewards farther into the future. It focuses especially on off-policy actor-critic learning, where the policy being improved can differ from the one that produced the training experience. The authors identify this combination as relatively underexplored.

They derive deterministic policy-gradient theorems for both on-policy and off-policy average-reward learning. These results underpin ARO-DDPG, an off-policy deep reinforcement learning algorithm. The paper also provides asymptotic convergence analysis using an ordinary-differential-equation method, connecting the learning updates to a mathematical account of their long-run behavior.

A separate finite-time analysis addresses the stochastic approximation scheme with a linear function approximator. It reports an epsilon-optimal stationary policy with sample complexity Ω(epsilon^−2.5); this statement specifically concerns that linear setting. Experiments in MuJoCo-based environments show better average-reward performance than the compared state-of-the-art on-policy average-reward actor-critic methods, providing empirical support for the proposed off-policy algorithm.
summary.tldr: ARO-DDPG brings deterministic off-policy actor-critic learning to average reward, supported by gradient theorems, convergence analysis, and MuJoCo results.

title: Off-Policy Average Reward Actor-Critic with Deterministic Policy Search

abstract: We introduce Dynamic Contextual Markov Decision Processes (DCMDPs) , a novel reinforcement learning framework for history-dependent environments that generalizes the contextual MDP framework to handle non-Markov environments, where contexts change over time. We consider special cases of the model, with a focus on logistic DCMDPs, which break the exponential dependence on history length by leveraging aggregation functions to determine context transitions. This special structure allows us to derive an upper-confidence-bound style algorithm for which we establish regret bounds. Motivated by our theoretical results, we introduce a practical model-based algorithm for logistic DCMDPs that plans in a latent space and uses optimism over history-dependent features. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on a recommendation task (using MovieLens data) where user behavior dynamics evolve in response to recommendations.

paragraphs: Some environments change in ways that depend on earlier interactions, so a fixed context does not adequately describe them. This paper introduces Dynamic Contextual Markov Decision Processes to represent contexts that evolve over time. The framework extends contextual MDPs to history-dependent environments whose behavior is non-Markovian.

The authors focus on a special case called logistic DCMDPs. Aggregation functions determine context transitions, allowing this structure to avoid exponential dependence on history length. They use it to derive an algorithm based on upper confidence bounds and establish regret bounds. The tractability result is tied to this structured special case.

A recommendation task using MovieLens data demonstrates its effectiveness when user behavior evolves in response to recommendations. This links the formal model to a setting where actions influence both immediate outcomes and the context of later decisions.
summary.tldr: Dynamic contextual MDPs model evolving, history-dependent environments, with tractable learning guarantees and a practical algorithm for a structured logistic case.

title: Reinforcement Learning with History Dependent Dynamic Contexts

abstract: When estimating target parameters in nonparametric models with nuisance parameters, substituting the unknown nuisances with nonparametric estimators can introduce "plug-in bias." Traditional methods addressing this suboptimal bias-variance trade-off rely on the influence function (IF) of the target parameter. When estimating multiple target parameters, these methods require debiasing the nuisance parameter multiple times using the corresponding IFs, which poses analytical and computational challenges. In this work, we leverage the targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) framework to propose a novel method named kernel debiased plug-in estimation (KDPE). KDPE refines an initial estimate through regularized likelihood maximization steps, employing a nonparametric model based on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. We show that KDPE: (i) simultaneously debiases all pathwise differentiable target parameters that satisfy our regularity conditions, (ii) does not require the IF for implementation, and (iii) remains computationally tractable. We numerically illustrate the use of KDPE and validate our theoretical results.
