paragraphs: Estimating a quantity often requires first estimating other, supporting quantities called nuisance parameters. Substituting those estimates into the final calculation can introduce plug-in bias. Existing correction methods rely on a target's influence function, and estimating several targets can require repeated, target-specific debiasing work. This creates analytical and computational burdens.

Kernel Debiased Plug-in Estimation, or KDPE, refines an initial estimate through regularized likelihood-maximization steps. It works within the targeted maximum likelihood framework and uses a nonparametric model built from a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The implementation avoids requiring a separate influence function for each target.

The theoretical result is simultaneous debiasing for all pathwise differentiable targets that meet the paper's regularity conditions. Thus, the coverage is broad but explicitly conditional on properties of the targets and model setting. The authors also establish computational tractability and provide numerical illustrations supporting the theory. The approach matters because one refinement procedure can serve many eligible target quantities, reducing the need for repeated custom corrections.
summary.tldr: KDPE simultaneously debiases eligible target estimates under regularity conditions without requiring influence functions in its implementation.

title: Kernel Debiased Plug-in Estimation: Simultaneous, Automated Debiasing without Influence Functions for Many Target Parameters

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated great potential for generating diverse images. However, their performance often suffers from slow generation due to iterative denoising. Knowledge distillation has been recently proposed as a remedy which can reduce the number of inference steps to one or a few, without significant quality degradation. However, existing distillation methods either require significant amounts of offline computation for generating synthetic training data from the teacher model, or need to perform expensive online learning with the help of real data. In this work, we present a novel technique called BOOT, that overcomes these limitations with an efficient data-free distillation algorithm. The core idea is to learn a time-conditioned model that predicts the output of a pre-trained diffusion model teacher given any time-step. Such a model can be efficiently trained based on bootstrapping from two consecutive sampled steps. Furthermore, our method can be easily adapted to large-scale text-to-image diffusion models, which are challenging for previous methods given the fact that the training sets are often large and difficult to access. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets in the DDIM setting, achieving comparable generation quality while being orders of magnitude faster than the diffusion teacher. The text-to-image results show that the proposed approach is able to handle highly complex distributions, shedding light on more efficient generative modeling.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate images through repeated denoising, making generation slow. Distillation aims to transfer their behavior into a model requiring far fewer steps. Existing approaches can demand either substantial offline work to produce synthetic training examples or expensive online learning that depends on real data.

BOOT introduces a data-free alternative. It trains a time-conditioned model to predict the pretrained teacher's output from any timestep. Training uses bootstrapping between two consecutive sampled steps, providing an efficient way to learn from the teacher without the data requirements described for prior approaches. The method can also be adapted to large text-to-image models, whose original training collections may be difficult to access.

Its text-to-image results also demonstrate the ability to handle complex distributions. The contribution is both a faster generation model and a training procedure that reduces the practical burden of obtaining that model.
summary.tldr: BOOT uses data-free bootstrapping to distill diffusion teachers into much faster generators with comparable quality in the reported DDIM experiments.

title: Data-free Distillation of Diffusion Models with Bootstrapping

abstract: Multi-fidelity surrogate modeling aims to learn an accurate surrogate at the highest fidelity level by combining data from multiple sources. Traditional methods relying on Gaussian processes can hardly scale to high-dimensional data. Deep learning approaches utilize neural network based encoders and decoders to improve scalability. These approaches share encoded representations across fidelities without including corresponding decoder parameters. This hinders inference performance, especially in out-of-distribution scenarios when the highest fidelity data has limited domain coverage. To address these limitations, we propose Multi-fidelity Residual Neural Processes (MFRNP), a novel multi-fidelity surrogate modeling framework. MFRNP explicitly models the residual between the aggregated output from lower fidelities and ground truth at the highest fidelity. The aggregation introduces decoders into the information sharing step and optimizes lower fidelity decoders to accurately capture both in-fidelity and cross-fidelity information. We show that MFRNP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art in learning partial differential equations and a real-world climate modeling task. Our code is published at: https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/MFRNP

Traditional methods relying on Gaussian processes can hardly scale to high-dimensional data. Deep learning approaches utilize neural network based encoders and decoders to improve scalability. These approaches share encoded representations across fidelities without including corresponding decoder parameters. This hinders inference performance, especially in out-of-distribution scenarios when the highest fidelity data has limited domain coverage. To address these limitations, we propose Multi-fidelity Residual Neural Processes (MFRNP), a novel multi-fidelity surrogate modeling framework. MFRNP explicitly models the residual between the aggregated output from lower fidelities and ground truth at the highest fidelity. The aggregation introduces decoders into the information sharing step and optimizes lower fidelity decoders to accurately capture both in-fidelity and cross-fidelity information. We show that MFRNP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art in learning partial differential equations and a real-world climate modeling task. Our code is published at: https://github.com/Rose-STL-Lab/MFRNP

paragraphs: Multi-fidelity surrogate modeling combines sources with different levels of accuracy to predict the highest-fidelity result. Neural approaches improve scalability over traditional Gaussian-process methods, but often share only encoded representations across fidelity levels. The paper identifies this omission of decoder parameters as a weakness, particularly when high-fidelity training data covers only a limited part of the input domain.

Multi-fidelity Residual Neural Processes addresses the problem by combining outputs from lower-fidelity models and explicitly learning the residual between that combination and the highest-fidelity target. Because aggregation happens through decoded outputs, the decoders participate in information sharing. Lower-fidelity decoders are optimized to capture relationships both within their own fidelity and across fidelity levels.

The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on partial differential equation learning and a real-world climate modeling task. The architectural contribution is a concrete way to make lower-fidelity predictions useful to the final target: learn their combined contribution and then model its remaining error. This directly addresses the information-sharing weakness identified in earlier neural surrogate approaches.
summary.tldr: MFRNP combines lower-fidelity model outputs and learns their residual error to improve high-fidelity surrogate predictions.

title: Multi-Fidelity Residual Neural Processes for Scalable Surrogate Modeling

abstract: Conventional state representations in reinforcement learning often omit critical task-related details, presenting a significant challenge for value networks in establishing accurate mappings from states to task rewards. Traditional methods typically depend on extensive sample learning to enrich state representations with task-specific information, which leads to low sample efficiency and high time costs. Recently, surging knowledgeable large language models (LLM) have provided promising substitutes for prior injection with minimal human intervention. Motivated by this, we propose LLM-Empowered State Representation (LESR), a novel approach that utilizes LLM to autonomously generate task-related state representation codes which help to enhance the continuity of network mappings and facilitate efficient training. Experimental results demonstrate LESR exhibits high sample efficiency and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by an average of 29% in accumulated reward in Mujoco tasks and 30% in success rates in Gym-Robotics tasks. Codes of LESR are accessible at https://github.com/thu-rllab/LESR.

paragraphs: LESR addresses the information an agent receives as its state representation. Conventional representations can leave out details that matter for a task, making it harder for a value network to connect states with rewards. Learning those connections from extensive interaction can require many samples and substantial training time.

The method uses a large language model to generate task-related state-representation code autonomously. This puts the language model's knowledge into the representation used by reinforcement learning, with minimal human intervention. The generated representations are intended to improve the continuity of the network's mappings and make training more efficient.

Experiments report high sample efficiency and improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, averaging 29% in accumulated reward on MuJoCo tasks and 30% in success rates on Gym-Robotics tasks. These are separate improvements in different measures, each tied to its evaluated task family. The results support using language-model-generated representation code as a practical way to supply task information that the learner would otherwise need to extract through experience.
summary.tldr: LESR uses language models to generate task-specific state-representation code that improves reinforcement-learning sample efficiency and performance.

title: LLM-Empowered State Representation for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Use of machine learning to perform database operations, such as indexing, cardinality estimation, and sorting, is shown to provide substantial performance benefits. However, when datasets change and data distribution shifts, empirical results also show performance degradation for learned models, possibly to worse than non-learned alternatives. This, together with a lack of theoretical understanding of learned methods undermines their practical applicability, since there are no guarantees on how well the models will perform after deployment. In this paper, we present the first known theoretical characterization of the performance of learned models in dynamic datasets, for the aforementioned operations. Our results show novel theoretical characteristics achievable by learned models and provide bounds on the performance of the models that characterize their advantages over non-learned methods, showing why and when learned models can outperform the alternatives. Our analysis develops the distribution learnability framework and novel theoretical tools which build the foundation for the analysis of learned database operations in the future.

paragraphs: Machine learning can accelerate database operations such as indexing, cardinality estimation, and sorting. However, changing data distributions can erode those gains and sometimes make learned methods worse than conventional alternatives. This paper addresses the lack of theoretical understanding needed to judge their performance after deployment on dynamic datasets.

The authors develop a framework called distribution learnability and use it to characterize the performance of learned versions of these operations. Their bounds describe achievable behavior and the circumstances in which learned models can outperform non-learned methods. The focus is therefore on explaining the conditions behind an advantage, rather than assuming that training a model automatically produces one.

The paper presents this as the first known theoretical characterization covering these learned operations in dynamic datasets. Its contribution is a set of guarantees and analytical tools for reasoning about performance as datasets change. These results provide a foundation for future analysis of learned database systems and help connect observed speed benefits with a more explicit account of when those benefits are achievable.
summary.tldr: Distribution learnability provides theoretical bounds explaining when learned database operations can outperform conventional methods as data distributions change.

title: Theoretical Analysis of Learned Database Operations under Distribution Shift through Distribution Learnability

abstract: Neural Temporal Point Processes (TPPs) have emerged as the primary framework for predicting sequences of events that occur at irregular time intervals, but their sequential nature can hamper performance for long-horizon forecasts. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that incorporates a diffusion generative model. The model facilitates sequence-to-sequence prediction, allowing multi-step predictions based on historical event sequences. In contrast to previous approaches, our model directly learns the joint probability distribution of types and inter-arrival times for multiple events. The model is composed of two diffusion processes, one for the time intervals and one for the event types. These processes interact through their respective denoising functions, which can take as input intermediate representations from both processes, allowing the model to learn complex interactions. We demonstrate that our proposal outperforms state-of-the-art baselines for long-horizon forecasting of TPPs.

paragraphs: Event-sequence forecasting must predict both what happens and how much time passes between events. Neural temporal point processes are a common framework for this task, but their sequential structure can hamper long-horizon forecasting. This paper instead uses diffusion generation to predict multiple future events from a historical event sequence.

The model directly learns a joint distribution over future event types and the intervals between them. It contains two diffusion processes: one handles time intervals, and the other handles event categories. Their denoising functions can access intermediate representations from both processes, allowing predictions about timing and event identity to inform each other.

This interaction is the key distinction from treating the two kinds of output separately. The sequence-to-sequence formulation also makes multi-step forecasting part of the model’s direct objective. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines for long-horizon temporal point-process forecasting. The results support jointly modeling timing, categories, and their interactions when predicting an extended sequence of future events.
summary.tldr: Two interacting diffusion processes jointly forecast event types and time intervals, improving reported long-horizon event-sequence predictions.

title: Interacting Diffusion Processes for Event Sequence Forecasting

abstract: This paper introduces a family of learning-augmented algorithms for online knapsack problems that achieve near Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness trade-offs through a simple combination of trusted learning-augmented and worst-case algorithms. Our approach relies on succinct, practical predictions—single values or intervals estimating the minimum value of any item in an offline solution. Additionally, we propose a novel fractional-to-integral conversion procedure, offering new insights for online algorithm design.

Additionally, we propose a novel fractional-to-integral conversion procedure, offering new insights for online algorithm design.

paragraphs: Online knapsack algorithms must make selection decisions as items arrive, without the complete information available to an offline solution. Predictions can help guide those decisions, but trusting them introduces a trade-off. Consistency captures the benefit of useful predictions, while robustness concerns performance when predictions are unreliable. This paper develops algorithms that balance those objectives.

The proposed family combines a trusted learning-augmented algorithm with an algorithm designed for worst-case performance. Its predictions are compact: a single value or an interval estimating the minimum item value in an offline solution. This gives the method a specific, succinct piece of predictive information to use when making online decisions.

The authors establish near Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness trade-offs, meaning the resulting balance is close to the frontier of what can be jointly achieved. They also introduce a procedure for converting fractional solutions into integral ones. That conversion contributes to the design of online algorithms that must ultimately make discrete selections, while the main result shows how combining predictive and worst-case methods can approach the attainable trade-off.
summary.tldr: Combining prediction-guided and worst-case algorithms yields near-optimal trade-offs between consistency and robustness for online knapsack problems.

title: Near-Optimal Consistency-Robustness Trade-Offs for Learning-Augmented Online Knapsack Problems

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized artificial intelligence with capabilities in reasoning, coding, and communication, driving innovation across industries. Their true potential depends on effective alignment to ensure correct, trustworthy and ethical behavior, addressing challenges like misinformation, hallucinations, bias and misuse. While existing Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based alignment methods are notoriously complex, direct optimization approaches offer a simpler alternative. In this work, we introduce a novel direct optimization approach for LLM alignment by drawing on established Information Retrieval (IR) principles. We present a systematic framework that bridges LLM alignment and IR methodologies, mapping LLM generation and reward models to IR’s retriever-reranker paradigm. Building on this foundation, we propose LLM Alignment as Retriever Preference Optimization (LarPO), a new alignment method that enhances overall alignment quality. Extensive experiments validate LarPO’s effectiveness with 38.9 % and 13.7 % averaged improvement on AlpacaEval2 and MixEval-Hard respectively. Our work opens new avenues for advancing LLM alignment by integrating IR foundations, offering a promising direction for future research.

paragraphs: This paper approaches language-model alignment through information retrieval. Alignment seeks to improve how models behave, while reinforcement-learning-based approaches can be complex to implement. The authors develop a direct optimization framework that connects language generation and reward modeling to the retriever-and-reranker pattern used in information retrieval, providing another foundation for designing alignment methods.

Within this mapping, the generation model corresponds to a retriever and the reward model corresponds to a reranker. That correspondence connects the production of candidate responses with their evaluation according to preferences. The resulting method, LLM Alignment as Retriever Preference Optimization, or LarPO, uses this framework to improve alignment through direct optimization.

Experiments report average improvements of 38.9% on AlpacaEval2 and 13.7% on MixEval-Hard. These results provide empirical support for LarPO on the evaluated benchmarks and for the usefulness of the retrieval perspective. The paper’s contribution combines a concrete alignment method with a systematic connection between two research areas, creating a basis for further methods informed by information retrieval.
summary.tldr: LarPO uses a retriever-reranker interpretation of generation and reward models to improve alignment through direct preference optimization.

title: LLM Alignment as Retriever Optimization: An Information Retrieval Perspective

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are regularly evaluated using benchmark datasets. But what justifies making inferences about an LLM’s capabilities based on its answers to a curated set of questions? This paper first introduces a formal framework to address this question. The key is to note that the benchmarks used to test LLMs—such as AP exams—are also those used to test people. However, this raises an implication: such benchmarks are only valid tests if LLMs misunderstand concepts in ways that mirror human misunderstandings. Otherwise, success on benchmarks only demonstrates potemkin understanding: the illusion of understanding driven by answers irreconcilable with how any human would interpret a concept. We present two procedures for quantifying the existence of potemkins: one using a specially designed benchmark in three domains, the other using a general procedure that provides a lower-bound on their prevalence. We find that potemkins are ubiquitous across models, tasks, and domains. We also find that these failures reflect not just incorrect understanding, but deeper internal incoherence in concept representations.

paragraphs: A model’s correct answers on a benchmark are often treated as evidence that it understands the tested concepts. This paper develops a formal framework for examining that inference, especially when the benchmark was also designed to test people. The issue is whether the same observed answers justify the same interpretation of ability.

Within the framework, those benchmarks are valid tests only if model misunderstandings mirror human misunderstandings. The authors call apparent success based on answers incompatible with any human interpretation of a concept potemkin understanding. This makes the coherence of answers across uses of a concept central to assessing what benchmark success actually establishes.

The paper introduces two measurement procedures: a purpose-built benchmark spanning three domains and a general method that gives a lower bound on the prevalence of these failures. The authors find them widespread across the examined models, tasks, and domains. They interpret the failures as evidence of internal incoherence in concept representations, beyond simply holding an incorrect understanding. The result challenges straightforward human-style interpretations of model benchmark performance.
summary.tldr: The paper finds widespread incoherence in LLM concept use that can make correct benchmark answers misleading evidence of human-like understanding.

title: Potemkin Understanding in Large Language Models

abstract: Large language model training with 8-bit floating point (FP8) formats promises significant efficiency improvements, but reduced numerical precision makes training challenging. It is currently possible to train in FP8 only if one is willing to tune various hyperparameters, reduce model scale, or accept the overhead of computing dynamic scale factors. We demonstrate simple, scalable FP8 training that requires no dynamic scaling factors or special hyperparameters, even at large model sizes. Our method, $\bm{\mu}$nit Scaling ($\bm{\mu}$S), also enables simple hyperparameter transfer across model widths, matched numerics across training and inference, and other desirable properties. $\bm{\mu}$nit Scaling is straightforward to implement, consisting of a set of minimal interventions based on a first-principles analysis of transformer operations. We validate our method by training models with parameters ranging from 1B to 13B, performing all hidden linear layer computations in FP8. We achieve quality equal to higher-precision baselines while also training up to 33% faster.

paragraphs: Training with eight-bit floating point numbers promises greater efficiency, but the reduced precision makes numerical behavior harder to manage. Existing approaches can require special tuning, smaller models, or dynamically computed scale factors. This paper presents μnit Scaling, a method designed to make FP8 training straightforward at larger model sizes.

The method consists of minimal changes derived from an analysis of transformer operations. It requires neither dynamic scaling factors nor special hyperparameters. It also supports transferring hyperparameters across model widths and matching numerical behavior between training and inference. These properties address practical complications beyond the arithmetic format itself.

The authors validate μnit Scaling by training models ranging from one billion to thirteen billion parameters, with all hidden linear layer computations performed in FP8. They report quality matching higher-precision baselines and training speed improvements of up to 33%. The evidence supports low-precision training at the tested scales without the usual scaling machinery described in the paper. The stated FP8 coverage applies specifically to hidden linear layer computations, preserving the scope of the demonstrated result.
summary.tldr: μnit Scaling enables FP8 hidden linear computations without dynamic scaling, matching higher-precision quality with up to 33% faster training.

title: $\mathrmμ$nit Scaling: Simple and Scalable FP8 LLM Training

abstract: We present a new method for generating confidence sets within the split conformal prediction framework. Our method performs a trainable transformation of any given conformity score to improve conditional coverage while ensuring exact marginal coverage. The transformation is based on an estimate of the conditional quantile of conformity scores. The resulting method is particularly beneficial for constructing adaptive confidence sets in multi-output problems where standard conformal quantile regression approaches have limited applicability. We develop a theoretical bound that captures the influence of the accuracy of the quantile estimate on the approximate conditional validity, unlike classical bounds for conformal prediction methods that only offer marginal coverage. We experimentally show that our method is highly adaptive to the local data structure and outperforms existing methods in terms of conditional coverage, improving the reliability of statistical inference in various applications.

Our method performs a trainable transformation of any given conformity score to improve conditional coverage while ensuring exact marginal coverage. The transformation is based on an estimate of the conditional quantile of conformity scores. The resulting method is particularly beneficial for constructing adaptive confidence sets in multi-output problems where standard conformal quantile regression approaches have limited applicability. We develop a theoretical bound that captures the influence of the accuracy of the quantile estimate on the approximate conditional validity, unlike classical bounds for conformal prediction methods that only offer marginal coverage. We experimentally show that our method is highly adaptive to the local data structure and outperforms existing methods in terms of conditional coverage, improving the reliability of statistical inference in various applications.

paragraphs: A prediction set can achieve its intended coverage on average while being less reliable for particular kinds of inputs. This paper addresses that difference within split conformal prediction. It introduces a trainable transformation of an existing conformity score, aiming to improve coverage conditional on the input while preserving exact marginal coverage across the overall data distribution.

The transformation uses an estimate of a conditional quantile of the conformity scores. This lets the method adapt to local data structure rather than treating the score’s behavior as uniform across inputs. Because it transforms a supplied score, the approach is especially useful for multi-output prediction problems where standard conformal quantile regression has limited applicability.

The theoretical analysis bounds approximate conditional validity in terms of how accurately that conditional quantile is estimated. Thus, exact marginal coverage and improved conditional coverage have different guarantees in the result. Experiments show strong local adaptation and better conditional coverage than existing methods. The contribution provides both a practical adjustment to prediction sets and a mathematical connection between the quality of that adjustment and its conditional reliability.
summary.tldr: Learning a quantile-based transformation of conformity scores improves conditional coverage while retaining exact marginal coverage.

title: Rectifying Conformity Scores for Better Conditional Coverage

abstract: Generative replay (GR) has been extensively validated in continual learning as a mechanism to synthesize data and replay past knowledge to mitigate forgetting. By leveraging synthetic rather than real data for the replay, GR has been adopted in some federated continual learning (FCL) approaches to ensure the privacy of client-side data. While existing GR-based FCL approaches have introduced improvements, none of their enhancements specifically take into account the unique characteristics of federated learning settings. Beyond privacy constraints, what other fundamental aspects of federated learning should be explored in the context of FCL? In this work, we explore the potential benefits that come from emphasizing the role of clients throughout the process. We begin by highlighting two key observations: (a) Client Expertise Superiority, where clients, rather than the server, act as domain experts, and (b) Client Forgetting Variance, where heterogeneous data distributions across clients lead to varying levels of forgetting. Building on these insights, we propose CAN (Clients As Navigators), highlighting the pivotal role of clients in both data synthesis and data replay. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that this client-centric approach achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, it requires a smaller buffer size, reducing storage overhead and enhancing computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Continual learning systems can forget earlier knowledge as they learn new material. Generative replay addresses this by synthesizing examples that revisit past knowledge. In federated continual learning, synthetic replay also provides a way to avoid replaying real client data. This paper asks how replay can make better use of the distinctive roles and differences of participating clients.

The approach starts from two observations: clients can have greater expertise in their own domains than the server, and clients with different data distributions can experience different amounts of forgetting. CAN, short for Clients As Navigators, incorporates clients into both the generation of synthetic data and the replay process.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across extensive evaluations while using a smaller replay buffer. That reduction lowers storage overhead and improves computational efficiency. The broader contribution is to make client knowledge and client-specific forgetting central to replay design, showing that these characteristics can matter alongside the privacy motivation for using synthetic data.
summary.tldr: CAN uses client expertise and differences in forgetting to guide generative replay, reporting stronger performance with a smaller buffer.

title: CAN: Leveraging Clients As Navigators for Generative Replay in Federated Continual Learning

abstract: Kernel methods are powerful tools for nonlinear learning with well-established theory. The scalability issue has been their long-standing challenge. Despite the existing success, there are two limitations in large-scale kernel methods: (i) The memory overhead is too high for users to afford; (ii) existing efforts mainly focus on kernel ridge regression (KRR), while other models lack study. In this paper, we propose Joker, a joint optimization framework for diverse kernel models, including KRR, logistic regression, and support vector machines. We design a dual block coordinate descent method with trust region (DBCD-TR) and adopt kernel approximation with randomized features, leading to low memory costs and high efficiency in large-scale learning. Experiments show that Joker saves up to 90% memory but achieves comparable training time and performance (or even better) than the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Kernel methods provide a theoretically established way to learn nonlinear relationships, but their memory demands can make large datasets difficult to handle. The paper identifies another imbalance: much work on scalable kernel learning concentrates on kernel ridge regression. Joker aims to address both the memory burden and the narrower coverage of existing approaches.

Joker supplies a joint optimization framework for kernel ridge regression, logistic regression, and support vector machines. It combines a dual block coordinate descent procedure with a trust-region mechanism and approximates kernels using randomized features. These choices bring optimization and kernel approximation into the same framework, with the stated goal of making several types of kernel model practical at larger scales.

Experiments report memory savings of up to 90% relative to state-of-the-art methods, with comparable or sometimes better training time and predictive performance. The result suggests that substantial memory reduction need not require a corresponding loss of speed or accuracy in the tested settings. Its broader significance is extending that efficiency strategy beyond a single kernel model.
summary.tldr: Joker combines randomized kernel features with joint optimization to support several kernel models while saving up to 90% memory in experiments.

title: Joker: Joint Optimization Framework for Lightweight Kernel Machines

abstract: Recent advances in bioengineering have enabled the creation of biological neural networks in vitro, significantly reducing the cost, ethical hurdles, and complexity of experimentation with genuine biological neural computation. In this position paper, we argue that this trend offers a unique and timely opportunity to put our understanding of neural computation to the test. By designing artificial neural networks that can interact and control living neural systems, it is becoming possible to validate computational models beyond simulation and gain empirical insights to help unlock more robust and energy-efficient next-generation AI systems. We provide an overview of key technologies, challenges, and principles behind this development and describe strategies and opportunities for novel machine learning research in this emerging field. We also discuss implications and fundamental questions that could be answered as this technology advances, exemplifying the longer-term impact of increasingly sophisticated in vitro neural networks.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that biological neural networks grown in laboratory settings offer a timely opportunity to test ideas about neural computation. Advances in bioengineering have reduced the cost, complexity, and ethical hurdles of working with these systems. The authors see this as a way to bring computational theories into closer contact with living neural activity.

The proposed research direction involves artificial neural networks that interact with and control living neural systems. Such interaction could allow computational models to be evaluated beyond simulation. The paper surveys relevant technologies, principles, and challenges, and describes strategies through which machine learning researchers could investigate this emerging experimental setting.

The longer-term motivation is to learn principles that may help build more robust and energy-efficient AI. The authors also discuss fundamental questions that increasingly sophisticated laboratory neural networks could help answer. These benefits are presented as opportunities enabled by technological progress. The paper’s central contribution is a research case and overview, rather than a claim that biological experimentation has already produced the proposed next generation of AI systems.
summary.tldr: Laboratory-grown neural networks could help test computational theories and inform more robust, energy-efficient AI.

title: Position: It Is Time We Test Neural Computation In Vitro

abstract: Adapting large-scale pre-trained video generators for Video Super-Resolution (VSR) in novel domains remains computationally prohibitive. Methods that reformulate generation as direct Low-Quality to High-Quality mappings deviate from the original generative formulation, demanding extensive fine-tuning. ControlNet-style adapters lose their efficiency under modern Diffusion Transformers since the absence of encoder-decoder hierarchy forces duplication of the entire backbone. We observe that flow matching offers a principled alternative for cross-domain VSR adaptation. By predicting a constant velocity field across all timesteps, the adaptation task reduces to learning a fixed injection pattern rather than time-varying transformations. Building on this insight, we propose LiteVSR, a minimalist framework that performs VSR using a completely frozen Diffusion Transformer with a lightweight State-Aware Adapter. The adapter employs a dual-stream architecture that extracts static structural cues from the LQ input and dynamic cues from intermediate denoising states, aligning them through time-dependent cross-attention to enable adaptive transition from structural alignment to texture refinement as denoising proceeds. LiteVSR achieves competitive restoration quality with only 11.25% trainable parameters and 12 GPU-hours of training on a single A100, while maintaining fast sampling (down to a single step) compatibility.

abstract: Large language model inference is often bounded by memory footprint and bandwidth in resource-constrained deployments, making quantization fundamental to efficient serving. While post-training quantization (PTQ) maintains high fidelity at 4-bit, it deteriorates at 2-3 bits. In essence, existing methods enforce a shape-invariant quantization grid (e.g., the fixed uniform intervals of UINT2) for each group, severely restricting the feasible set for error minimization. To address this, we propose Bit-Plane Decomposition Quantization (BPDQ), which constructs a variable quantization grid via bit-planes and scalar coefficients, and iteratively refines them using second-order information while progressively compensating for quantization errors to minimize output discrepancy. In the 2-bit regime, BPDQ enables serving Qwen2.5-72B on a single RTX 3090 with 83.85% GSM8K accuracy (vs. 90.83% at 16-bit). Moreover, we theoretically show that the variable grid expands the feasible set, and that the quantization process consistently aligns with the optimization objective in Hessian-induced geometry. The code is available at github.com/KingdalfGoodman/BPDQ.

title: BPDQ: Bit-Plane Decomposition Quantization on a Variable Grid for Large Language Models

abstract: We present learning-augmented algorithms for two general classes of online minimization problems: metrical task systems and laminar set cover. Both algorithms achieve improved theoretical guarantees using machine-learned predictions of an optimal solution to the dual linear program. Unlike optimal primal solutions, which can change drastically under tiny instance perturbations, these dual solutions are much more stable, which ensures the existence of good (and learnable) predictions for families of similar instances. While previous work has used dual predictions in offline settings and for online maximization problems, our algorithms are, to the best of our knowledge, the first demonstration that such dual predictions can be effective for online minimization. Our theoretical results are complemented by experiments on the $k$-server problem and the parking permit problem.

This paper studies how learned predictions can improve algorithms for metrical task systems and laminar set cover. Its central choice is to predict an optimal solution of the dual linear program rather than the original, or primal, optimization problem.

The motivation is stability across related instances. An optimal primal solution may change sharply after a small change to the problem, making it a difficult prediction target. The authors argue that the corresponding dual solutions are substantially more stable, ensuring the existence of good, learnable predictions for families of similar instances.

Using these dual predictions, the paper develops algorithms with improved theoretical guarantees for both problem classes. Experiments on the k-server and parking permit problems complement the theory. The authors position the work as, to their knowledge, the first demonstration of effective dual predictions for online minimization, extending an approach previously used in offline optimization and online maximization.
summary.tldr: Predicting more stable dual solutions improves theoretical guarantees for online algorithms in metrical task systems and laminar set cover.

title: Learning-Augmented Online Minimization with Dual Predictions

abstract: In this paper, we present the convergence analysis of the proximal Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) for problems with block anti-upper triangular constraints. While the linear constraints can be treated separately, most analyses of ADMM and its variants predominantly regard the linear constraints as one. Hence, it relies on assumptions related to the entire constraint matrix, such as the full column rank. However, some problems with block anti-upper triangular constraints that can be solved by ADMM do not satisfy these assumptions. To fill this gap, a new assumption is proposed and used to guarantee the global convergence of the proximal ADMM for nonconvex problems. In the strongly convex setting, we also prove the global convergence of the proximal ADMM and establish the linear convergence under four different scenarios. This work extends the theoretical understanding of the multi-block ADMM to more general cases with block anti-upper triangular constraints.

Its focus is a particular arrangement of linear constraints, called block anti-upper triangular structure. Existing analyses often combine all constraints into one matrix and require properties of that entire matrix, such as full column rank.

That approach leaves a gap: some problems with this block structure can be solved by ADMM even though they fail the usual matrix assumptions. These results broaden the theoretical coverage of multiblock proximal ADMM; the guarantees remain tied to the stated assumptions and scenarios, rather than applying to every problem with multiple variable blocks.
summary.tldr: A new convergence analysis extends proximal ADMM guarantees to structured multiblock problems that can fall outside standard matrix assumptions.

title: A proximal ADMM for multiblock problems with block anti-upper triangular constraints

abstract: Rectified-flow-based diffusion transformers, particularly FLUX, have demonstrated outstanding performance in high-quality image generation. However, achieving fast and accurate inversion—transforming images back to latent noise for faithful reconstruction and editing—remains a challenging bottleneck due to the discretization errors of linear solvers. This paper introduces SlerpFlow, a straightforward yet highly effective zero-shot approach that unlocks the full potential of FLUX for high-fidelity inversion and editing. Unlike existing approaches (e.g., RF-Solver) that rely on complex numerical approximations such as high-order Taylor expansions to correct trajectory errors, we present a geometric view based on the Manifold Hypothesis: the empirically observed trajectory curvature is not a numerical artifact, but rather serves as a necessary “centripetal force” that constrains the flow to remain on the data manifold. Guided by this insight, SlerpFlow integrates Spherical Linear Interpolation (Slerp) to rectify flow velocity directions on the hypersphere, strictly adhering to the intrinsic curvature of the latent space. Crucially, by caching the corrected velocity for subsequent steps, SlerpFlow achieves high-precision inversion while maintaining the computational efficiency of a first-order Euler solver. Extensive experiments on FLUX-based reconstruction and editing tasks demonstrate that SlerpFlow improves reconstruction fidelity and achieves stronger semantic alignment in editing without requiring additional training. Code is available at https://github.com/0answer0/SlerpFlow.

title: SlerpFlow: Spherical Trajectory Correction for Rectified Flow Inversion

abstract: In this work, we propose One-shot Entropy Minimization (EM), a simple and fully unsupervised post-training approach that significantly improves reasoning and generation performance using only a single unlabeled data and approximately ten gradient steps. To avoid data contamination, we pretrain a 7-billion-parameter language model from scratch with strictly decontaminated data. Despite its extreme simplicity, one-shot EM yields substantial performance gains and improves reasoning abilities across a broad range of domains, including mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, and coding. We further show that entropy minimization induces a characteristic right-skewed logit shift, amplifying high-probability tokens while suppressing low-probability tails, in contrast to reinforcement learning. Our findings suggest that entropy minimization primarily acts as a distribution shaping mechanism rather than a conventional learning process, offering an efficient and practical algorithm for post-training large language models.

paragraphs: The paper studies an unusually small post-training intervention: entropy minimization using one unlabeled example and roughly ten gradient steps. Entropy measures how spread out a model’s predicted probabilities are, so minimizing it encourages a more concentrated output distribution. The approach is fully unsupervised and does not depend on labeled answers for this update.

To address data contamination, the authors pretrain a seven-billion-parameter language model from scratch using strictly decontaminated data. They report substantial improvements in generation and reasoning across mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, and coding. The breadth of the reported gains is central to the finding, given the very small amount of data and optimization used.

Their analysis finds a characteristic right-skewed change in logits, the scores underlying token probabilities: high-probability tokens are amplified and low-probability tails suppressed. They distinguish this pattern from reinforcement learning. The findings suggest that the intervention mainly reshapes the model’s output distribution rather than functioning as conventional learning, offering an efficient post-training procedure in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Entropy minimization with one unlabeled example and about ten gradient steps improves reasoning by reshaping token probabilities.

title: One-shot Entropy Minimization for Language Model Reasoning

abstract: A key challenge in normalizing flows is finding expressive invertible scalar bijections. Existing approaches face trade-offs: affine transformations are smooth and analytically invertible but lack expressivity; monotonic splines offer local control but are only piecewise smooth and act on bounded domains; residual flows achieve smoothness but need numerical inversion. We introduce three families of analytic bijections that are globally smooth ($C^\infty$), defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$, and analytically invertible in closed form, combining the favorable properties of prior approaches. Beyond serving as drop-in replacements in coupling flows, where they match or exceed spline performance, we develop radial flows: a novel architecture using direct parametrization that transforms the radial coordinate while preserving angular direction. Radial flows exhibit exceptional training stability, produce geometrically interpretable transformations, and on targets with radial structure can achieve comparable quality to coupling flows with $1000\times$ fewer parameters. We provide comprehensive evaluation on 1D and 2D benchmarks, and demonstrate applicability to higher-dimensional physics problems through experiments on $\phi^4$ lattice field theory, where our bijections outperform affine baselines and enable problem-specific designs that address mode collapse.

Existing scalar transformations trade off useful properties: affine maps have limited expressivity, splines are only piecewise smooth and operate on bounded domains, and residual approaches require numerical inversion. These choices affect how a flow represents a distribution and how conveniently it can be evaluated.

The paper introduces three transformation families that are smooth everywhere, operate across the entire real line, and have closed-form inverses. Used inside coupling flows, they match or exceed spline performance. The authors also build radial flows that change distance from a center while preserving direction, giving the transformation a direct geometric interpretation.

For targets with radial structure, radial flows can reach comparable quality to coupling flows with 1,000 times fewer parameters. The paper also reports strong training stability and improvements over affine baselines in the physics setting, where tailored designs address mode collapse.
summary.tldr: New analytically invertible transformations give normalizing flows global smoothness and support compact, interpretable radial architectures.

title: Analytic Bijections for Smooth and Interpretable Normalizing Flows

abstract: Conformal prediction provides rigorous, distribution-free uncertainty guarantees, but often yields prohibitively large prediction sets in structured domains such as routing, planning, or sequential recommendation. We introduce graph-based conformal compression, a framework for constructing compact subgraphs that preserve statistical validity while reducing structural complexity. We formulate compression as selecting a smallest subgraph capturing a prescribed fraction of the probability mass, and reduce to a weighted version of densest-k-subgraphs in hypergraphs, in the regime where the subgraph has a large fraction of edges. We design efficient approximation algorithms that achieve constant factor coverage and size trade-offs. Crucially, we prove that our relaxation satisfies a monotonicity property, derived from a connection to parametric minimum cuts, which guarantees the nestedness required for valid conformal calibration. Our results therefore not only highlight an algorithmic regime, distinct from classical densest-k-subgraph hardness settings, where the problem can be approximated efficiently, but also bridge conformal prediction with combinatorial graph compression via monotonicity. We finally validate our algorithmic approach via simulations for trip planning and navigation, and compare to natural baselines.

For routing or planning, that set can become structurally unwieldy. This paper asks how to represent uncertainty with a compact subgraph while preserving the validity of conformal calibration.

The authors formulate compression as finding the smallest subgraph that retains a specified share of probability mass. They connect this problem to a weighted hypergraph version of densest-k-subgraph, focusing on a regime where the selected subgraph contains a large fraction of edges. summary.tldr: Graph-based compression builds smaller conformal prediction subgraphs while preserving the nestedness needed for valid calibration.

title: Compact Conformal Subgraphs

abstract: Most semi-supervised learning frameworks rely on a single teacher that transfers zero-order supervision through pseudo-labels, constraining the student to imitate categorical outputs without perceiving the loss geometry. This design often leads to unstable optimization and limited generalization under scarce labels. We propose TTN (Two-Teachers Newton-guided Learning), a dual-teacher framework that integrates complementary supervision from MAE and DINOv3 and optimizes the student through a Newton step update. The two teachers provide multi-scale structural and semantic cues whose pseudo-labels and local Hessians are fused by confidence weighting, forming a unified second-order supervision signal. The student updates parameters preconditioned by the fused curvature, enabling stable convergence and geometry-consistent learning. TTN consistently improves over existing single-teacher and consistency-based semi-supervised learning methods on ImageNet, CIFAR-10, SVHN, and STL-10, demonstrating that combining multi-view self-supervised teachers with curvature-guided optimization yields robust and efficient semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning often trains a student using pseudo-labels supplied by a teacher. Those labels identify desired outputs but do not describe the local geometry of the training loss. This paper links that restricted supervision to unstable optimization and limited generalization when labeled data are scarce, then proposes a framework with two complementary teachers.

TTN combines supervision from MAE and DINOv3. Their structural and semantic cues operate at multiple scales, and the framework fuses both their pseudo-labels and local Hessians using confidence weights. The Hessians provide curvature information about the loss. A Newton-guided student update uses this combined curvature to precondition parameter changes, making the optimization responsive to geometry as well as predicted categories.

Across ImageNet, CIFAR-10, SVHN, and STL-10, TTN consistently improves on the evaluated single-teacher and consistency-based methods. The findings support coupling complementary self-supervised teachers with curvature-guided optimization. Its central contribution is to enrich what the student receives: supervision includes both the teachers’ predictions and second-order information that helps guide how the student moves toward those predictions.
summary.tldr: TTN combines two teachers’ predictions and loss curvature to guide more effective semi-supervised student learning.

title: Newton-coupled Dual-Teacher Semi-supervised Learning Framework

abstract: Rapid expansion of urban areas and population growth is causing an immense increase in waste production, which demands the need for efficient and automated waste management. In this scenario, automated waste recycling (AWR) using deep learning methods can assist humans in optimal waste management. Recent deep learning approaches for AWR provide promising waste segmentation performance, however, these methods rely on large backbone networks that are inefficient for AWR systems and suffer from performance deterioration in cluttered scenes. To this end, an optimal waste segmentation network is introduced which effectively utilizes the spatial domain to capture localized structural dependencies and the spectral domain to efficiently extract global contextual relationships. This cascaded design allows the network to progressively leverage both local and global representations across complementary domains to highlight the semantic information necessary for effective segmentation of various waste objects. Furthermore, auxiliary feature enhancement module (AFEM) is introduced to enhance the target objects’ boundaries and blob amplification for better segmentation in cluttered scenarios. Extensive experimentation on ZeroWaste-aug, ZeroWaste-f and SpectralWaste datasets reveals the merits of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Automated recycling needs systems that can separate waste objects from their surroundings in images. Existing deep-learning approaches can rely on large backbones and lose segmentation quality in cluttered scenes. This paper proposes a waste-segmentation network designed to combine useful local detail with broader contextual information efficiently.

The network uses a cascaded design spanning spatial and spectral processing. Spatial processing captures localized structural relationships, while spectral processing extracts global contextual relationships. Passing through these complementary representations progressively helps the model emphasize semantic information needed to identify different waste objects. The approach therefore addresses both the structure of individual objects and their relationship to the wider scene.

An auxiliary feature enhancement module further strengthens object boundaries and amplifies object regions, targeting the difficulty of separating waste from clutter. Experiments on ZeroWaste-aug, ZeroWaste-f, and SpectralWaste support the proposed method’s merits. The stated contribution is the combined segmentation design and its evaluation across these datasets, with local structure, global context, and boundary enhancement serving complementary roles.
summary.tldr: A cascaded spatial-and-spectral network combines local structure, global context, and boundary enhancement for waste segmentation in clutter.

title: Towards Effective Waste Segmentation for Automated Waste Recycling in Cluttered Background

abstract: Role specialization in multi-LLM agent systems is often realized via multi-LoRA, where agents share a pretrained backbone and differ only through lightweight adapters. Despite sharing base model weights, each agent independently builds and stores its own KV cache for the same long, tool-augmented trajectories, incurring substantial memory and compute overhead. Existing KV cache sharing methods largely overlook this multi-LoRA setting. We observe that, across agents, cache differences are dominated by adapter outputs, while activations from the shared pretrained backbone remain highly similar. Based on this observation, we propose LRAgent, a KV cache sharing framework for multi-LoRA agents that decomposes the cache into a shared base component from the pretrained weights and an adapter-dependent component from LoRA weights. LRAgent reduces memory overhead by sharing the base component and storing the adapter component in its inherent low-rank form, and further reduces compute overhead, enabled by shared-$A$ multi-LoRA architectures, by also sharing the low-rank cache and avoiding redundant computations for contexts already processed by other agents. To efficiently reconstruct adapter contributions at runtime, we introduce Flash-LoRA-Attention, a kernel that reorders attention computation to avoid materializing the low-rank cache to full dimension. LRAgent achieves throughput and time-to-first-token latency close to fully shared caching, while preserving accuracy near the non-shared caching baseline across agentic question-answering benchmarks.

paragraphs: Multi-agent language systems can specialize agents through lightweight LoRA adapters while sharing a pretrained backbone. Yet each agent may still build a separate attention cache for the same long interaction history. LRAgent targets this duplicated storage and computation, using the observation that backbone activations remain highly similar while adapter outputs dominate differences between agents.

The framework separates the cache into a shared backbone component and an adapter-dependent component stored in low-rank form. With shared-A multi-LoRA architectures, it can also share the low-rank cache and reuse computation for contexts another agent has processed. Its Flash-LoRA-Attention kernel reorders attention operations so adapter contributions need not be expanded into a full-dimensional cache.

On agentic question-answering benchmarks, LRAgent achieves throughput and time-to-first-token latency close to fully shared caching, while maintaining accuracy near the separate-cache baseline. The results show that exploiting the structure of adapter differences can recover much of sharing’s efficiency while retaining agent specialization. The additional low-rank sharing benefits specifically rely on the stated shared-A architecture.
summary.tldr: LRAgent shares backbone and structured adapter caches to reduce multi-LoRA agent overhead while preserving accuracy near separate caching.

title: LRAgent: Efficient KV Cache Sharing for Multi-LoRA LLM Agents

abstract: Diffusion models generate highly realistic images but often struggle with precise text–image alignment. While recent post-training methods improve alignment using external rewards or human preference signals, their performance heavily depends on reward quality and does not directly address alignment within the diffusion process itself. Recent reward-free approaches such as SoftREPA demonstrate that optimizing soft text tokens via contrastive learning can effectively improve text-image representation alignment, outperforming standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning baselines. However, the contrastive formulation can excessively penalize negative pairs, which manifests as characteristic failure cases such as over-counting and repetition. To address this issue, we propose a lightweight, reward-free post-training method that refines soft tokens by integrating contrastive alignment guidance directly into the score-matching objective of diffusion models. By assigning alignment directions at the score level, our approach mitigates these limitations and yields more coherent and semantically faithful generations. Experiments show that our method matches SoftREPA while substantially improving its failure cases, achieving over 35% improvement in counting accuracy on the GenEval benchmark. Our method is seamlessly applicable to existing diffusion backbones (SD1.5, SDXL, and SD3), and is complementary to existing RL-based diffusion post-training methods.

title: Alignment-Guided Score Matching for Text-to-Image Alignment in Diffusion Models

abstract: The design of environments plays a critical role in shaping the development and evaluation of cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms. While existing benchmarks highlight critical challenges, they often lack the modularity required to design custom evaluation scenarios. We introduce the Totally Accelerated Battle Simulator in JAX (TABX), a high-throughput sandbox designed for reconfigurable multi-agent tasks. TABX provides granular control over environmental parameters, permitting a systematic investigation into emergent agent behaviors and algorithmic trade-offs across a diverse spectrum of task complexities. Leveraging JAX for hardware-accelerated execution on GPUs, TABX enables massive parallelization and significantly reduces computational overhead. By providing a fast, extensible, and easily customized framework, TABX facilitates the study of MARL agents in complex structured domains and serves as a scalable foundation for future research. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TABX-00CA.

paragraphs: The environment used to train and evaluate cooperative agents shapes which behaviors and difficulties researchers can study. Existing multi-agent benchmarks expose important challenges, but limited modularity can make custom scenarios hard to construct. TABX provides a reconfigurable battle sandbox intended to make those experimental choices more accessible.

The simulator gives researchers fine-grained control over environmental parameters. This supports systematic investigation of emerging agent behavior and algorithmic trade-offs across tasks with different levels of complexity. Its implementation uses JAX and GPU acceleration to run many simulations in parallel, reducing the computational overhead associated with collecting experience from multi-agent environments.

The paper’s contribution is a fast, extensible research environment rather than a new agent-learning algorithm. Its stated value combines customization with throughput: researchers can vary task conditions while retaining the ability to run large numbers of simulations. That combination provides a scalable basis for studying cooperative learning in complex, structured domains and for constructing evaluations around specific research questions.
summary.tldr: TABX is a customizable, GPU-accelerated battle simulator designed for high-throughput cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning research.

title: TABX: A High-Throughput Sandbox Battle Simulator for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Social interactions are characterized by both adversarial and cooperative aspects. Communications between agents may also involve adversarially motivated actors. Messages can pass through intermediaries with malicious intent before reaching the intended receiver. These actors may modify the message to induce misunderstanding from the receiver while preserving the overall characteristics of the message. This form of misinformation is prevalent in real-world communications and may affect the dynamics under which communication protocols are developed. However, this aspect of social interaction is relatively underexplored in many emergent communication studies that aim to understand the environmental factors behind the emergence of languages’ characteristics. This work explores how misinformation affects language emergence with a focus on compositionality. We design a communication game containing a malign intermediary between the sender and receiver. We find that risks of malign misrepresentation promote the emergence of compositional languages in simulations of communicative agents. Furthermore, we observe that adaptability of malign intermediaries is a crucial factor in forming a consistent pressure toward compositionality and that partial misinformation, in which the intermediary targets only a subset of attributes, can also induce compositionality.

paragraphs: Studies of emergent communication examine how agents develop ways to exchange information. This paper adds a social complication: a message may pass through an intermediary that deliberately changes it to mislead the receiver while preserving its overall characteristics. The authors ask how that risk influences the language that communicating agents develop, focusing on compositionality.

Compositionality concerns how message parts combine to express meaning. To investigate its emergence, the authors build a communication game with a sender, a receiver, and a malign intermediary. This makes interference part of the environment in which communication develops, allowing the simulations to examine how the possibility of misrepresentation shapes the resulting communication system.

The simulations find that risks of malicious misrepresentation promote compositional languages. The intermediary’s adaptability is crucial for producing consistent pressure in that direction. Interference targeting only some attributes can also induce compositionality. Together, these findings identify adversarial communication as a possible influence on language structure in simulated agents, with the nature of the intermediary affecting how that influence operates.
summary.tldr: Communication-game simulations show that adaptive malicious intermediaries can promote the emergence of compositional languages.

title: Emergent Communication Under Misinformation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in settings that require reliable long-context understanding, such as retrieval-augmented generation and multi-document reasoning. A common strategy is to fine-tune pretrained short-context models at the target sequence length. However, we find that standard long-context adaptation can remain brittle: model accuracy depends strongly on the absolute placement of relevant evidence, exhibiting high positional variance even when controlling for task format and difficulty. We propose RoPE-Perturbed Self-Distillation, a training regularizer that improves positional robustness. The core idea is to form alternative “views” of the same training sequence by perturbing its RoPE indices—effectively moving parts of the context to different positions—and to train the model to produce consistent predictions across views via self-distillation. This encourages reliance on semantic signals instead of brittle position dependencies. Experiments on long-context adaptation of Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B demonstrate consistent gains on long-context benchmarks, including up to 12.04 percent-point improvement on RULER-64K for Llama-3-8B and 2.71 percent-point gain on RULER-256K for Qwen-3-4B after SFT, alongside improved length extrapolation beyond the training context window.

paragraphs: Extending a language model’s context window does not necessarily make it equally reliable at every position. The paper finds that standard long-context fine-tuning can leave accuracy strongly dependent on where relevant evidence appears, even when task format and difficulty are controlled. This makes placement itself a source of brittleness in long-context understanding.

RoPE-Perturbed Self-Distillation creates alternative views of a training sequence by changing its rotary position indices. These changes effectively move portions of the context to different positions. A self-distillation objective encourages consistent predictions across the resulting views, pushing the model to rely more on semantic evidence and less on fragile associations with absolute placement.

Experiments adapting Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B show consistent benchmark gains. Reported improvements include up to 12.04 percentage points on RULER-64K for Llama and 2.71 percentage points on RULER-256K for Qwen after supervised fine-tuning. Improved extrapolation beyond the training window further supports positional consistency as a useful training objective for long-context adaptation.
summary.tldr: RoPE-Perturbed Self-Distillation improves long-context robustness by training models to agree across different positional views of the same sequence.

title: Shuffle the Context: RoPE-Perturbed Self-Distillation for Long-Context Adaptation

abstract: Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) has significantly advanced self-supervised representation learning on graphs, yet its practical efficacy remains hindered by random augmentations that induce semantic distortion and rigid one-to-one sampling strategy that amplifies inter-class entanglement and intra-class dispersion. To address these limitations, we develop CL-GCL, a Comprehensive and Lightweight Graph Contrastive Learning framework. Specifically, we exploit graph coarsening to preserve structural semantics through community-level representations and manifold learning to capture local geometric relations without costly pairwise distance computations. This design naturally aligns with the neighborhood aggregation principle of Graph Convolutional Networks, enhancing structural consistency while eliminating negative sampling bias. We theoretically prove that CL-GCL approximates node-level contrastive loss under mild conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent superiority in both accuracy and efficiency over state-of-the-art GCL methods.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning builds representations without supervised labels, but its training choices can distort the relationships it should preserve. Random graph changes may alter meaning, while rigid one-to-one sampling can mix different classes and scatter members of the same class. CL-GCL addresses these problems by organizing learning around graph structure and local geometry.

The framework uses graph coarsening to represent communities, preserving structural meaning at a broader scale. It also uses manifold learning to capture local geometric relationships without expensive pairwise distance calculations. Together, these components fit the neighborhood aggregation used by graph convolutional networks, strengthen structural consistency, and eliminate the negative-sampling bias identified in the paper.

The authors prove that the resulting objective approximates a node-level contrastive loss under mild conditions. This connects the lighter formulation to the finer-grained learning objective it aims to replace. Experiments report consistent gains in both accuracy and efficiency over state-of-the-art graph contrastive methods, suggesting that preserving meaningful structure can improve representation quality while also reducing computational burden.
summary.tldr: CL-GCL combines community representations and local geometry to improve graph contrastive learning accuracy and efficiency.

title: CL-GCL: Comprehensive and Lightweight Graph Contrastive Learning

abstract: Online conformal prediction (OCP) seeks prediction intervals that achieve long-run $1-\alpha$ coverage for arbitrary (possibly adversarial) data streams, while remaining as informative as possible. Existing OCP methods often require manual learning-rate tuning to work well, and may also require algorithm-specific analyses. Here, we develop a general regret-to-coverage theory for interval-valued OCP based on the $(1-\alpha)$-pinball loss. Our first contribution is to identify linearized regret as a key notion, showing that controlling it implies coverage bounds for any online algorithm. This relies on a black-box reduction that depends only on the Fenchel conjugate of an upper bound on the linearized regret. Building on this theory, we propose UP-OCP, a parameter-free method for OCP, via a reduction to a two-asset portfolio selection problem, leveraging universal portfolio algorithms. We show strong finite-time bounds on the miscoverage of UP-OCP, even for polynomially growing predictions. Extensive experiments support that UP-OCP delivers consistently better size/coverage trade-offs than prior online conformal baselines.

paragraphs: Online conformal prediction aims to produce informative prediction intervals while maintaining a target long-run coverage rate, even for arbitrary or adversarial data streams. Existing methods often depend on learning-rate tuning. This paper develops a general theoretical connection between an online algorithm’s regret and the coverage of the intervals it produces.

The key quantity is linearized regret under the pinball loss. The authors show that controlling this quantity yields coverage bounds through a black-box reduction involving the Fenchel conjugate of a regret bound. This provides a reusable route from an online learning guarantee to a coverage guarantee, rather than requiring a separate coverage analysis for each algorithm.

Using that connection, they construct UP-OCP by reducing interval prediction to a two-asset portfolio selection problem and applying universal portfolio algorithms. The resulting method is parameter-free and has finite-time miscoverage bounds, including for polynomially growing predictions. Experiments report consistently better interval-size and coverage trade-offs than prior online conformal baselines. The contribution combines a general analytical tool with a concrete method that avoids manual learning-rate selection.
summary.tldr: UP-OCP uses universal portfolio algorithms and a regret-to-coverage theory to produce prediction intervals without learning-rate tuning.

title: Online Conformal Prediction via Universal Portfolio Algorithms

abstract: In recent years, multi-view outlier detection (MVOD) has gained increasing attention, with the primary objective of recovering the underlying structure of normal data from outlier-contaminated multi-view datasets. However, this objective is hindered by two fundamental challenges:(i) outlier propagation, (ii) scale discrepancy. To address these issues, we propose RNAMOD (Reliable Neighborhood-Aware Multi-View Outlier Detection), which introduces the concept of reliability and constructs a reliable neighborhood structure to avoid outlier propagation. We introduce a leave-one-out directional consensus mechanism to align cross-view neighborhood structures while preventing scale discrepancy by aligning geometric directions that remain invariant to scaling. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that RNAMOD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
