paragraphs: Multi-view outlier detection seeks the structure of normal data when each item has multiple representations and some items are anomalous. The paper identifies two obstacles: outliers can contaminate neighborhood information, and differences in scale across views can interfere with comparing their structures. Both affect the evidence used to distinguish normal patterns.

RNAMOD introduces reliability into neighborhood construction to avoid propagating outlier influence. It also uses a leave-one-out directional consensus mechanism to align neighborhood structures across views. The alignment focuses on geometric directions, which remain unchanged under scaling. This addresses scale discrepancy through the type of geometric information being compared.

Experiments on six benchmark datasets report consistent improvements over the evaluated state-of-the-art methods. The contribution joins two related ideas: construct neighborhoods with attention to reliability, then reconcile views using scale-invariant directions. Reliable construction targets contamination within neighborhood evidence, while directional consensus targets disagreement caused by different scales. The reported results support combining these mechanisms when recovering normal structure from contaminated multi-view datasets.
summary.tldr: RNAMOD combines reliable neighborhoods with scale-invariant directional alignment to improve multi-view outlier detection.

title: Reliable Neighborhood-Aware Multi-View Outlier Detection

abstract: Recent multimodal large language models have demonstrated strong reasoning ability, yet their reliability as automated evaluators remains limited by a critical weakness: when visual evidence conflicts with textual cues, MLLM judges tend to reward plausible narratives over perceptually correct answers. We identify and systematically analyze this phenomenon, which we term Perceptual Judgment Bias. Through controlled visual perturbations, existing multimodal judges frequently anchor on the response text instead of their own visual perception, leading to inconsistent and non-verifiable evaluations. To address this issue, we introduce the Perceptually Perturbed Judgment Dataset, which constructs minimally edited counterfactual responses that isolate perceptual errors and enable verifiable supervision. Building on this dataset, we develop a unified training framework that combines a structured GRPO-based reward with a batch-ranking objective, achieving coherent global ordering without explicit pairwise labels. Experiments across diverse MLLM-as-a-Judge benchmarks show that our approach substantially improves perceptual fidelity, ranking coherence, and alignment with human evaluation. Our results establish a scalable and generalizable pathway for training multimodal judges that are perceptually grounded, interpretable, and robust to visual–reasoning conflicts.

paragraphs: A multimodal model judging an answer may favor a convincing explanation even when it conflicts with the image. The authors call this Perceptual Judgment Bias. Through controlled visual perturbations, they show that existing judges frequently anchor on response text instead of visual evidence, making their evaluations inconsistent and difficult to verify.

To train against this failure, they construct the Perceptually Perturbed Judgment Dataset. Minimally edited counterfactual responses isolate perceptual errors, supplying supervision whose correctness can be checked against the visual evidence. The training framework combines a structured GRPO-based reward with a batch-ranking objective, encouraging coherent ordering across responses without requiring explicit pairwise labels.

Across diverse multimodal judging benchmarks, the approach substantially improves fidelity to visual evidence, consistency of rankings, and agreement with human evaluations. These findings connect the diagnosed bias to a targeted training intervention: isolate visual mistakes, then reward judgments that recognize them. The authors present this as a scalable route toward interpretable judges that are more robust when persuasive reasoning and visual evidence disagree.
summary.tldr: Targeted counterfactual training helps multimodal judges prioritize visual correctness over persuasive but perceptually wrong responses.

title: Mitigating Perceptual Judgment Bias in Multimodal LLM-as-a-Judge via Perceptual Perturbation and Reward Modeling

abstract: While there are many applications of machine learning (ML) to scientific problems that look promising, the eye test can be misleading compared to the quantitative values. Using numerical analysis techniques, we rigorously quantify the accuracy, convergence rates, and generalization bounds of certain ML models applied to linear differential equations (DEs) for parameter discovery or solution finding. Beyond the quantity and discretization of data, we identify that the function space of the data is critical to the generalization of the model which can lead to divergence. Similar lack of generalization is empirically demonstrated for commonly used models. Surprisingly, we find that different classes of models can exhibit opposing generalization behaviors. Based on our theoretical analysis, we also introduce a new mechanistic interpretability lens on scientific models whereby Green’s function representations can be extracted from the weights of black-box models. Our results inform a new cross-validation technique for measuring generalization in physical systems, and can be useful as a benchmark of future methods.

paragraphs: A learned physical solution can look convincing while still being quantitatively inaccurate. This paper uses numerical analysis to study certain machine-learning models applied to linear differential equations, covering both parameter discovery and solution finding. It derives accuracy estimates, convergence rates, and generalization bounds to make performance assessable beyond visual resemblance.

The analysis identifies the function space containing the data as a crucial factor in generalization, alongside data quantity and discretization. A mismatch can lead to divergence, and experiments show related generalization failures in commonly used models. Different model classes can even exhibit opposing generalization behavior, so conclusions about one class need not transfer directly to another.

The authors also develop an interpretability approach that extracts Green's function representations from black-box model weights. This connects learned parameters to a mathematical representation of the physical system. Their theory informs a new cross-validation technique for measuring generalization in physical problems, offering both a diagnostic method and a potential benchmark for evaluating future scientific learning methods.
summary.tldr: Numerical analysis reveals how data function spaces affect learned physics and provides generalization bounds and a Green's-function interpretability method.

title: Interpretability and Generalization Bounds for Learning Spatial Physics

abstract: Efficient sampling of molecular systems at thermodynamic equilibrium is a hallmark challenge in statistical physics. This challenge has driven the development of Boltzmann Generators (BGs), which allow rapid generation of uncorrelated equilibrium samples by combining a generative model with exact likelihoods and an importance sampling correction. However, modern BGs predominantly rely on Normalizing Flows (NFs), which either suffer from limited expressivity due to strict invertibility constraints (discrete time) or computationally expensive likelihoods (continuous time). In this paper, we propose Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators (ArBG), a novel autoregressive modelling framework that overcomes these limitations by departing from the flow-based BG paradigm. ArBG circumvents the topological constraints of flows and enables sequential inference-time interventions, while offering enhanced scalability by leveraging architectures effective in Large Language Models. We empirically demonstrate that ArBG leads to significant improvements over flow-based models across all benchmarks, but particularly in larger peptide systems such as the 10-residue Chignolin. Furthermore, we introduce Robin, a 132M parameter transferable model trained with the ArBG framework which improves over the previous state-of-the-art, reducing the zero-shot energy error, $\mathcal{E}$-$\mathcal{W}_2$, on 8-residue systems by $\sim 60$%.

paragraphs: Boltzmann Generators aim to sample molecular configurations at thermodynamic equilibrium efficiently. They combine a generative model with exact likelihoods and an importance-sampling correction. Most rely on normalizing flows, which introduce a tradeoff: discrete-time flows impose strict invertibility constraints, while continuous-time flows can make likelihood computation expensive.

This paper replaces the flow-based architecture with an autoregressive framework called ArBG. Generating configurations sequentially avoids the topological constraints associated with flows and allows interventions during the generation sequence. The approach also draws on architectures effective in large language models to improve scalability. Its contribution is a different modeling foundation for Boltzmann Generators, retaining the focus on efficient equilibrium sampling.

Experiments show improvements over flow-based models across all evaluated benchmarks, especially for larger peptides such as ten-residue Chignolin. The authors also introduce Robin, a transferable 132-million-parameter model trained with ArBG. On eight-residue systems, Robin reduces the reported zero-shot energy error by about 60% relative to the previous state of the art, demonstrating transfer benefits within the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators replace flow-based molecular sampling with sequential generation, improving benchmark performance and transfer to evaluated peptide systems.

title: Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators

abstract: Online structured prediction, including online classification as a special case, is the task of sequentially predicting labels from input features. In this setting, the surrogate regret—the cumulative excess of the actual target loss (e.g., the 0-1 loss) over the surrogate loss (e.g., the logistic loss) incurred by the best fixed estimator—has gained attention because it admits a finite bound independent of the time horizon $T$. However, such guarantees break down in non-stationary environments, where every fixed estimator may incur surrogate loss that grows linearly with $T$. To address this limitation, we obtain an upper bound of $F_T+O(1+P_T)$ on the cumulative target loss, where $F_T$ is the cumulative surrogate loss of any comparator sequence and $P_T$ is its path length. This bound depends on $T$ only through $F_T$ and $P_T$, thus offering stronger guarantees under non-stationarity. Our core idea is to combine the dynamic regret analysis of online gradient descent (OGD) with the exploit-the-surrogate-gap technique. This viewpoint sheds light on the usefulness of a Polyak-style learning rate for OGD, which systematically yields target-loss bounds and performs well empirically. We then extend our approach to broader settings beyond prior work via the convolutional Fenchel–Young loss. Finally, a lower bound shows that the dependence on $F_T$ and $P_T$ is tight.
originalAbstract: Online structured prediction, including online classification as a special case, is the task of sequentially predicting labels from input features. However, such guarantees break down in non-stationary environments, where every fixed estimator may incur surrogate loss that grows linearly with $T$. To address this limitation, we obtain an upper bound of $F_T+O(1+P_T)$ on the cumulative target loss, where $F_T$ is the cumulative surrogate loss of any comparator sequence and $P_T$ is its path length. This bound depends on $T$ only through $F_T$ and $P_T$, thus offering stronger guarantees under non-stationarity. This viewpoint sheds light on the usefulness of a Polyak-style learning rate for OGD, which systematically yields target-loss bounds and performs well empirically. paragraphs: Online structured prediction makes label predictions sequentially as inputs arrive. Existing surrogate-regret guarantees compare performance with a single fixed estimator, but that reference can become poor when the environment changes. Even a bounded excess over its surrogate loss may offer little reassurance if the reference loss itself grows linearly with time.

The paper instead compares cumulative target loss with a sequence of estimators that can change. Its bound is F_T + O(1 + P_T), where F_T is that sequence's cumulative surrogate loss and P_T measures how far it moves. Time enters only through these two quantities, connecting performance to how well a changing reference predicts and how much adaptation it requires.

The approach combines dynamic regret analysis for online gradient descent with a technique that exploits the gap between target and surrogate losses. It explains the usefulness of a Polyak-style learning rate, which also performs well empirically, and extends the framework using convolutional Fenchel–Young loss. A matching lower-bound result shows that the dependence on F_T and P_T is tight.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds online prediction loss against a changing comparator, with tight dependence on its surrogate loss and amount of movement.

title: Non-Stationary Online Structured Prediction with Surrogate Losses

abstract: We propose a sequential test for distribution-shift detection that allows conformal test martingales (CTMs) to work under a fixed, reference-conditional setting. Existing CTM detectors construct test martingales by continually growing a reference set with each incoming sample, using it to assess how atypical the new sample is relative to past observations. While this design yields anytime-valid type-I error control, it suffers from test-time contamination: after a change, post-shift observations enter the reference set and dilute the evidence for distribution shift, increasing detection delay and reducing power. In contrast, our method avoids contamination by design by comparing each new sample to a fixed null reference dataset. Our main technical contribution is a robust martingale construction that remains valid conditional on the null reference data, achieved by explicitly accounting for the estimation error in the reference distribution induced by the finite reference set. This yields anytime-valid type-I error control together with guarantees of asymptotic power one and bounded expected detection delay. Empirically, our method detects shifts faster than standard CTMs, providing a powerful and reliable distribution-shift detector.

paragraphs: A distribution-shift detector compares arriving observations with what normal data should look like. Standard conformal test martingales continually enlarge their reference set. After a shift, however, changed observations enter that set and make the new behavior appear less unusual, weakening evidence and potentially delaying detection.

The paper instead compares every incoming sample with a fixed dataset representing the null distribution. Keeping that reference unchanged prevents post-shift contamination, but a finite reference set estimates the null distribution imperfectly. The main technical contribution is a robust martingale construction that explicitly accounts for this estimation error and remains valid conditional on the observed reference data.

The construction provides anytime-valid type-I error control, so repeatedly checking for an alarm preserves the stated false-alarm guarantee. It also comes with asymptotic power-one and bounded expected detection-delay guarantees. Experiments show faster detection than standard conformal test martingales. The work therefore addresses both the statistical validity of a fixed-reference approach and the practical loss of sensitivity caused by updating references after a change.
summary.tldr: A fixed-reference conformal detector avoids contamination after distribution shifts while retaining anytime-valid false-alarm control.

title: Testing For Distribution Shifts with Conditional Conformal Test Martingales

abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are fundamentally constrained by context length on long-horizon tasks. Existing agent frameworks usually rely on manually defined context engineering pipelines, such as multi-agent or post-hoc summary. We introduce Context Folding, a framework that empowers agents to actively manage their working context. An agent can procedurally branch into a sub-trajectory to handle a subtask and then fold it upon completion, collapsing the intermediate steps while retaining a concise summary of the outcome. To make this behavior learnable, we propose FoldGRPO, an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework with specific process rewards to encourage effective task decomposition and context management. On long-horizon tasks, our agent matches the performance of baselines while using an active context up to 10x smaller, and significantly outperforms models constrained to the same context size. Code is available at https://github.com/sunnweiwei/FoldAgent.

paragraphs: Long tasks can overwhelm a language-model agent’s context with intermediate actions and observations. Existing frameworks often handle this through manually designed context-management procedures. Context Folding gives the agent an explicit way to manage its own working context as part of carrying out the task.

The agent can branch into a separate sub-trajectory for a subtask. After completing that work, it folds the branch: intermediate steps are collapsed, while a concise summary of the outcome remains available. FoldGRPO trains this behavior end to end with reinforcement learning. Its process rewards encourage useful task decomposition and effective context management, making the decisions about branching and folding learnable.

On long-horizon tasks, the resulting agent matches baseline performance while using an active context up to ten times smaller. It also significantly outperforms models given the same context-size constraint. These findings indicate that learned management of intermediate work can make limited active context more useful, while the reported context reduction specifically concerns what remains in the agent’s working context.
summary.tldr: Context Folding trains agents to summarize completed subtask branches, matching baseline performance with active context up to ten times smaller.

title: Scaling Long-Horizon Agent via Context Folding

abstract: Existing code reasoning methods primarily supervise final code outputs, ignoring intermediate states, often leading to reward hacking where correct answers are obtained through inconsistent reasoning. We propose StepCodeReasoner, a framework that introduces explicit intermediate execution-state supervision. By automatically inserting structured print-based execution-trace anchors into code, the model is trained to predict runtime states at each step, transforming code reasoning into a verifiable, stepwise execution modeling problem. Building on this execution-aware method, we introduce Dual-Granularity GRPO (DG-GRPO), a reinforcement learning algorithm for structured credit assignment at two complementary granularities: inter-trajectory comparison across sampled execution paths and intra-trajectory shaping based on downstream correctness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that StepCodeReasoner achieves state-of-the-art performance in code reasoning. In particular, our 7B model achieves 91.1% on CRUXEval and 86.5% on LiveCodeBench, outperforming the CodeReasoner-7B baseline (86.0% and 77.7%) and GPT-4o (85.6% and 75.1%). Furthermore, on the execution-trace benchmark REval, our model scores 82.9%, outperforming baseline CodeReasoner-7B (72.3%), its 14B counterpart (81.1%), and GPT-4o (77.3%). In addition, StepCodeReasoner improves code generation, achieving 90.1 on HumanEval, 85.0 on MBPP, and 19.4 on LiveCodeBench generation, with an average score of 64.8 versus 62.6 for CodeReasoner-7B.

summary.tldr: StepCodeReasoner trains on verifiable intermediate execution states, improving reported code reasoning, trace prediction, and generation results.

title: StepCodeReasoner: Aligning Code Reasoning with Stepwise Execution Traces via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In standard reinforcement learning (RL) settings, the interaction between the agent and the environment is typically modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP), which assumes that the agent observes the system state instantaneously, selects an action without delay, and executes it immediately. In real-world dynamic environments, such as cyber-physical systems, this assumption often breaks down due to delays in the interaction between the agent and the system. These delays can vary stochastically over time and are typically unobservable when deciding on an action. Existing methods deal with this uncertainty conservatively by assuming a known fixed upper bound on the delay, even if the delay is often much lower. In this work, we introduce the interaction layer, a general framework that enables agents to adaptively handle unobservable and time-varying delays. Specifically, the agent generates a matrix of possible future actions, anticipating a horizon of potential delays, to handle both unpredictable delays and lost action packets sent over networks. Building on this framework, we develop a model-based algorithm, Actor-Critic with Delay Adaptation (ACDA), which dynamically adjusts to delay patterns. Our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across a wide range of locomotion benchmark environments, including real-world measured delays.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often assumes that observations arrive immediately and chosen actions take effect without delay. Networked systems can violate both assumptions: delays fluctuate, and an agent may not know the current delay when choosing an action. Planning around a fixed maximum delay can therefore be unnecessarily conservative when actual delays are shorter.

The paper introduces an interaction layer that lets an agent prepare for several possible delays at once. Instead of producing only one immediate action, the agent generates a matrix of possible future actions over a delay horizon. This framework addresses unpredictable timing as well as action packets that fail to arrive over a network.

The authors build Actor-Critic with Delay Adaptation, or ACDA, on this framework. This model-based algorithm adjusts to changing delay patterns. Across locomotion benchmarks, including experiments using measured real-world delays, it substantially outperforms the compared approaches. The findings support preparing adaptable future actions as a way to improve control when communication timing is uncertain.
summary.tldr: ACDA prepares alternative future actions to improve reinforcement learning under hidden, changing delays and lost action packets.

title: Adaptive Reinforcement Learning for Unobservable Random Delays

abstract: We study simultaneous confidence bounds for aggregated effects over downward-closed subset families of independent statistical tests. The bounds are obtained by bootstrap calibration of the maximum normalized aggregated effect over the relevant subset family, yielding valid post-hoc inference for data-selected subsets and tighter bounds than classical methods that protect all linear contrasts. A central challenge is that the required maximization is a nonlinear combinatorial optimization problem. We cast it as a weighted densest-subgraph problem and derive exact linear and mixed integer linear program reformulations, and we further develop a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme that exploits the rank-1 structure of the objective to scale to large families. On the statistical side, we establish a finite-sample coverage guarantee with a lighter dependence on the subset family size than high-dimensional central limit theorems provide. We illustrate the method on synthetic and real machine learning applications.

On the statistical side, we establish a finite-sample coverage guarantee with a lighter dependence on the subset family size than high-dimensional central limit theorems provide. paragraphs: Researchers may want confidence bounds for a combined effect after choosing a subset of results from observed data. This paper studies simultaneous bounds over downward-closed families of subsets of independent statistical tests. Such families retain all smaller subsets of an allowed set, defining which aggregated effects receive protection.

The procedure uses bootstrap calibration of the largest normalized aggregate across the relevant family. That maximization is a nonlinear combinatorial problem, so the authors reformulate it as a weighted densest-subgraph problem and derive exact linear and mixed-integer linear programs. The statistical analysis provides finite-sample coverage with a lighter dependence on family size than high-dimensional central limit theorems offer. Targeting the relevant subsets also yields tighter bounds than methods protecting all linear contrasts. Synthetic and real machine-learning applications illustrate the approach. Its contribution joins computational optimization with uncertainty guarantees that remain valid when the reported subset is selected after seeing the data.
summary.tldr: Subset optimization enables tighter simultaneous confidence bounds for aggregated effects selected after observing independent test results.

title: Simultaneous Confidence Bounds for Aggregated Effects via Exact Subset Optimization

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on structured visual understanding tasks such as chart and document question answering. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate these domains in isolation, leaving underexplored a key capability: whether models can use textual context to determine how chart evidence should be selected, interpreted, and aggregated. We introduce DocHop, a benchmark for integrated chart–context reasoning in document-style images. In DocHop, the document narrative specifies multi-step compositional constraints, while charts provide the corresponding data values. Questions are grounded on a semantic reference label defined in the narrative, requiring models to resolve target entities from context before aggregating evidence across multiple charts. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct DocHop via a stochastic logic-first generation pipeline with controllable reasoning depth and visual density, covering 2,074 examples across six task categories. Experiments on a wide range of proprietary and open-source MLLMs show a substantial gap to human performance: annotators achieve over 90% accuracy, while the best model reaches only 62.83%. Reasoning-enhanced models consistently show improved results, but performance degrades as reasoning complexity increases. Overall, DocHop provides a controlled testbed for challenging multi-hop document reasoning.

paragraphs: DocHop tests whether a model can combine document text with evidence from several charts. Reading chart values alone is insufficient: the surrounding narrative determines which entities matter and how their values should be combined. This targets a capability that benchmarks evaluating charts and documents separately leave underexplored.

Each question refers to a semantic label defined in the narrative. A model must interpret that label, resolve the relevant entities, follow multiple constraints, and aggregate the corresponding chart evidence. The benchmark uses a randomized generation process that establishes the logic first, allowing the authors to control reasoning depth and visual density across 2,074 examples in six task categories.

Human annotators exceed 90% accuracy, while the best evaluated model reaches 62.83%. Models enhanced for reasoning perform better, but accuracy declines as the reasoning becomes more complex. The findings expose a substantial gap in connecting textual instructions to visual evidence through multiple steps, even among models with strong performance on other structured visual tasks.
summary.tldr: DocHop reveals a substantial human–model gap when document text determines how evidence from multiple charts must be interpreted and combined.

title: DocHop: Benchmarking Out-of-domain Multi-hop Reasoning in Information-Dense Documents

abstract: Recently, Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have emerged in Real-World Image Super-Resolution (Real-ISR) to generate high-quality textures, yet their heavy inference burden hinders real-world deployment. While Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) is a promising solution for acceleration, existing methods in super-resolution mostly focus on U-Net architectures, whereas generic DiT quantization is typically designed for text-to-image tasks. Directly applying these methods to DiT-based super-resolution models leads to severe degradation of local textures. Therefore, we propose Q-DiT4SR, the first PTQ framework specifically tailored for DiT-based Real-ISR. We propose H-SVD, a hierarchical SVD that integrates a global low-rank branch with a local block-wise rank-1 branch under a matched parameter budget. We further propose Variance-aware Spatio-Temporal Mixed Precision: VaSMP allocates cross-layer weight bit-widths in a data-free manner based on rate-distortion theory, while VaTMP schedules intra-layer activation precision across diffusion timesteps via dynamic programming (DP) with minimal calibration. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our Q-DiT4SR achieves SOTA performance under both W4A6 and W4A4 settings. Notably, the W4A4 quantization configuration reduces model size by 5.8$\times$ and computational operations by 6.14$\times$. Our code and models will be available at https://github.com/xunzhang1128/Q-DiT4SR.

paragraphs: Diffusion Transformers can generate detailed textures for real-world image super-resolution, but their inference cost makes deployment difficult. Applying existing quantization approaches can severely degrade local texture. Q-DiT4SR designs post-training quantization specifically around the demands of these super-resolution models, where preserving fine detail is central to the task.

The framework combines a global low-rank branch with a local block-wise rank-one branch through hierarchical singular-value decomposition, keeping the parameter budget matched. It also distributes numerical precision in two ways. A data-free procedure allocates weight bit-widths across layers using rate-distortion theory, while a minimally calibrated dynamic-programming procedure schedules activation precision across diffusion timesteps.

Experiments on multiple real-world datasets report state-of-the-art performance with four-bit weights and either six-bit or four-bit activations. The four-bit weight and activation configuration reduces model size by 5.8 times and computational operations by 6.14 times. These findings show how tailoring approximation structure and precision allocation to super-resolution can support substantial compression while addressing texture degradation.
summary.tldr: Q-DiT4SR tailors quantization to diffusion-transformer super-resolution, preserving detail while substantially reducing model size and computation.

title: Q-DiT4SR: Exploration of Detail-Preserving Diffusion Transformer Quantization for Real-World Image Super-Resolution

abstract: The reliance of machine learning (ML) models on large-scale, high-quality labeled training data incurs significant challenges in specialized domains where such data is expensive and difficult to obtain. A promising solution is the automatic creation of synthetic training data. However, current approaches — including data generation, automated annotation, and domain adaptation — often fail to explicitly use downstream model performance to guide the creation and refinement of synthetic training data. This position paper argues that multi-level optimization (MLO) is essential for producing high-fidelity synthetic data by enabling joint optimization of data generation, annotation, adaptation, and selection, all informed by downstream model performance. We advocate for MLO as a unified framework to address three critical challenges: (1) improving data generation by aligning synthetic data with model needs, particularly targeting class-specific deficiencies and worst-case robustness; (2) enhancing automated annotation through sequential verification and the use of large language models for more accurate labeling; and (3) enabling example-specific adaptation and selection to maximize data utility while preventing excessive over-adaptation. By facilitating end-to-end coordination across multiple learning stages, MLO offers a potential paradigm shift in synthetic data creation for data-scarce domains.

paragraphs: This position paper examines how to create useful synthetic training data when obtaining high-quality labeled examples is difficult or expensive. The authors argue that existing generation, labeling, and adaptation approaches often fail to use the eventual model’s performance as explicit feedback. Consequently, the process of producing data can remain disconnected from what the learner needs.

They propose multi-level optimization as a common framework for coordinating these stages. Data generation would respond to weaknesses such as poor performance on particular classes and inadequate worst-case robustness. Automated labeling would incorporate sequential verification and language models. Adaptation and selection would operate at the level of individual examples, seeking useful training signals while avoiding excessive adaptation.

The key idea is that decisions across the data pipeline should be optimized together using downstream performance. An example’s value would therefore depend on how it helps the model, rather than solely on its properties at creation. The paper presents this coordination as a potential change in how data-scarce domains develop synthetic training sets.
summary.tldr: The authors advocate jointly optimizing synthetic data generation, labeling, adaptation, and selection using feedback from downstream model performance.

abstract: We consider the problem of computing low rank approximations of matrices. The novelty of our approach is that the low rank approximations are on a sequenceof matrices. Unlike the problem of low rank approximations of a single matrix,which was well studied in the past, the proposed algorithm in this paper does notadmit a closed form solution in general. We did extensive experiments on face imagedata to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm and compare thecomputed low rank approximations with those obtained from traditional Singular Value Decomposition based method.

Unlike the problem of low rank approximations of a single matrix,which was well studied in the past, the proposed algorithm in this paper does notadmit a closed form solution in general. paragraphs: Low-rank approximation seeks a simpler matrix representation by restricting its rank. This paper changes the scope of that problem from a single matrix to a sequence of matrices. The contribution is a generalized approximation algorithm designed around this collection of matrix-valued inputs, extending a problem that was already well studied for individual matrices.

The extension has an important computational consequence: the proposed algorithm does not generally admit a closed-form solution. Thus, the familiar single-matrix setting does not directly supply a general explicit solution for the new formulation. This is a stated property of the proposed approach, and it helps explain why extending low-rank approximation to a sequence requires separate algorithmic treatment.

The authors evaluate the algorithm through extensive experiments on face-image data. They compare the resulting approximations with those produced by a traditional singular-value-decomposition-based method. This evaluation examines the practical effectiveness of the sequence-oriented formulation against an established approximation approach. The abstract identifies the comparison and its purpose without stating a particular numerical advantage or a universal improvement.
summary.tldr: The paper extends low-rank approximation to sequences of matrices and evaluates its algorithm against an SVD-based method on face images.

title: Generalized low rank approximations of matrices

abstract: We present MI-CRF, a conditional random field (CRF) model for multiple instance learning (MIL). MI-CRF models bags as nodes in a CRF with instances as their states. It combines discriminative unary instance classifiers and pairwise dissimilarity measures. We show that both forces improve the classification performance. Unlike other approaches, MI-CRF considers all bags jointly during training as well as during testing. This makes it possible to classify test bags in an imputation setup. The parameters of MI-CRF are learned using constraint generation. Furthermore, we show that MI-CRF can incorporate previous MIL algorithms to improve on their results. MI-CRF obtains competitive results on five standard MIL datasets.

MI-CRF obtains competitive results on five standard MIL datasets.

paragraphs: Multiple-instance learning organizes examples into bags containing individual instances. This paper introduces MI-CRF, a conditional random field that represents each bag as a node and its instances as possible states. This representation lets the model connect decisions about individual instances with relationships across bags, rather than treating every bag as an isolated classification problem.

The model combines two kinds of evidence: discriminative classifiers that score individual instances and pairwise measures of dissimilarity. The authors report that both contribute to better classification. A distinctive feature is that MI-CRF considers all bags together during both training and testing. This joint treatment also makes it possible to classify test bags in an imputation setting.

The authors learn the model parameters through constraint generation and show that earlier multiple-instance learning algorithms can be incorporated to improve their results. Evaluation on five standard datasets produces competitive performance. The contribution is therefore both a particular classifier and a framework for combining existing instance-level methods with information connecting bags.
summary.tldr: MI-CRF jointly classifies bags by combining instance classifiers with relationships between bags, achieving competitive multiple-instance learning results.

title: A Conditional Random Field for Multiple-Instance Learning

abstract: We propose Shotgun, a parallel coordinate descent algorithm for minimizing L1-regularized losses. Though coordinate descent seems inherently sequential, we prove convergence bounds for Shotgun which predict linear speedups, up to a problem-dependent limit. We present a comprehensive empirical study of Shotgun for Lasso and sparse logistic regression. Our theoretical predictions on the potential for parallelism closely match behavior on real data. Shotgun outperforms other published solvers on a range of large problems, proving to be one of the most scalable algorithms for L1.

Shotgun outperforms other published solvers on a range of large problems, proving to be one of the most scalable algorithms for L1.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent solves an optimization problem through updates to individual coordinates, an arrangement that can appear inherently sequential. This paper introduces Shotgun, a parallel version for losses with L1 regularization. It asks how much simultaneous updating can accelerate these problems while preserving a theoretical account of convergence.

The authors prove convergence bounds that predict linear speedups up to a limit determined by the particular problem. That limit is central to the result: the analysis supports useful parallelism without claiming that speed will continue increasing proportionally as more updates run at once. The theory provides a prediction of the available acceleration.

A comprehensive empirical study evaluates Shotgun on Lasso and sparse logistic regression. The predicted potential for parallelism closely matches observed behavior on real data, and Shotgun outperforms other published solvers on a range of large problems. These findings connect the convergence analysis to practical scalability and support Shotgun as an effective solver for the evaluated L1-regularized tasks.
summary.tldr: Shotgun parallelizes coordinate descent with convergence bounds predicting linear speedups up to a problem-dependent limit, supported by large-scale experiments.

title: Parallel Coordinate Descent for L1-Regularized Loss Minimization

abstract: Algorithms for learning distributions over weight-vectors, such as AROW were recently shown empirically to achieve state-of-the-art performance at various problems, with strong theoretical guaranties. Extending these algorithms to matrix models poses a challenge since the number of free parameters in the covariance of the distribution scales as n^4 with the dimension n of the matrix. We describe, analyze and experiment with two new algorithms for learning distribution of matrix models. Our first algorithm maintains a diagonal covariance over the parameters and is able to handle large covariance matrices. The second algorithm factores the covariance capturing some inter-features correlation while keeping the number of parameters linear in the size of the original matrix. We analyze the diagonal algorithm in the mistake bound model and show the superior precision of our approach over other algorithms in two tasks: retrieving similar images, and ranking similar documents. The second algorithms is shown to attain faster convergence rate.

paragraphs: Learning a distribution over model parameters allows a method to represent uncertainty about those parameters. Extending this idea from weight vectors to matrices creates a substantial storage problem: for a matrix with dimension n, a full covariance description requires a number of parameters proportional to n to the fourth power. This paper develops two ways to make such matrix models manageable.

The first algorithm keeps only a diagonal covariance, providing a simpler uncertainty representation that can handle large parameter collections. The second factors the covariance, retaining some correlations between features while keeping the parameter count linear in the size of the original matrix. These are different compromises between the richness of the uncertainty model and the cost of maintaining it.

The authors analyze the diagonal method through a mistake bound and evaluate their approach on similar-image retrieval and similar-document ranking. They report better precision than competing algorithms on these tasks. The factored algorithm is also shown to converge faster, supporting the usefulness of retaining some correlation information without constructing the full covariance.
summary.tldr: Two compact covariance representations make learning distributions over similarity matrices practical, with improved precision and faster convergence reported.

title: Adaptive Regularization for Similarity Measures

abstract: This paper investigates two feature-scoring criteria that make use of estimated class probabilities: one method proposed by shen and a complementary approach proposed below. We develop a theoretical framework to analyze each criterion and show that both estimate the spread (across all values of a given feature) of the probability that an example belongs to the positive class. Based on our analysis, we predict when each scoring technique will be advantageous over the other and give empirical results validating those predictions.
originalAbstract: This paper investigates two feature-scoring criteria that make use of estimated class probabilities: one method proposed by shen and a complementary approach proposed below. We develop a theoretical framework to analyze each criterion and show that both estimate the spread (across all values of a given feature) of the probability that an example belongs to the positive class. Based on our analysis, we predict when each scoring technique will be advantageous over the other and give empirical results validating those predictions.

paragraphs: Feature selection requires a way to judge which input variables are informative for prediction. This paper studies two scoring criteria that use estimated class probabilities: an existing method and a complementary method introduced by the authors. The focus is on understanding what these probability-based scores actually measure and when one is preferable.

The theoretical analysis shows that both criteria estimate the spread of the probability of belonging to the positive class across a feature's possible values. In plain language, they examine how much the estimated chance of a positive label changes as the feature changes. This gives the scores a shared interpretation while leaving room for differences in how effectively they capture that variation.

The authors use this framework to predict conditions under which each scoring method should have an advantage over the other. Empirical results validate those predictions. The contribution is therefore both a complementary feature score and an explanation of comparative behavior, providing a basis for choosing between the two criteria rather than treating either as universally superior.
summary.tldr: Two probability-based feature scores measure variation in positive-class probability, and theory predicts when each has an advantage.

title: Feature Selection via Probabilistic Outputs

abstract: Item neighbourhood methods for collaborative filtering learn a weighted graph over the set of items, where each item is connected to those it is most similar to. The prediction of a user's rating on an item is then given by that rating of neighbouring items, weighted by their similarity. This paper presents a new neighbourhood approach which we call item fields, whereby an undirected graphical model is formed over the item graph. The resulting prediction rule is a simple generalization of the classical approaches, which takes into account non-local information in the graph, allowing its best results to be obtained when using drastically fewer edges than other neighbourhood approaches. A fast approximate maximum entropy training method based on the Bethe approximation is presented which utilizes a novel decomposition into tractable sub-problems. When using precomputed sufficient statistics on the Movielens dataset, our method outperforms maximum likelihood approaches by two orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Item-neighbourhood recommendation methods predict a user's rating by combining that user's ratings of similar items. These similarities form a weighted graph: items are nodes, and connections indicate which items help predict one another. The paper turns this graph into an undirected probabilistic model called item fields.

Its prediction rule extends the usual neighbourhood calculation by incorporating information beyond immediate connections. This makes the graph useful as a connected system, rather than only as a collection of local weighted averages. The authors report that their approach achieves its best results with drastically fewer edges than other neighbourhood methods, suggesting that broader information can make a sparse graph effective.

The paper also develops an approximate maximum entropy training procedure using the Bethe approximation. A new decomposition breaks training into tractable subproblems. With sufficient statistics already computed on Movielens, the method reports a two-orders-of-magnitude advantage over maximum likelihood approaches in the training comparison. That qualification matters: the reported advantage is tied to the precomputed-statistics setting.
summary.tldr: Item fields extend neighbourhood recommendation with non-local graph information and an efficient approximate maximum entropy training method.

title: A Graphical Model Formulation of Collaborative Filtering Neighbourhood Methods with Fast Maximum Entropy Training

abstract: Modified policy iteration (MPI) is a dynamic programming (DP) algorithm that contains the two celebrated policy and value iteration methods. Despite its generality, MPI has not been thoroughly studied, especially its approximation form which is used when the state and/or action spaces are large or infinite. In this paper, we propose three approximate MPI (AMPI) algorithms that are extensions of the well-known approximate DP algorithms: fitted-value iteration, fitted-Q iteration, and classification-based policy iteration. We provide an error propagation analysis for AMPI that unifies those for approximate policy and value iteration. We also provide a finite-sample analysis for the classification-based implementation of AMPI (CBMPI), which is more general (and somehow contains) than the analysis of the other presented AMPI algorithms. An interesting observation is that the MPI's parameter allows us to control the balance of errors (in value function approximation and in estimating the greedy policy) in the final performance of the CBMPI algorithm.

paragraphs: Modified policy iteration is a dynamic programming framework that includes both policy iteration and value iteration. Its approximate versions matter when state or action spaces are too large, or infinite, for exact computation. This paper develops that approximate setting and examines how errors made during learning affect the resulting policy.

The authors introduce three algorithms extending fitted-value iteration, fitted-Q iteration, and classification-based policy iteration. They give a shared error propagation analysis that brings approximate policy iteration and approximate value iteration into the same framework. They also analyze the classification-based implementation with a finite amount of data, providing a treatment broader than the analyses of the other proposed implementations.

A central observation concerns the parameter in modified policy iteration. It controls the balance between errors in approximating values and errors in estimating the greedy policy, which chooses actions using those values. This makes the parameter relevant to final policy performance: it changes how the two kinds of approximation error contribute, rather than merely selecting between familiar algorithm names.
summary.tldr: Three approximate modified policy iteration algorithms share an analysis showing how a parameter balances value approximation and policy estimation errors.

title: Approximate Modified Policy Iteration
